darwin-orchids-contrivances-1877:
Charles Darwin published his book on orchids in 1877, in a revised edition of his 1862 work on how insects fertilise orchids. Darwin had spent years with live plants, watching bees and moths visit flowers. Orchids, with their odd shapes, were his test case for natural selection in flowers.

Flower by flower, Darwin showed how tubes, lids, and sticky pollen masses fit the bodies of visiting insects. Each odd structure, he argued, helped the plant set seed through insect help. No designer was needed, only slow change guided by what worked. The book is a patient, hands-on proof that small advantages, summed over ages, can build very strange beauty.
dryden-all-for-love-1677:
John Dryden wrote All for Love in 1677, retelling the story Shakespeare had told in Antony and Cleopatra. Dryden admired Shakespeare but wanted a tighter, more regular tragedy. He kept to the classical unities and wrote in blank verse rather than his usual rhymed couplets.

The play covers only the last days of Antony and Cleopatra in Alexandria. Antony must choose between his Roman duty and his love, while Cleopatra fights to keep him. Dryden strips away Shakespeare's sprawling scenes and focuses on the lovers' final choice. Many critics rank it as the finest heroic tragedy of the Restoration stage.
dunham-homoeopathy-science-of-therapeuti:
Carroll Dunham gathered his papers into Homoeopathy, the Science of Therapeutics in 1877, the year after his death. Dunham led the American school of homeopathy, and friends brought his scattered essays together in one volume. Each paper works to explain and show the law of similars, the rule that like cures like.

Dunham writes as both thinker and working doctor, moving from broad claims to cases at the bedside. He defends careful study of each drug's full effects before any use in illness. The book became the great statement of theory for American homeopaths, read long after the papers first appeared in journals.
edwards-thousand-miles-nile-1877:
Amelia Edwards sailed the Nile and wrote the book that changed her life in A Thousand Miles up the Nile, out in 1877. Edwards was a famed tale smith who went for a warm trip. Tombs, shrines, and digs in the sand seized her heart. She came home set to save them from harm and theft.

Her warm, bright prose made crowds in Britain care. Funds she raised soon backed true digs, Petrie midst them. The book is both a trek tale and a call to arms. It marks the start of a new age.
etienne-de-bourbon-anecdotes-historiques:
Etienne de Bourbon, a Dominican inquisitor in Languedoc, filled his preaching book with stories, legends, and apologies gathered in a life of hunting heresy. He died in 1261. A. Lecoy de la Marche edited the Anecdotes Historiques from his Latin treatise in 1877, and the text here is that French edition. It is an anecdotal archive of the Albigensian aftermath.

Etienne tells of Cathar believers, Waldensian preachers, false saints, and the strange cult of Saint Guinefort, a holy greyhound honored by peasants. He names towns, roads, and practices he saw himself. Preachers mined the book for sermon tales for centuries. For the daily texture of heresy and faith in the 1200s, few sources are richer.
europmc-pmc10134577:
Zhou and co-authors review exosomes from stem cells as a treatment to help wounds heal, in a 2023 paper. Wound healing moves through stages of clotting, inflammation, growth, and remodeling. Stem cells can aid that process, and much of their effect comes from tiny parcels they release, called exosomes.

The review explains how these parcels carry signals that calm inflammation and spur new tissue. It gathers lab and early clinical evidence across wound types. It also lists hurdles, such as making pure batches at scale, before such treatments reach routine care.
europmc-pmc10171177:
Rojas and a large team report a phase one trial of personalized RNA vaccines in pancreatic cancer, in a 2023 study. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, yet its tumors carry mutations that the immune system can learn to spot. The team built a custom vaccine for each patient from the mutations in that patient's own tumor.

After surgery, patients received the vaccine along with standard care. In many patients the vaccine roused strong T cell responses against their tumors. The results support wider trials of custom vaccines after surgery.
europmc-pmc10318377:
Crowley and a large team set out a 2023 plan to read the DNA of British land arthropods. Arthropods are animals with jointed legs, such as insects and spiders. The plan sits inside the Darwin Tree of Life project. That project aims to read the full DNA code of each species in Britain and Ireland.

Crowley covers four steps in the first phase of the work. The team checked which species appear on UK lists and picked which ones to sample first. Staff then had to collect each bug and keep its DNA in good shape. Set rules also guide how staff name, check, and store each specimen. The team shares lessons from the pilot phase and the Covid years.
europmc-pmc10517477:
Alowais and co-authors reviewed the role of AI in clinical practice in 2023. AI tools can learn patterns in large health data sets. Clinics hope they will sharpen care and lift quality of life. The team searched major data banks for past work on AI in health settings, with no date limits.

Their survey found gains in finding disease, picking treatments, and running lab tests. AI can beat human scores on some tasks and can cut costs, time, and errors. Alowais also lists wider uses: drug doses tuned to one patient, virtual health aides, and mental health support. Risks stand out too, from data privacy to bias. Human skill stays vital, the authors stress.
europmc-pmc10639077:
Müller-Dott and co-authors built a larger, signed map of gene control in 2023. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on or off. Each factor's target set is called its regulon. Software can guess a factor's activity from gene data, if the regulons are sound.

Their resource, CollecTRI, merges many sources into one set of factor-gene links. It covers 1,186 factors and marks each link as a boost or a brake. Müller-Dott tested it on lab data where factors were cut or spiked. The signed set beat past public sets at reading true activity shifts. Case work in three cancers showed how the maps expose which factors drive a tumour.
europmc-pmc10767877:
Agrawal and co-authors gave the 2024 update of WikiPathways, a free bank of biological pathway maps. A pathway map charts the steps of a cell process, from signal to response. The bank is built and kept by its user community, in an open science model. Growth of content and joint work headline this release.

The bank has been rebuilt at its core, Agrawal reports. That overhaul aims at stability for community curation in years ahead. The website was redesigned for a smoother user experience. New functions ease how users add and fix maps, with more steps run by automation. Past features all still work on the new base.
europmc-pmc10784577:
Tan and colleagues survey a cell-free option for healing in this 2024 review. Stem cells can help treat some diseases, but their use in surgery has real limits. Exosomes are tiny sacs that stem cells release, and they carry some of the same healing signals. Unlike live cells, these sacs do not trigger immune rejection and carry no risk of forming tumours.

Drawing on five years of studies, the review covers uses across many fields of surgery. These range from bone and brain surgery to heart, eye, and skin work. Exosomes from bone marrow, fat, nerve, and other stem cells each show promise for distinct problems. The authors urge surgeons, nano-scale drug experts, and stem cell scientists to work together on trials. They present the sacs as a safer path to the gains of stem cell care.
europmc-pmc11592877:
Mustafa and colleagues give a comprehensive overview of apoptosis in this 2024 review. Apoptosis is meticulously controlled programmed cell death. It facilitates embryonic development and maintains tissue balance and immune function. Two main routes trigger it. The extrinsic route starts when death ligands such as TNF-alpha and Fas bind receptors on the cell surface.

The intrinsic route raises the permeability of the mitochondrial outer membrane, releasing factors such as cytochrome c. A protein family called Bcl-2 regulates that gate. Both routes converge on caspases, enzymes that dismantle the cell, causing DNA fragmentation and orderly break-up. Dysregulation is implicated in cancer, autoimmune and cardiovascular diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders. The review details morphological changes, meaning the visible shape changes of dying cells. It closes with therapeutic implications of pushing or blocking the program.
europmc-pmc12021777:
Zafar and co-authors reviewed classic cancer treatments in 2025. Cancer is the second leading cause of death worldwide. Four long-used treatments anchor much of care. They are surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and hormonal therapy.

Surgery now gains from glowing dyes and robotic arms. Radiation has sharper focus and three-dimensional planning. Chemotherapy drugs have grown stronger and more targeted over time. Hormonal therapy curbs cancers that feed on hormones. Zafar also stresses the limits each method still faces. The review helps readers weigh gains against harms. It appeared in Discover Oncology in 2025.
europmc-pmc1224877:
Roberts surveyed salt-loving microbes and their inner chemistry in 2005. Microbes in salty places must fight drying pressure from outside. They stock small molecules inside to balance that pull. Many of those molecules are organic, not simple salts.

The stock can carry charge, no charge, or pair with potassium ions. Roberts reviews what kinds exist and how cells make them. These solutes also protect proteins and keep them stable. Cells can raise or lower levels fast when salt shifts. The survey links survival tricks to basic cell physics. It appeared in the journal Saline Systems.
europmc-pmc1247377:
Oberdörster tested manufactured carbon nanoparticles in young largemouth bass in 2004. Fullerenes, or C60, are ball-shaped carbon particles made by the ton. They slip into fatty cell membranes and react chemically. Spills could expose wildlife through water.

Fish exposed to suspended fullerene particles showed brain damage markers. Lipid peroxidation, a sign of oxidative attack on fats, rose significantly. The study also tracked protein damage and a key antioxidant, glutathione. Oberdörster gives early proof that engineered nanoparticles can stress fish brains. Safety checks should precede wide release of such materials.
europmc-pmc1431577:
Do young children and adults share one brain system for number? Cantlon and co-authors scanned brains in 2006 to find out. Adults and four-year-olds watched sets of dots while a scanner tracked blood flow. Most sets kept the same count, then a new count or a new shape broke the pattern.

In adults, a groove in the parietal lobe, a top rear brain area, reacted more to count changes than to shape changes. That same area handles number symbols like written digits. The child scans tested whether the response exists early in life. Cantlon argues the work links a basic feel for amount to later school math skills.
europmc-pmc1829477:
Eden, Yakhini and colleagues tackled in 2007 a flaw in how researchers hunt for short DNA patterns that proteins bind. Such motifs are usually found by splitting sequences into a target set and a background set, an arbitrary cut. Older tools also lacked exact significance values and could report motifs even in random data.

Their method, called DRIM, works directly on ranked lists of sequences instead of split sets. It supplies a rigorous model, an exact p-value for enrichment, and a way to handle motifs that appear many times. On yeast data from protein-DNA binding chips, DRIM found 50 new candidate transcription factor binding sites. Some were followed up for biological function. The framework was also applied to DNA methylation data, showing its wider reach.
europmc-pmc1945077:
Osborne, Fraser and co-authors watched in 2007 as an activated gene physically moves to a shared workbench inside the nucleus. Mammalian genes are read in transcription factories, nuclear spots rich in the copying enzyme RNA polymerase II. Different genes can share one factory, implying genes travel to preassembled sites.

In mouse B lymphocytes, switching on immediate early genes triggered rapid relocation to factories. The cancer-linked gene Myc, on chromosome 15, was preferentially recruited to the very factory occupied by Igh, a heavily read antibody gene on chromosome 12. Myc and Igh are also the most frequent swap partners in two blood cancers, plasmacytoma and Burkitt lymphoma. The authors propose that sharing a factory explains why certain chromosome swaps recur: partners that work side by side can be wrongly joined.
europmc-pmc2000477:
Dietrich and co-authors showed in 2006 that common chemotherapy drugs can harm brain precursor cells. Cancer patients often report memory problems and white matter damage after treatment. The cell basis for those effects was poorly understood. The team tested carmustine, cisplatin and cytarabine at doses used in patients. They compared brain cells with several cancer cell lines.

All three drugs killed central nervous system progenitor cells more readily than cancer cells. Non-dividing oligodendrocytes, cells that coat nerve fibres, were also highly sensitive. In mice, systemic treatment raised cell death and cut cell division in three brain regions. Some effects lasted for weeks after dosing ended. Lab tests predicted the animal results closely, offering a fast screen for safer therapies.

europmc-pmc2147077:
Velasco and a very large team produced a draft genome sequence in 2007 for the Pinot Noir grapevine. Grapes have a huge global market, and the cultivated species Vitis vinifera could model fruit tree genetics. Its high heterozygosity, meaning its two chromosome copies differ greatly, challenges standard sequencing. The team combined classic Sanger sequencing with newer synthesis methods and custom assembly programs to build a consensus sequence.

They estimate the genome at 504.6 million bases, with 477.1 million assembled and most anchored to the 19 chromosome groups. They predict 29,585 genes, and 96.1 percent were placed on chromosomes, giving breeders a dense map for selection work in vineyards and for tracing trait genes across this variety. About two million single-letter variants were found. Homologous chromosomes differ across 11.2 percent of their DNA. The team also dated a large duplication event specific to grape.
europmc-pmc2248177:
Howe, Hargreaves and Huttly examined wealth indices in 2008, a common tool for measuring socio-economic position in low-income countries. Such studies often lack income data, so researchers score households by assets owned, using principal components analysis to weight the items. Critics worry the method obscures meaning and mishandles yes-or-no data. Using Malawi household survey data from 2004 and 2005, the team built indices five different ways.

All indices agreed only modestly with per-capita consumption expenditure, the conventional comparison measure. Indices built from data coded the same way agreed strongly with each other. Agreement fell when coding differed. The choice of which assets to include mattered more than the weighting method used. Adjusting consumption for household size did not change the picture. The authors question wealth indices as proxies for spending.
europmc-pmc2292177:
Ishihama and co-workers profiled protein abundances in the Escherichia coli cytosol in 2008, the fluid interior of this model bacterium. Quantitative models of cell behaviour need to know how much of each protein exists, but mass spectrometry coverage was limited. Combining several fractionation and LC-MS/MS strategies, the team identified proteins and estimated each one's abundance from how many of its peptides were sequenced.

They identified 1,103 cytosolic proteins, the most complete bacterial abundance map then available. Abundance estimates matched independently measured copy numbers per cell. Ribosomal and other protein-synthesis proteins were most abundant, followed by energy metabolism and binding proteins. Proteins for transcription, transport and cell organisation were rare. Abundant proteins tended to be essential, shorter, and resistant to aggregation. Protein and messenger RNA levels correlated significantly. The dataset links a protein's amount to its function and properties.
europmc-pmc2359677:
Wu and colleagues reviewed soy foods and breast cancer risk in 2008. Soy contains isoflavones, plant compounds that act weakly like the hormone estrogen. Because estrogen itself can drive breast cancer, researchers had long debated whether soy protects or harms.

The authors focused on studies that measured soy intake well and adjusted for other risk factors. In eight studies of Asian women, who eat much soy, risk fell steadily as intake rose. Women eating the most soy, at least 20 milligrams of isoflavones a day, had an odds ratio of 0.71, and mid-level intake sat between that and the low group. In eleven Western studies, intake was far lower and no link appeared. They concluded Asian-level soy intake may protect against breast cancer.
europmc-pmc2361377:
Hwang and Mendell reviewed microRNAs in cancer in 2006. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces, about 18 to 24 letters long, that dial down the output of target genes. All complex animals use them to control basic cell jobs such as growth, maturation, and death.

The authors explained that faulty microRNA levels are a common feature of human cancers. Some microRNAs act like oncogenes, pushing cells to grow when present in excess. Others act as tumor suppressors, and losing them removes a brake on growth. Over 300 microRNAs were then known in humans, with estimates of up to 1,000 genes for them. As a group they were thought to regulate about 30% of human genes, which makes their failure in cancer a wide-reaching problem.
europmc-pmc2516577:
Wolff and colleagues measured chemical exposures during pregnancy and compared them with newborn size in this 2008 study. Phthalates and phenols are hormonally active chemicals found in plastics and personal care products. The team collected urine from 404 women in New York City during the last third of pregnancy and recorded each baby's birth measures.

Most of the 15 chemicals tested were found at clear levels in the women's urine. A few links with birth size stood out. Higher levels of one phenol, 2,5-dichlorophenol, predicted about 210 grams lower birth weight in boys. Another, benzophenone-3, was tied to lower weight in girls but higher weight in boys. Most chemicals showed no association with birth size.
europmc-pmc2573877:
Searle, Mitnitski, Gahbauer, Gill, and Rockwood set out a standard recipe in 2008 for building a frailty index, a score of how many health deficits an older person has accumulated. Such indices predict death and decline, but each research group built its own. The authors demonstrated their procedure on the Yale Precipitating Events Project, a cohort of 754 non-disabled people aged 70 and over around New Haven.

They selected 40 deficits covering function, thinking, disease, and physical performance, and recoded each onto a zero-to-one scale. The index values followed a smooth distribution, rose with age, and levelled near 0.6 to 0.7 even in the frailest. Together with age and sex, the index significantly predicted mortality. The authors offer the procedure so studies can be compared directly.
europmc-pmc2606177: A medical paper with studies upon Asiatic cholera. The great cholera. This article preserves that tropical medicine. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2654877:
Desailloud and Hober reviewed in 2009 whether viruses help cause thyroiditis, inflammation of the thyroid gland in the neck. Viruses are often blamed as the outside trigger for these diseases, which include a painful short-lived form and two slow autoimmune forms, Graves' disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

The authors sorted the proof by strength. Counts of past infections in patients hint at links but cannot prove cause. Stronger proof comes from finding virus parts inside thyroid tissue itself. Such direct traces exist for mumps and several retroviruses in the short-lived form. Lists for the two slow forms include HTLV-1, rubella, herpes viruses, and parvovirus, among others. Even then, the authors caution, a virus found in the gland may be an innocent bystander, not the culprit. More work is needed before prevention or treatment can build on these links.
europmc-pmc2714977:
Dostert and co-authors showed in 2009 that hemozoin, a crystal made by malaria parasites, triggers a strong immune alarm in the body. Parasites make the crystal to detoxify heme, a toxic part left when they digest hemoglobin in red blood cells. Fever and brain damage in malaria resemble signs seen when the Nalp3 inflammasome, an immune alarm complex, is overactive.

Hemozoin switched on that complex and released interleukin-1 beta, a potent fever signal, in lab tests. Blocking cell eating, potassium flow, or a key enzyme stopped the effect. Mice lacking the alarm parts had milder belly swelling after injection and milder brain malaria, though parasite counts stayed the same.
europmc-pmc2725977:
Tristan and co-authors tracked in 2007 the global spread of Panton-Valentine leukocidin-positive MRSA, community strains of a drug-resistant bacterium that infect healthy young people outside hospitals. Many such strains carry a toxin gene and a compact resistance cassette. In 2003 the main clones looked continent-specific, each region holding its own type.

Typing four hundred sixty-nine isolates from seventeen countries collected since 1999, they found some formerly local clones had now spread around the world. The European clone and the main United States clone were detected well beyond their home regions, and Asian-Pacific clones appeared in travel hubs. Community MRSA can no longer be read as a purely local problem.
europmc-pmc2768977:
Stabler and co-authors compared in 2009 the genomes and traits of epidemic and non-epidemic Clostridium difficile strains to explain how a hypervirulent form emerged. This spore-forming gut bacterium is the most frequent cause of hospital diarrhea worldwide. Its ribotype 027 strains had lately driven outbreaks with worse illness, higher deaths, and more relapses across North America and Europe.

Genome comparison revealed gene gains in the epidemic strains that could account for their success. The changes fit a picture of a lineage that picked up new tools for survival and spread in hospitals. Phenotype tests backed the genomic contrasts between old and new strains. Their results trace how a once-rare strain became a dominant hospital threat within a few years, and flag the gained genes as clues to its edge.
europmc-pmc2885077:
Aam and colleagues reviewed in 2010 how to make chitooligosaccharides, short chains built from the sugars in crab-shell chitin, and what medicine might do with them. The chains are cut from chitin or its treated form chitosan by enzymes, chemicals, or both. Their catch is purity: most studies used ragged mixtures of chain lengths and patterns, so effects cannot be pinned to a defined molecule.

The review sets out methods to produce and verify cleaner fractions with known length and chemistry. With defined material, reported effects can finally be tested properly, including slowing tumor growth, calming asthma-type airway inflammation, and strengthening bone. Other candidate uses range from gene delivery and wound dressings to fighting bacteria, fungi, and malaria parasites.
europmc-pmc2896477:
Giorgio and co-authors scanned in 2010 sixty-six adults aged twenty-three to eighty-one to chart how gray and white matter age differently. Gray matter holds nerve cell bodies, while white matter carries the insulated wiring between them. Earlier studies usually measured one property at a time, which produced a mixed picture of when decline begins in each tissue.

Gray matter volume held fairly steady into middle age and then shrank widely, though frontal cortex, the region behind the forehead, began earlier. White matter wiring quality, measured by how water diffuses along fibers, deteriorated from young adulthood onward across much of the brain. That wiring measure detected aging earlier and more sensitively than white matter volume did, suggesting insulation frays long before bulk is lost.
europmc-pmc3102077:
Shaye and Greenwald built in 2011 OrthoList, a vetted list of worm genes that have counterparts in humans, to make the tiny worm C. elegans a sharper tool for human biology. The worm is a favorite for gene knockdown screens, but screening its whole genome wastes effort on worm only genes. They merged the verdicts of four ortholog prediction programs and checked the union carefully.

The final list holds more than seven thousand six hundred worm genes with likely human matches, with strong coverage and low error in their tests. Two published genome wide screens suggest nearly every conserved hit would have been found by screening only this list, cutting the work by about three fifths. The list is sorted by protein family and function, so finding the worm version of a human disease gene takes minutes. The authors also refreshed counts of conserved signaling parts along the way.
europmc-pmc3111477:
Anatole Ghazalpour and colleagues published a 2011 mouse genetics study in PLoS Genetics asking how closely gene activity predicts protein levels. Earlier work in plants and yeast had found only a modest match. The team measured both layers in liver tissue from nearly a hundred mouse strains, using natural genetic differences as the test.

Thousands of gene messages and hundreds of proteins were measured reliably. Levels matched well for only about half of the genes, and the match varied with where a protein works and what it does. Places in the genome controlling message levels barely overlapped with those controlling protein levels. Surprisingly, message levels tracked body traits such as fatness more strongly than protein levels did, a caution for studies that read only one layer.
europmc-pmc3146877:
Claire Eades, Jill Ferguson, and Ronan O'Carroll reviewed attitudes toward public health work in community pharmacies in a 2011 paper in BMC Public Health. Pharmacists are being asked to add health promotion to their medicine roles, which demands change from staff and customers alike. The team gathered studies published over a decade, ending with more than sixty.

Most pharmacists rated public health work important but secondary, and their confidence in delivering it was middling at best. Lack of time was the barrier named again and again, alongside missing private space and fear of customer pushback. Most customers had never been offered such services and did not expect them, though those who had tried them reported high satisfaction. The authors call for training that builds confidence and more proactive offers.
europmc-pmc3207877:
Matteo Fumagalli and colleagues asked what force has shaped human genetic variation most strongly, in this 2011 study in PLoS Genetics. They matched allele frequencies from fifty-five human populations against local environmental factors, including climate, diet, and pathogen loads. The aim was to see which pressure left the clearest signature of local adaptation in the genome.

After correcting for population history, the diversity of local pathogens emerged as the dominant driver, ahead of climate and diet. About one hundred genes tracked the pathogen environment unusually closely. Strikingly, those genes were enriched for links to autoimmune illness. Celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, and multiple sclerosis were among them. The authors suggest some disease-risk variants may persist because they once helped fight infection.
europmc-pmc3248377:
Andrew Manning and Meta Kuehn showed that the bubbles bacteria shed from their outer membrane act as decoys in self-defense, in this 2011 paper in BMC Microbiology. Gram-negative bacteria constantly release these vesicles, which had been assigned roles in virulence and stress responses. The team tested whether vesicles also give immediate protection against attackers aimed at the membrane.

A mutant Escherichia coli that sheds extra vesicles survived treatment with antimicrobial peptides better than normal bacteria. Adding purified vesicles to normal cultures protected them too. The peptides themselves triggered more shedding. The same protection appeared in a disease-causing E. coli strain, though heavy vesicle doses blocked the bacteria from gaining lasting resistance. Vesicles also bound a bacterial virus quickly and for good, cutting its power to infect. The authors conclude the shed membrane soaks up threats.
europmc-pmc3260177:
Anna Falk and colleagues captured a renewable stem cell type for making human neurons in the dish, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Human embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells promise tools for studying brain development and modeling neurological disease, but comparative studies need standardized, reliable supplies of neural cells. The team derived long-term self-renewing neuroepithelial-like stem cells from several stem cell lines.

Produced independently in two laboratories, these cells showed consistent behavior. They expand nonstop with two growth factors. They keep a stable ability to become neurons or glia. They carry a characteristic set of active transcription factors. And they start with a hindbrain identity that can be steered to other regions. They mature into working neurons and differ developmentally from fetal-derived stem cells. The authors propose them as a standard system for comparing healthy and diseased lines.
europmc-pmc3280977:
Andrzej Pawlowski and colleagues reviewed the deadly partnership between tuberculosis and HIV in this 2012 primer in PLoS Pathogens. Each disease worsens the other. HIV is the strongest known risk factor for tuberculosis. It multiplies the chance that a latent infection reactivates many times over. Tuberculosis, in turn, is the commonest cause of AIDS-related death. Together they strain health systems and complicate diagnosis and treatment.

The review explains how the two pathogens act in synergy, each accelerating the collapse of immune defenses, and gathers what is known about the immunological events behind that breakdown. It also surveys animal models for studying the interaction, since much of the mechanism remains unclear. The authors close by naming the gaps in knowledge and the research needed to build preventive measures against the combined epidemic.
europmc-pmc3320277:
Tiemersma and colleagues, working with a European surveillance network, charted drug resistant staph infections across Europe from 1999 to 2002, reporting in 2004. The germ Staphylococcus aureus causes many hospital infections, and strains that shrug off the antibiotic methicillin leave doctors with few options. The network collects standardized blood test results from hundreds of laboratories in dozens of countries.

Resistant strains made up wildly different shares of staph blood infections from country to country. Some nations saw barely any, while others faced very high rates, and shares also varied sharply between hospitals in the same country. The report tracks how these patterns shifted over the four years within individual countries. The authors argue that steady, comparable surveillance is essential for targeting infection control and antibiotic policy.
europmc-pmc3346977:
Alander and colleagues reviewed a glowing dye technique that helps surgeons see hidden structures during operations, in a 2012 article. The dye, indocyanine green, shines under near infrared light when lit by special cameras, revealing blood flow and tissue borders in real time. It has a long safety record from eye and liver testing.

The review explains the physics of the dye and the cameras used, then walks through more than two hundred clinical reports. Surgeons use the glow to check blood supply in reconstructed tissue, find the first lymph node a tumor drains to, trace bile ducts, and spot tumors during removal. The authors also note newer uses beyond the operating room. They present the technique as a cheap, low risk aid that is steadily entering routine surgical practice.
europmc-pmc3348477:
Salminen, Kaarniranta, and Kauppinen linked the slow burn inflammation of aging to a breakdown in cellular housekeeping, in a 2012 article. Aging mammals drift into a mild, chronic inflammatory state the authors call inflammaging. At the same time, the cleanup system called autophagy weakens, letting damaged power plants of the cell, the mitochondria, pile up and leak reactive oxygen chemicals.

Those leaks can trip internal alarm platforms known as inflammasomes, especially one called NLRP3. Once tripped, it activates enzymes that release two potent inflammatory messengers, which in turn suppress autophagy further, locking in a vicious circle. The same platform is overactive in age linked diseases such as clogged arteries, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. The authors frame protecting autophagy as a promising way to cool inflammaging at its source.
europmc-pmc3355077:
Pradeepa and colleagues studied how a chromatin-reading protein links the chemical marks on DNA packaging to the splicing of messenger RNA. The protein Psip1, in its short p52 form, carries a domain that recognises a particular methylated histone mark found on active genes.

The team showed that p52 binds trimethylated histone H3 at lysine 36 and associates with splicing factors including Srsf1. In cells lacking Psip1, Srsf1 levels at that histone mark fell and the alternative splicing of specific genes changed, with altered factor distribution around the affected exons. The authors propose that p52 helps couple chromatin state to splicing choices.
europmc-pmc3364277:
Bouchard and a large group of collaborators asked an uncomfortable question about exercise: can regular training actually worsen some people's cardiovascular and diabetes risk factors? They pooled completers from six exercise studies, 1,687 men and women in total. An adverse response meant a change large enough to exceed measurement error in the harmful direction.

Adverse responses were far from rare. Depending on the risk factor, roughly one in twelve to one in eight participants got worse. The factors were blood pressure, fasting insulin, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol. About seven percent worsened on two or more factors. The authors argue for identifying who is susceptible, as a foundation for personalised exercise prescription.

The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc8307577: A fresh look at SARS-CoV-2 spike mutations, L452R, T478K, E484Q and P681R, in the second wave of COVID-19 in Maharashtra, India arrived with this 2021 research paper. As the global severe acute breathing syndrome coronavirus 2 pandemic expands, genomic epidemiology (how diseases spread in populations) and whole. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8403677: Yu and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on wnt/β-catenin signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) in cancers and aimed therapies. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc8440177: This 2021 research paper covers immunogenicity and reactogenicity of heterologous ChAdOx1 nCoV-19/mRNA vaccination (preventive shots). Heterologous priming with the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vector vaccine followed by boosting with a messenger RNA vaccine is currently recommended. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8480977: Barton and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on the effects of common mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD and its ligand, the human ACE2 receptor (docking point on a cell). The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8488577: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on autophagy (cell self-cleanup) in major human diseases. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8611377: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on the effect of natural mutations of SARS-CoV-2 on spike structure, conformation, and antigenicity. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8624977: This 2021 research paper covers obesity and cardiometabolic risk factors: from childhood to adulthood. Obesity has become a major epidemic (outbreak) in the 21st century. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment. The full text sits with this description in the library.
europmc-pmc8828877: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at single-cell (one cell at a time) analysis of human glioma and immune cells identifies S100A4. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc8941077: Doctors and scientists took on antibody (defense protein) drug conjugate: the "biological (from living things) missile" for aimed cancer therapy in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9044977: A fresh look at exposure to per and polyfluoroalkyl substances and markers of liver injury: a systematic review (a review of every study) arrived with this 2022 research paper. Experimental evidence indicates that exposure to certain pollutants is linked to liver damage. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc9046077: Douaud and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on SARS-CoV-2 is linked to changes in brain structure in UK biobank. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9164677: A fresh look at community spread of monkeypox in the united kingdom, April to May 2022 arrived with this 2022 research paper. Between 7 and 25 May, 86 monkeypox cases were confirmed in the united kingdom. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9188077: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on intermittent theta-burst stimulation improves motor function by inhibiting neuronal pyroptosis (a fiery form of cell death) and regulating microglial polarization. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9330677: A fresh look at clinical (in patients) application (use) of stem cell in regenerative medicine: a narrative review arrived with this 2022 review paper. The multipotency property of stem cells has attained worldwide consideration because of their immense for immunomodulation and their treatment function. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc9349777: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on evolution (gradual change) of the SARS-CoV-2 omicron variants ba-1 to ba-5: implications (what the findings mean) for immune escape and spread. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9832677: Zhao and co-authors published this review paper in 2023 on insulin resistance (cells ignoring insulin) in polycystic ovary syndrome across various tissues: an updated review of pathogenesis (how the disease develops), testing. The authors pull together the key findings from across the field. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9942077: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on lung cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system): progress, pitfalls, and promises. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
flaubert-simple-soul-1877:
Flaubert opens A Simple Soul in the town of Pont-l'Eveque in Normandy. For half a century, he writes, local housewives envied Madame Aubain her servant Felicite. For a hundred francs a year, Felicite cooked, cleaned, washed, ironed, and mended for her mistress.

Madame Aubain, widowed in 1809 with two children and many debts, was not an easy woman. Felicite stayed loyal all the same, through a plain and narrowing life. She pours her pure love on a nephew, an old man, and at last on Loulou, her parrot. Flaubert finds the sublime in that humble heart, with tenderness and quiet irony.
flaubert-three-short-works-1877:
Three short works share this Flaubert volume, and their span may surprise readers. The Dance of Death, a prose poem of 1838, comes first. The Legend of Saint-Julian the Hospitaller and A Simple Soul follow it.

In the opening piece Death speaks at night among cold tombs in winter. Death claims to have reaped countless generations with a scythe, like a nurse of earth itself. Saint Julian retells a medieval tale of sin and pardon in rich style. A Simple Soul then finds grandeur in a poor servant's plain life, and many call the late tales the finest short fiction in French.
freeman-ottoman-power-europe-1877:
Edward Freeman wrote The Ottoman Power in Europe in 1877, amid the Eastern Crisis. His history of Turkish rule in the Balkans doubles as a polemic. He argues that Ottoman power in Europe is alien and doomed to fall.

Atrocity reports and great-power rivalry heat his pages throughout. Freeman the liberal pleads the cause of the Balkan Christians with passion. Modern readers will find his views partisan and dated in places. Yet the book vividly shows Victorian opinion on the Eastern Question, and its learning on Balkan history still gives it weight beyond its moment of crisis.
frus-1861-d177:
On 20 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Carl Schurz for the second time in five days. The letter is document 177 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Madrid letters in five days show a post kept on a short rein. Schurz was able but new, and Seward guided him closely. The August notes form a small course in the Secretary's method: short, clear, and tied to one aim. A short rein in August gave Schurz room to grow without room to stray. Room to grow, on a short rein, is a fair sum of Seward's way with new men.
frus-1861-d277:
Seward heard from Mr. Angel on 4 June 1861, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 277 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the opening months of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d77:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 September 1861. It is document 77 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams and Seward again wrote on the same day, in ignorance of each other. Adams's page reports London as it stood in early autumn. His care with tone and fact made his reports the base on which Lincoln's cabinet judged British intent. His reports were later prized by scholars for their cool, exact prose. Cool, exact prose made his reports the base line for judging all other news.
frus-1862-d177:
Writing on 28 October 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report that appears as Document 177 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams spoke for the United States in London as its minister.

Reports written just before a mail steamer sailed tended to sum up the week, and this one closed October at the legation. The questions hanging over it were large: would Britain join France in pressing a truce, and would warships built in British yards reach the South? Adams's mail kept those questions in front of Washington. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d277:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton on 10 May 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 277 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter went by steamer to the Paris legation.

Mid-May 1862 found McClellan's army within sight of Richmond's church spires. Or so the phrase went, and Europe wondered if the war might end by summer. Seward's mail fed that hope where it helped and damped it where it hurt. Letters like this one were instruments of mood as much as of business, and Dayton knew how to use them. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d377:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Viscount Treilhard, in a letter printed as Document 377 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter came five days after the Bull Run defeat.

Early September found Lee's army crossing into Maryland and the capital recovering its nerve. Seward's correspondence in that week, across all channels, worked to project calm resolve. His letter to Treilhard is part of that effort, filed just before Antietam gave Washington a stronger story to tell Europe. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks. French citizens and ships caught by the war gave the legation a steady stream of case work.
frus-1862-d477:
James E. Harvey, the American minister in Lisbon, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 June 1862. It is Document 477 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the first Portuguese report in the file.

Harvey reported from a capital whose importance lay in its ports and islands rather than its armies. Portugal watched the war with care, trading with America and ruling Atlantic stations where belligerent ships might seek coal or shelter. His reports told Washington how Lisbon meant to apply the rules of neutrality. For the reader, the Portuguese file opens a side door on the war: the legal, port-by-port struggle that ran beneath the famous battles.
frus-1862-d577:
James Watson Webb sent this report from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 July 1862, though the printed file places it after later papers. It is Document 577 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The Brazilian file's loose order reflects the mails: letters from Rio arrived in batches, months apart, and were printed as the office gathered them. Webb's July report covered the imperial court's view of the war and the practical questions of ports and shipping that Brazil's long coast raised. For Washington, his letters fixed the southern reference point of its wartime map. Read by date, the file shows a correspondence conducted in slow motion, each side answering a world already changed.
frus-1862-d677:
On 29 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Anson Burlingame, the American minister to China. The letter is document 677 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It closes the spring set of orders in the China file.

Seward wrote knowing his words would not be read for months. That lag shaped the tone of all his far-off mail: clear aims, room for the envoy to judge, and news of home. This letter went out as the war at home turned grim. It is a fair sample of how the State Department kept faith with its distant posts when it could send them little else.
frus-1862-d77:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 7 June 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 77 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d177:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 April 1863. It is document 177 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d277:
The mail from London dated 3 September 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 277 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d377: On 29 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 377 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d477:
Among the day's business on 24 April 1863 was a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d577:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 24 June 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d677:
Dated 28 November 1863, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward went across the Atlantic to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams served as the United States minister to Britain. The letter is printed as document 677 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume.

Mail between Washington and London took days by ship, so each dispatch had to stand on its own. Seward used these letters to share news, set policy, and tell Adams what to say to British leaders. For a reader today, the value is the direct view. There is no retelling here, just the government's own words as they were sent during the war.
frus-1863p1-d77:
On 12 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 77 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet often held what would not fit the first: a talk recalled, a press cut, a name to note. Adams's pair of 12 February is of that kind. This letter is its second half. Set in the run, it shows how the London post turned a mass of news into clean, filed reports. A busy secretary could use them at once.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d177: Stettinius wrote to President Roosevelt on October 30, 1943, from his post as Acting Secretary of State. The letter is Document 177 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, in the Moscow section. While Hull closed the conference abroad, Stettinius closed the home end of the work, and this letter belongs to that handover day. The record names the two men and the date. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d277:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 26 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, open with Southeast Asia business. The chiefs approve amendments to paper C.C.S. 411 and order the revised plan sent to Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek through Lord Mountbatten without delay.

Reports from commanders follow, and General Eisenhower speaks first. He calls a single command for the Mediterranean absolutely essential, since air and naval commands already work that way. On the war there, he backs Italy as the main effort under a full push, with the Po valley as the goal and landing craft as his chief need. Under a limited push, he warns, only the line north of Rome could be held, on a strategic defensive with strong local attacks.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d377:
Harry Hopkins' handwritten notes, dated 1 December 1943 at one in the afternoon, jot the heads of a report by Foreign Secretary Eden from the foreign ministers' committee at Tehran. The notes break off in the middle of a page and appear incomplete, and no other Hopkins notes of the meeting have been found.

The surviving lines concern Turkey. Turkey should be asked to come into the war, and her president invited to Cairo to meet the President of the United States and the Prime Minister. Eden asked Marshal Stalin whether the Soviet government wished to send a representative to that meeting, and Stalin answered that he would send one. A proposed telegram to President Inönü was presented and discussed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d477:
The catalog heading misspells the form as “Memorandwn,” but the text is a memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff dated December 4, 1943. That was the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference. The State Department printed the paper in its Cairo-Tehran volume, among the records of the chiefs' sessions.

American position papers like this one gave the joint meetings their agenda and their friction. The United States chiefs used written memoranda to press their views on the combined body before decisions were entered in the minutes. A reader following the Cairo debate over strategy in Europe and Asia will find this paper part of the paper trail.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d77: Roosevelt answered Churchill on October 30, 1943, in a letter that is Document 77 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The exchange that day closed the Moscow chapter and opened the final planning for Cairo and Tehran, then four weeks off. The record states the parties and the date only. Readers can find the letter in the Foreign Relations volume, where the November papers begin soon after.
frus-1944-quebec-d177:
The McFarland minutes record the plenary session of September 13, 1944, where Churchill, at Roosevelt's request, opened the discussion. Since Sextant, he said, everything the United Nations had touched had turned to gold, with seven weeks of unbroken success. He congratulated the Americans on Dragoon, praised the integrated staff machine in France, and stressed that the British Empire's effort had reached its peak.

Churchill then pressed his Italian design. No forces should be withdrawn until Kesselring was beaten or on the run. Afterward the armies must not sit idle: he wanted a right-handed movement through Istria and Trieste toward Vienna, partly to reach it before the Russians. He also reviewed Burma's bitter campaign, where sickness had cost 288,000 men, and introduced Plan Dracula against Rangoon.
frus-1944-quebec-d277:
Two draft messages to Chiang Kai-shek, a long and a short version, were circulated on September 15, 1944, as C.C.S. 681/1. The longer draft, sent in Roosevelt's and Churchill's names, reports the Quebec decisions. Its delivery was tightly controlled: through General Stilwell and the two ambassadors in Chungking, closely paraphrased before presentation.

The message pledges all available resources toward the earliest practicable invasion of the Japanese homeland, with vigorous redeployment after Germany's defeat. For Southeast Asia, it promises continued operations under Mountbatten to secure the Myitkyina air bases and open overland communications between India and China. British forces would advance from Imphal toward Mandalay, Chinese and allied forces from Myitkyina, and Chiang's Salween armies toward Lashio, all under preponderant air strength.
frus-1944-quebec-d77:
Treasury Department officials prepared a memorandum dated September 1, 1944. The paper entered the files gathered for the Quebec Conference. The State Department later printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. Treasury handled war finance and aid to the allies.

Financial questions ran through the Quebec agenda that September. Britain depended on American aid to keep fighting. Germany's future also raised money and trade questions. A Treasury paper gave officials shared facts before the talks. For readers, the memorandum shows finance staff shaping summit choices. Their work stood behind decisions the leaders announced later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d177:
A memorandum dated 21 November 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Commanding General of the Manhattan Engineer District, Department of War (Groves). The reader was the Atomic Energy Commission. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 177 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The sender ran the wartime atomic bomb program, and the new Atomic Energy Commission was about to take charge of atomic work from the Army.
frus-1945-50-intel-d277:
On 20 May 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 11th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. It is document 277 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

After key talks, an aide would write up what was said for the file. The result is close to the room itself. Later memos cite such notes the way lawyers cite a witness: as the best proof of words once spoken. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d377:
A memorandum dated 24 March 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was the Assistant Secretary of State for Occupied Areas (Saltzman). It survives in print as document 377 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d77:
Secretary Byrnes wrote to McCormack on 23 October 1945. The secretary of state addressing his intelligence chief in person gave the young office a mark of standing. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

McCormack's interim service held the old OSS analysts, whose reports the secretary read with profit. Byrnes's letter shows the chief receiving direction from the very top of his department. Readers should weigh what that meant in the autumn contest. While the central fight ran on, the State office was quietly proving its worth to its own secretary. Its later eclipse makes these early marks of favor poignant reading.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d177:
London set a deadline for King Peter, and asked Washington's view of its next step. The Secretary of State's note to Ambassador Halifax of 23 January 1945 answers the British Embassy's inquiry of the day before. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Britain had asked what the United States thought of the course London proposed if the King failed to accept the Tito–Subasic agreement by midday. Stettinius points to the lines already sent to Ambassador Patterson on 17 January. Some points in the King's reservations, Washington holds, can be judged fairly only once the government is back in Yugoslavia. Friendly missions should also be set up in Belgrade at an early date. On the goal of a government returning home to work as one, the two capitals agree.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d277:
Hold your hand, Grew told the American officers drafting a prisoners agreement at SHAEF. His urgent cable of 27 January 1945 went to the embassy in London, for Murphy, and was repeated to Moscow. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The Foreign Office had shared its cables on the proposed Soviet agreements covering freed prisoners and civilians. One British message shows SHAEF at work on a joint British-American text for the Big Three meeting. That text, Grew warns, stands at considerable variance with what the State, Army, and Navy committee is proposing to the Joint Chiefs. The American men at SHAEF must make no commitments until further instructions arrive, which Washington hopes to send through the Joint Chiefs on 29 January.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d377:
Roosevelt's letter to Stalin of February 6, 1945, is among the most direct he wrote at Yalta. He says he has thought hard about their afternoon meeting. On the Polish government, he is greatly disturbed. The three great powers have no meeting of minds about Poland's political setup, and the world can see it.

Moscow recognizes one Polish government; Washington and London recognize another, in London. Roosevelt insists the split must not continue. People would think a breach had opened between the allies, which is not the case. He is determined, he writes, that there shall be no breach. Surely, he pleads, their differences can be reconciled.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d477:
China and Moscow move toward each other in these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 5, 1945. Chiang Kai-shek and T. V. Soong had told Ambassador Hurley that Moscow agreed to receive Soong as the Generalissimo's personal representative. The visit would come late in February or early in March. Talks would cover closer relations and Soviet participation in the war against Japan.

Korea, Manchuria, postwar economic matters, and the Sino-Soviet border filled out the agenda. Hurley relayed Molotov's September assurance: the Russians were not supporting the Chinese Communists, who, Molotov claimed, were not communists at all. Grew's digest gave the traveling delegation a window on the Far East bargain forming behind Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d77:
Trusteeship for dependent territories had been kept off the table at Dumbarton Oaks, and this 15 November 1944 memorandum explains why. Sent to the President by Acting Secretary Stettinius, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The paper asks permission to move the subject forward quietly.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff had not wanted the topic discussed while the war ran on. The Soviet, British, and Chinese delegations all wished to take it up later, and the State Department had draft proposals ready. Stettinius recommends further study with the military and naval authorities. If the President approves the proposals, they would go to the three allied governments before the founding conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d177:
Acting Secretary Grew sent Truman the State Department's full briefing agenda on June 30, 1945. His covering memorandum is document 177 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Truman had asked before leaving Washington for a fully documented agenda for the meeting in Germany.

Grew apologizes that the papers lack the clearance he would have wished, with no Secretary of State in place. But time is too short to hold them back. The attached memo has three parts. The first lists items the United States should raise, with the recommended American position on each. The second lists items the British intend to raise. The third covers other important matters likely to come up. The first item proposes no formal peace conference, and instead a council of foreign ministers of the great powers. Copies went to James Byrnes and Admiral Leahy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d277:
Winant sent on Britain's twin caveat on Austrian reparations in a cable dated July 7, 1945. The cable is document 277 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It quotes the words the British member gave his own government on July 4.

London accepts in principle that Austria must furnish reparations, the British words run. But London is not to be taken as settling in advance the form or sum of such payments, or Austria's capacity to make them. The group in London had no power to weigh the real question. London holds that the four powers should now take it up in light of Austria's economic prospects. The wording matches the U.S. caveat sent three days before.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d377:
A draft letter for President Truman, prepared by the American delegation, would report the Reparations Commission's progress to Stalin and Churchill. Pauley, the draft says, reports two main gains. The Commission's members have agreed on a percentage split of reparations among the three powers: 56 for the Soviet Union, 22 for Britain, and 22 for the United States.

To meet the proven claims of other nations, each of the three would give up part of its share in proportion. The members also agreed a procedure for dividing reparations among the other claimant countries. The draft further treats all property removed from Germany as reparations, save paid exports, war booty, and restitutions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d477: Three conditions for an Italian government's success are stated in an extract of Kirk's cable from Rome of July 6, 1945. The full text is printed as document No. 469. In present circumstances, Kirk writes, no government, however gifted, can prove its worth without three things. The armistice regime must be abolished. Allied troops must stay in the country, to give confidence to a people in a state of demoralization. And material aid must come at once, to prevent unrest through wide unemployment and hunger.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d577:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent a top secret report from Moscow on July 12, 1945. Addressed to the President and the Secretary of State, it is document 577 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It covers that night's talk between China's T. V. Soong and Stalin.

Harriman says Soong and Stalin agree on most points, but not on the railways and ports. Stalin gave way on guards, who will be Chinese, and on moving Soviet troops in Manchuria. He still demands a majority of railway directors, which Soong resists. Stalin also wants Dairen inside a Soviet military zone with a naval base. Soong offers Port Arthur as the base and Dairen as a free port under Chinese rule. Stalin wants a deal before he meets Truman, so the date of Soviet entry into the war can be set.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d677:
Ambassador Winant sent an urgent secret survey of the Tangier tangle from London on July 14, 1945. It is document 677 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. His source was again Hoyer Millar of the Foreign Office.

Millar said the Dutch had now pressed their interest in Tangier with some force. The Portuguese and Belgians had registered interest as well. Churchill himself was taking a hand from Hendaye, and London's line was fixed. Nothing could be done until after the Big Three meeting. In Paris, France talked of separate soundings to reconcile the four governments' views. London would discourage that course and saw any meeting before August as out of the question. Millar even weighed a Spanish exit with Sherifian troops moving in, which a tactful French approach might make acceptable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d77:
General Eisenhower pressed Moscow for instant access to Berlin in an urgent telegram to General Deane on June 19, 1945. The message, sent from Frankfurt, is document 77 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Soviet officers wanted to delay the American survey party until Marshal Zhukov returned to Berlin on June 28.

Eisenhower calls that impossible. A meeting of this size cannot be arranged in two weeks, he says, and General Parks's party of some 275 men and 50 vehicles must go in the next day. He also demands open running rights on the Dessau-Berlin highway and the Halle-Berlin air route. Talks with Zhukov can wait, he adds; the groundwork cannot. The cable shows how tight the Potsdam timetable already was.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1077:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled the Secretary of State at Potsdam on July 24, 1945. Yugoslavia's Foreign Office had sent the American embassy in Belgrade two protest notes, dated July 18 and 19. They charge the Greek government with breaking the Atlantic Charter and the United Nations Charter in Aegean Macedonia.

Belgrade claims Athens fails to stop fascist gangs, backs them, and persecutes Slav Macedonians through its own forces. Testimony from 20,000 peasants who fled is cited as proof of a drive to expel or destroy them. Greek troops are also said to have fired across the Yugoslav border. Washington suggests the clash now needs joint international action, perhaps agreed at Potsdam itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1177:
The Soviet team tabled this proposal on 19 July 1945, the summit's third day. In the opening round, each side's papers staked out its starting demands. Only after all three hands were shown did the hard trading over words begin.

Moscow's papers pressed the Soviet case on the shape of postwar Europe. Borders, payments from Germany, and the rule of freed lands all ran through them. This proposal is the formal Soviet bid from that first round. Set beside the final protocol, it shows where Moscow started and how far the talks moved it, if at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1277:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to the President on 21 July 1945. Their messages to Truman ran through the summit on a steady rhythm. This one dates from the end of the first week, when the team had its full measure of the bargaining.

The chiefs wrote as the president's military house: forces, fronts, and the plans that bound them. Their word balanced the envoys' reports on the president's desk. This message is one turn of that exchange. It shows the commander in chief being served by his chiefs in writing, at the distance the summit imposed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1377:
Norman Brook, a senior secretary to the British cabinet, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on 28 July 1945. Brook served the British government at the staff level, much as Dunn served the American. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Staff-to-staff letters between allies are the grease of coalition work. Brook and Dunn could settle wording and timetables that leaders had no time to touch. This letter came just after Attlee took over the British delegation, when staff ties mattered most in keeping the talks smooth. Readers see here the level at which summits actually run: trusted aides passing paper so that principals can agree in public.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-77:
Department of State minutes record an informal foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945, at 4 p.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Byrnes opened by returning to reparations and to his morning talk with Molotov.

The Secretary said he would not repeat all he had said to Molotov. He merely wished to state the U.S. view in Eden's hearing. Certain Soviet positions, he held, were hard to reconcile with an overall reparation plan. Since Maisky was present, Byrnes asked him to confirm or clarify the Soviet definition of war booty. As reported to him, it covered all supplies and equipment, plants and materials included. Molotov then handed in what he called the true Soviet definition, printed as an annex. Byrnes closed with a question: was it true that Soviet authorities had taken quantities of equipment from their zone?
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d777:
Kirk reported from Rome to the Acting Secretary of State on July 20, 1945, in document 777. The ambassador in Italy wrote during the Potsdam Conference's first week. Italy's place in the coming peace was unsettled. Kirk's report was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Rome's view reached Washington through Kirk's steady hand. He had served in many capitals and wrote with a cool eye. Readers get Italy as its government wished to be seen, filtered by a skeptic. The document shows a former enemy state lobbying for mercy while the victors met. Its timing ties the plea to the summit's first decisions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d877: Emilio Collado cabled Willard Thorp and Jacob Reinstein from Babelsberg on July 23, 1945, in this secret telegram. Collado directed the Office of Financial and Development Policy. His news was blunt: four-power joint planning of imports, exports, and reparations now looked unworkable. The team was therefore drafting on a zonal basis instead. Western zones might still combine their handling and financing. Collado adds that he, McCloy, and Hilldring were drafting a directive on War Department financing duty.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d977: Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov answered Secretary Byrnes from Berlin on August 2, 1945. He agrees fully that the Potsdam reparations deal should be carried out as soon as possible. He also agrees the Reparations Commission should work closely with the Control Council and set up its organization in Berlin. One point he qualifies. The commission's permanent seat, he says, should naturally remain Moscow, as the Crimea Conference decided. He adds that the commission's work will bind it most closely to the Soviet Union, given the Berlin decisions.
frus-1948v02-d577: A 1948 FRUS document from the U.S. Military Governor for Germany. The occupation authorities reported from Berlin. This entry holds that report. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. Time has kept the file intact.
gao-gaoreports-b-295877: BTC Contract Services took its May 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297077: Haworth doubled its November 2005 protest — two case numbers, one furniture fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer each, and the record stays clean.
gao-gaoreports-b-298077: Critical Incident Solutions took its May 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298277: MadahCom took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299477: Phoenix Management took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Every protest gets the full fair-play reading, no matter the firm's size.
gao-gaoreports-b-299577: Forest City Military Communities took its June 2007 housing-contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Military family housing deals get the same fair-play ruling as any federal buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-400177: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by ECI Defense Group. The July 25, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-277: DOD's excess property was being wasted in 2005, and GAO's report says management control breakdowns caused substantial waste. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the surplus deserved better handling. The breakdowns had to be fixed. The surplus deserved better handling.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-377: Hardrock mining bonds needed better management in 2005, and GAO's report says BLM had to improve financial assurances for reclamation. The findings demand the guarantees. The report warns that the mined lands deserved real cleanup. The assurances had to be better.
