gao-gaoreports-gao-05-477: Passport fraud detection needed strengthening in 2005, and GAO's report says improvements were required. The findings demand the vigilance. The report warns that the travel documents should not be faked. The improvements had to come. The travel documents should not be faked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-577: Disaster backup plans were better but not battle-tested in 2005, and GAO's report says agency plans improved, with oversight needed to finish the job. The review checks who could keep working through an emergency. The continuity plans were maturing. The continuity plans were maturing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-677: TSA's sensitive information designation needed clear policies in 2005, and GAO's report says oversight was required. The findings demand the rules. The report warns that the secrecy stamps deserved honest use. The policies had to be clear. The secrecy stamps deserved honest use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-777: E-rulemaking progress got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says centralized system development was advancing. The findings give the credit. The report shows the digital democracy was being built. The progress had to be sustained. The digital democracy was being built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-177: Energy workers' compensation needed better oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says adjustments had been made, though more planning was required. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report warns that the atomic workers deserved fair pay. The oversight had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-277: The 2010 Census buying was mostly sound in 2006, and GAO's report says the bureau generally followed good acquisition practices, though management needed continuing. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the headcount's contracts needed watching. The management had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-577: UN procurement controls were weak in 2006, and GAO's report says the internal controls needed strengthening. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the world body's shopping needed locks. The controls had to be fixed. The world body's shopping needed locks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-677: The down-payment aid program's results were murky in 2006, and GAO's report says data limitations constrained the assessment of the initiative. The findings admit the fog. The report warns that the dream-home dollars needed proof. The data had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1077: Guarding bases and depots took more than fences in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon's risk game needed sharper management. The findings press defense brass to run base protection like a discipline, not a checklist. In an age of asymmetric threats, the report argues, ad-hoc security is no security.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-277: America's logo on its aid needed measuring in 2007, and GAO's report says the agencies should better assess their marking and publicity efforts. The findings demand proof of impact. The report's question: did the flag on the grain buy any goodwill?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-677: Iraq's lights and oil needed one master plan in 2007 — GAO's report says the rebuild of the power and petroleum sectors wanted an integrated strategy. The findings demand joined-up thinking. The report's warning: megawatts and barrels rise or fall together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-77: Kidney-care payments needed bundling in 2007, and GAO's report says bundling Medicare's drug payments with all end-stage renal disease services would promote efficiency. The findings make the case. The report argues that one price for the whole treatment would curb the gaming. The bundle had to be tied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-877: Uncle Sam's ad buys got an audit in 2007 — GAO's report finds the established ad programs mostly served the White House's small-business push. The findings track where the government's marketing dollars went. The report asks whether the public's airtime served the public.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-477: The Government Accountability Office dug into traffic Safety: Improved Reporting and Performance Measures Would Enhance Evaluation of High-Visibility Campaigns in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-77: GAO found in 2007 that the aid agency and the space agency were slack about chasing wrong payments. A 2002 law tells each agency to size up, report, and claw back money paid in error — but both fell short. The report grades their thin efforts and presses both shops to hunt down mistaken payouts and get the cash back.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-877: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at defense Acquisitions: Department of Defense Needs Framework for Balancing Investments in Tactical Radios. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
how-to-teach-according-to-temperament-an: How to Teach According to Temperament, 1877. The phrenological teaching. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Kept for readers. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
jewett-deephaven-1877:
Deephaven, Jewett's first book from 1877, follows two young Boston women through a summer in Maine. They stay in a sleepy coastal town in a house left by a great-aunt. Contents name Kate Lancaster's plan, the Brandon house and lighthouse, and Lady Brandon among the early sketches.

City girls learn country wisdom as they meet weathered houses and salty local folk. Jewett tells the tale in linked sketches rather than one tight plot. The gentle comedy already shows her fine ear and her love of place. No one before her had written New England village life with such close and loving care, and critics saw a major talent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucifer-10177:
Lucifer, the name of the morning star, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Kaufmann Kohler. The word renders a Hebrew phrase in Isaiah, “the brilliant one, son of the morning,” whose fall is compared to the fall of the king of Babylon. Kohler treats the passage as a borrowed star myth.

The article links the proud star, hurled down from the mountain of the gods, to Greek and Babylonian tales and to the fall of the angels on Mount Hermon. It then shows how, in the century before Christianity, the myth passed to Satan, once an archangel cast down for raising his throne too high. Early Christian writers completed that identification. For readers, the entry traces one word from a Hebrew prophecy about Babylon to the later figure of Satan himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micah-book-of-1:
The Book of Micah, sixth among the Twelve Minor Prophets, is summarized chapter by chapter in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn, published in 1906. The book is ascribed to Micah the Morasthite and runs to seven chapters. A critical section after the summary takes up scholarly questions about the prophet's period.

Chapter one denounces the idolatry of Samaria and Jerusalem, and chapter two attacks oppression while promising Israel's restoration. Chapter three reproves cruel princes and false prophets, and chapter four turns to Jerusalem restored and victorious. The summary closes with reproof for injustice, a lament over corruption, and comfort that Israel will return to its land and triumph.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morais-henry-sa:
Henry Samuel Morais, born at Philadelphia on May 13, 1860, was a writer and minister raised inside American Judaism's founding family, as Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father, Sabato Morais, gave him his religious instruction. He taught twelve years in Philadelphia's Hebrew schools before turning to print.

He was the principal founder of the Jewish Exponent and its managing editor for two years, with newspaper work at the Philadelphia Public Ledger beside. Pulpits followed at Mikve Israel, at Syracuse, and at Newport. His books made his name: Eminent Israelites of the Nineteenth Century at twenty, and in 1894 The Jews of Philadelphia, called here the most important local history of American Jews yet published.
kabbala-denudata-knorr-tome1-1677:
Christian Knorr von Rosenroth published the first tome of his Kabbala Denudata at Sulzbach in 1677. The text is in Latin, the learned tongue of his Europe. Knorr gathered Kabbalistic writings, above all from the Zohar and the school of Isaac Luria, and rendered them into Latin with long introductions of his own.

Through this anthology, Jewish mysticism reached Christian scholars who read no Hebrew or Aramaac. Thinkers from Leibniz onward consulted Knorr's volumes on the sefirot and the souls of men. No English translation of the work is in the public domain. Tome one is the principal vehicle by which Lurianic Kabbalah entered the Christian West. Its influence on early modern thought is still being mapped.
la-tete-humaine-etudes-de-phrenologie-et: La tête humaine, 1877. The human head studies. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
lalita-vistara-mitra-1877:
Rajendralala Mitra translated the Lalita Vistara into English in 1877. The Sanskrit text tells the Buddha's life as cosmic pageant. Mitra was a pioneering Indian scholar of the nineteenth century.

Miracles attend every episode of the ornate biography. A heaven-sent conception, a painless birth, and gods in attendance frame the story. The young prince's encounters lead toward the enlightenment beneath the tree. Beloved across Asia, the Lalita Vistara shaped Buddhist art for centuries. Mitra's translation captures its jeweled, devotional style in English. The work reads less as history than as devotion. Its gorgeous excess is precisely its point and charm.
lemery-course-of-chymistry-1677:
Nicolas Lemery was a Paris apothecary whose Cours de Chymie taught chemistry to fashionable crowds in his own laboratory. This 1677 English translation, A Course of Chymistry, was the bestselling chemistry textbook of the late seventeenth century. Lemery wrote for students, doctors, and curious householders alike.

He explains acids, alkalis, metals, and medicines with models of sharp and porous particles that a beginner can picture. Recipes and operations fill the course, from distilling spirits to preparing the drugs of his shop. The book's clarity helped turn chymistry from a secret craft into a public, teachable science.
mackenzie-royal-masonic-cyclopaedia-1877:
Kenneth Mackenzie built a vast word book of the craft in The Royal Masonic Cyclopaedia, out in 1877. Mackenzie was a sage of signs and rites in London. He later helped seed the Golden Dawn. Here he glosses each term, rank, rite, and tale of the Masons in A to Z form.

Lore of the craft sits by lore of the East and old myths. His own sly views slip in past the dry gloss. The book is a rich store for fans of rite. It shows the mind that shaped an age of magic. Mackenzie roamed the clubs and bands of the occult in his day. Few men of his age could match the breadth of lore packed here.
maclean-manual-antiquity-of-man-1877:
J. P. MacLean, an American writer on archaeology, published A Manual of the Antiquity of Man in 1877. The book is an early American synthesis of human prehistory for general readers. MacLean gathered what the 1870s knew of fossil man and the first ages of human life.

He surveys cave deposits with their extinct beasts, the shell mounds of the coasts, and the great earthworks of the mound-builders. European finds and American ones are weighed side by side. The manual's judgments belong to its decade, but its range is impressive. It stands as a snapshot of prehistoric archaeology while the field was still young and forming.
mccrindle-ancient-india-megasthenes-arri:
J. W. McCrindle collected Greek accounts of ancient India in his 1877 volume. Megasthenes' Indica and Arrian's Indica form the core of the book. McCrindle spent his career translating classical sources on India into English.

Megasthenes served as ambassador at Chandragupta's court around 300 BCE. His Indica survives only in quotations by later writers, which McCrindle assembled. Elephants, gold-digging ants, and seven castes fill the ambassador's report. Arrian's Indica adds Alexander-era knowledge and the voyage of Nearchus. Together they give the West's earliest systematic description of India. Wonder and sober reporting sit side by side throughout these fragments.
menghi-flagellum-daemonum-1577:
Girolamo Menghi was an Italian Franciscan exorcist whose Flagellum Daemonum, The Scourge of Demons, appeared in 1577. The book is a working manual of exorcism for priests facing possessed persons. It became the most reprinted Catholic exorcist's handbook of the early modern period.

Menghi gives the rites in order: prayers, adjurations, signs of the cross, and questions to put to the demon. He also teaches how to tell true possession from illness, fraud, and melancholy before any rite begins. Later exorcists copied his forms for two centuries, making his book the standard of the trade. Priests carried his manual into sickrooms and prisons across Catholic Europe.
miln-excavations-carnac-1877:
James Miln dug among the great stone rows at Carnac in Brittany in the 1870s. His book, printed in 1877, gives the first true dig report from the site. Carnac holds long lines of huge upright stones set in the far past. Miln worked at the Bossenno and Mont Saint-Michel sites.

He tells what the digs found layer by layer: tools, pots, and signs of old huts. Plans and views show the rows and the mounds near them. Miln's care set a mark for field work at such sites. The report launched the true study of Carnac.
mkultra-senate-hearings-1977:
The Senate dragged the CIA's mind-control program into the light in the summer of 1977. Project MKULTRA hearings, held jointly on August 3, laid out the agency's years of work on drugs and the mind. New-found money records had just shown the program was wider than first known.

Senators heard how the agency dosed men without their knowledge and hid the work behind cut-outs and shredders. The transcript prints the charges, the agency's defense, and the names of the dead and harmed. It is the base public record of the whole grim program. Later accounts of MKULTRA all build on this hearing.
morgan-ancient-society-1877:
Lewis Henry Morgan, a Rochester lawyer who studied the Iroquois for decades, published Ancient Society in 1877. His subtitle traces human progress from savagery through barbarism to civilization. The book is built on kinship systems, his great discovery as a fieldworker and theorist.

Morgan argues that mankind climbed one main ladder, marked by inventions: fire, the bow, pottery, farming, and iron. Family forms climb with them, from group marriage toward monogamy. Marx and Engels read the book closely; Engels built his Origin of the Family on it. Modern anthropology rejects Morgan's single ladder but honors his kinship work. The book is a foundation stone of American anthropology.
openalex-w1531900177: Ankylosing spondylitis — a painful arthritis of the spine — runs in genes. A 2015 Nature Communications study by Cortés and colleagues mapped the immune-gene associations of the disease, including links with ERAP1. The work untangled the complex genetics behind the condition.
openalex-w2784936077: The axolotl — the Mexican salamander that regrows limbs, jaws, and spinal cords — is biology's regeneration champion. This 2018 Nature paper reports its genome, one of the largest ever sequenced, and uses it to study the regulators of tissue formation. The genomic toolkit promises to reveal how the axolotl rebuilds what mammals cannot.
openalex-w2891646477: Guillain-Barré syndrome — the immune system attacking peripheral nerves — looks different in different places. This 2018 Brain paper systematically compares its clinical presentation, electrophysiological subtypes, and outcomes across regions. The analysis moves beyond single-country reports to map the syndrome's global diversity.
openalex-w2904186977: IllustrisTNG simulates universes — vast cosmological volumes with gas, stars, magnetic fields, and dark matter. This 2019 paper announces the full public release of the TNG100 and TNG300 simulation data, run with the Arepo moving-mesh code. The open dataset lets any astronomer explore galaxy formation in silico.
openalex-w2943031177: Mesenchymal stromal cells promise to calm immune overreactions and regenerate tissue — but results have been uneven. This 2019 Stem Cell Research & Therapy paper reviews priming approaches that boost MSC efficacy before therapy. Pre-treating the cells, the evidence suggests, can sharpen their immunosuppressive and regenerative powers.
openalex-w2951276077: What doesn't hydrology know? This 2019 Hydrological Sciences Journal paper — born of public consultation and workshops — lists 23 unsolved problems in hydrology. The community perspective aims to harmonize research toward the field's biggest open questions, from groundwater to floods.
openalex-w2951287977: As healthcare turns patient-centered, the patient's verdict matters. This 2019 Frontiers in Public Health mixed-method study assesses satisfaction — and its determinants — among outpatients at Suva's subdivisional health center in Fiji. The findings give administrators a patient-eyed view of what their clinics get right and wrong.
openalex-w3035590377: Teenagers' mental health is worsening — and those who need help most seek it least. This 2020 BMC Psychiatry systematic review examines barriers, facilitators, and interventions for help-seeking among adolescents. Understanding the reluctance is the first step to overcoming it.
openalex-w4384652177: PacBio HiFi reads — long (15–20 kb) and highly accurate — have revolutionized genome assembly. This 2023 BMC Bioinformatics paper presents MitoHiFi: a Python pipeline for assembling mitochondrial genomes from HiFi reads. The tool brings the HiFi revolution to the cell’s powerhouses.
openalex-w7204159777: A patient with HIV developed a rare, life-threatening clotting disorder before starting antiretroviral therapy. This case report traces the recovery from immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, untangling it from HIV-related look-alikes. The authors detail the diagnostic puzzle and the treatment. A hematology case where telling two similar diseases apart saved a life.
openalex-w7204194277: Brazil's new high school model asks students to investigate, not just absorb. This article presents a ready-to-use lesson sequence on science, health, and well-being built for that model. The authors designed it to build scientific literacy and student voice. Practical and timely, it hands teachers a tested plan for curious classrooms.
peirce-fixation-belief-1877:
The Fixation of Belief, published in 1877 in Popular Science Monthly, opens Peirce's series Illustrations of the Logic of Science. It is the paper in which pragmatism begins, though the word itself comes a year later.

Peirce asks how beliefs get fixed, and finds four methods: tenacity, authority, the a priori method of taste, and the method of science. Only science, he argues, ties belief to something real outside our wishes, and so only science settles doubt for good. The essay's calm logic hides a revolution. Every later pragmatist, James and Dewey included, built on this paper.
plos-pbio-0020077:
Gregory C. DeAngelis and William T. Newsome studied how the brain reads its own visual maps in PLOS Biology in 2004. In area MT, neurons respond to both motion direction and depth. The two kinds of information are woven into the same patch of cortex.

The puzzle is how a later brain area picks out one kind of signal without mixing in the other. The authors test how well the joint map supports judging depth from motion cues. Their work speaks to a broad problem in brain science: tidy readout from messy, mixed signals. Lessons from MT apply to many areas where one cell group carries several kinds of news at once.
plos-pbio-0020277:
Chung-I Chang, Sébastien Pili-Floury, Mireille Hervé, and their team solved the shape of a fly immune sensor in PLOS Biology in 2004. The sensor spots peptidoglycan, a mesh material in bacterial cell walls. Its structure shows a groove where that mesh fits, like a key in a lock.

The same protein also has an odd cutting activity that can trim the bacterial material it detects. Sensing and trimming in one molecule is a compact design. Structures like this show how insect immunity, which lacks antibodies, still tells friend from foe with precision. They also offer drug design lessons, since bacterial wall pieces are classic antibiotic targets.
plos-pbio-0020377:
R. Daniel Rudic, Peter McNamara, Anne-Maria Chang, and their team linked body clocks to blood sugar in PLOS Biology in 2004. BMAL1 and CLOCK are core gear proteins of the circadian clock, the daily timer in our cells. Mice with broken clocks showed faults in how they handle glucose.

The finding connects two systems once studied apart: daily rhythms and sugar control. Organs like the liver and pancreas run on clock time, and their sugar work follows the day. When the clock breaks, that work slips. The study helps explain why shift work and broken sleep raise diabetes risk. It also suggests the time of day may matter for diabetes care.
plos-pone-0000077:
Samantha Kerry, Michael TeKippe, Nathan C. Gaddis, and their team hunted an immunity gene in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their study organism fights off bacterial and fungal infections with the help of GATA transcription factors, proteins that switch gene groups on. One such factor proved required for a working defense.

Without it, the host could not mount the proper response to either kind of germ. A single switch controlling defense against both bacteria and fungi marks it as a high-level control. That makes it a strong lead for understanding immune failure. It may also point to ways of boosting defense, in crops or in animals, by tuning one central switch rather than many small ones.
plos-pone-0000177:
Benjamin A. Onwuegbusi, Jonathan R. E. Rees, Pierre Lao-Sirieix, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. In oesophageal adenocarcinoma, a cancer of the food pipe, they study the TGF-beta signaling pathway. The title reports that losing the Smad-dependent arm of that pathway stops cells arresting their cycle and instead promotes invasion.

A pathway that normally restrains growth can be cut in a way that frees the tumor. The authors show this selective loss in cancer cell lines. The result helps explain how this aggressive cancer spreads, and it marks a step that future treatments might target.
plos-pone-0000277:
Bénédicte Lafay and Jeremy J. Burdon published this plant microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Legumes house bacteria in root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air, fertilizing the plant. The authors survey the molecular diversity of those root-nodule bacteria in Kakadu National Park in Australia's Northern Territory, a landscape little sampled for such microbes.

Australia's native legumes and their bacteria evolved apart from the farm species most studies use. Cataloguing their diversity shows what nitrogen-fixing partnerships exist in wild ecosystems. The work also supplies baseline data for a protected landscape, useful as climates and land use change.
plos-pone-0000377:
Sean O. Sean O. Henderson and colleagues tackled a public health question in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They asked why death rates from heart and blood vessel disease differ between racial groups. Known causes like smoking, blood pressure, and cholesterol are often blamed only in part. The team tested how much of the gap those established risk factors can explain.

Their analysis concludes that the established factors account for most of the racial differences in deaths from cardiovascular disease. That finding points prevention efforts toward the known, changeable risks rather than toward unknown causes. It also frames unequal exposure to those risks as a central reason the death rates differ.
plos-pone-0000477:
Kirsten Moll and colleagues described a new piece of the malaria parasite's surface machinery, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, sticks to human red blood cells as part of its life cycle. The team identified a novel DBL-domain of the parasite's 332 molecule and proposed it is involved in erythrocyte adhesion.

Sticking to red cells helps the parasite hide from the spleen and cause disease. A domain that does the sticking is a candidate target for drugs or vaccines meant to break the grip. Malaria surface proteins are notoriously variable, so each well-mapped piece adds to the search for stable targets.
plos-pone-0000577:
Tal Murthy and colleagues built a checked gene library for a dangerous germ, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia and is feared as a possible bioweapon. The team built a full set of its protein-coding genes, each one checked by reading its sequence.

A checked set like this lets any lab order a gene and test what its protein does. No one has to clone genes from the live germ to start work. That speeds the hunt for drug targets and tests. Papers that build shared tools like this rarely win fame, but they lift the work of a whole field.
plos-pone-0000677:
François Meurens, Mustapha Berri, Richard H. Siggers and colleagues studied how gut bacteria relate to two immune signals in the intestine. Their 2007 PLOS ONE subject was chemokines, small proteins that call immune cells to a location. TECK, also called CCL25, and MEC, or CCL28, are made mainly in the thymus and in mucosal surfaces. Their receptors, CCR9 and CCR10, sit mostly on T and B lymphocytes.

In humans, mice, pigs, and sheep, these chemokines help sort immune cells into the gut. Commensal bacteria, the normal residents of the intestine, are the variable under study. If resident microbes tune these signals, the gut's immune traffic partly answers to its own bacteria.
plos-pone-0000777:
Sander H. Diks, Kaushal Parikh, Marijke van der Sijde and colleagues asked how small the core set of protein phosphorylation sites might be. Reversible phosphorylation, run by enzymes called kinases, is probably the most important regulatory mechanism in eukaryotes. The team studied phosphorylation in vitro with peptide arrays. The arrays carried most protein sequences held in the PhosphoBase database. Cell lysates supplied the enzymes that act on them.

Their title poses the question of a minimal eukaryotic phosphoproteome: a basic set of sites that many species share. If such a core exists, it defines the essential wiring of cell regulation. Comparing lysates from representative species tests how universal that wiring is.
plos-pone-0000877:
Hua Wong, Jean-Marc Victor and Julien Mozziconacci built an atom-by-atom model of the chromatin fiber, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inside the cell nucleus, histone proteins wrap DNA into a packed, ordered structure. That packing controls which genes can be read and when.

The team built their model from known structures: the nucleosome core, plain DNA and part of a linker histone called H5. Their fiber includes those linker histones, which many simpler models leave out. The result is a flexible structure whose shape shifts with the spacing between nucleosomes. Such models help turn static pictures of DNA packing into testable ideas.
plos-pone-0000977:
Frederic Pincet examined how pulling scaffold proteins to the cell membrane drives specific signaling, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. A cell must answer each signal with the right response, not a generic one. Scaffold proteins help by holding the right partners together, steering the signal down one path.

Pincet focuses on the step where scaffolds are recruited to the membrane, the cell's inner surface. That move can decide which response fires. The paper works at the level of molecular mechanisms, the physical details of binding and place. Getting those details right is what separates a true explanation from a diagram.
plos-pone-0001077:
Etay Ziv, Ilya Nemenman and Chris Wiggins measured how network shape affects signal handling in small gene circuits, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A transcriptional network has to sense environmental signals and answer well. The team quantify how the network's topology, its wiring pattern, influences that ability.

They pose the problem in information theory terms, which frees the analysis from assuming one specific function. A wiring pattern can then be scored for how much signal it can carry. Small biochemical networks are the kind synthetic biologists actually build. General rules for their design, not tied to one job, are the paper's aim.
plos-pone-0001177:
Leishmania donovani is a parasite that causes visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly disease also called kala-azar. Rosario Díaz González and colleagues studied one of the parasite's enzymes, DNA topoisomerase IB, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The parasite's version of this enzyme differs substantially from the human one, which makes it a promising drug lead.

The authors deleted parts of the enzyme to search for the smallest working form, a minimal functional heterodimer. Mapping which pieces are essential shows where a drug might grip. Structural differences between the parasite and human enzymes are exactly what selective drug design needs.
plos-pone-0001277:
Microsporidia are intracellular parasites with some of the smallest genomes known, highly derived relatives of fungi. Nicolas Corradi and colleagues compared the genomes of three species, Encephalitozoon cuniculi, Antonospora locustae, and Enterocytozoon bieneusi, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Despite fast sequence evolution, far-related microsporidia can share much the same gene order.

The authors describe patterns of genome evolution across the three parasites. Only two microsporidian genomes had been studied before. Matching compacted genomes shows what a parasite can throw away and what it must keep. It is a lesson in how small a genome can get.
plos-pone-0001377:
Timothée Masquelier, Rudy Guyonneau, and Simon Thorpe published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how nerve cells learn from timing. When one nerve cell fires just before a second one, their link tends to grow strong. When the order flips, the link tends to grow weak. The team built a model based on this timing rule.

In their tests, the model learned to spot the start of a pattern that repeats in a stream of spikes. It did so without being told what to look for. The result shows how a simple timing rule can pull order out of noise. It may also hint at how real brains pick up rhythms and habits.
plos-pone-0001477:
Emmanuel Boucrot and Tomas Kirchhausen wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on cell size during division. Using films of single cells, they found that a cell shrinks as it rounds up to divide. The smallest size comes at a key stage, just before the split. Size then grows back fast as the cell moves to part.

A set size dip during division had not been charted this clearly before. It hints that cells shed or take up fluid on a strict clock. That clock may help the split go right. The work adds a plain but new fact to the base account of how cells divide.
plos-pone-0001577:
Stephanie Prady and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how well acupuncture trials are reported. Two rule sets had been issued to lift trial reporting: one for all trials, one for acupuncture. Poor reports block readers from judging a trial's worth. The team rated reports from before and after the rules came out.

They checked whether scores for report quality rose over that span. Gains would show the rules work in practice, not just on paper. Weak gains would urge stronger steps by journals. Either way, the study tests a cheap tool for lifting science quality across the field.
plos-pone-0001677:
Lucia Banci, Ivano Bertini, Mirela Boca, and their co-authors studied a protein tied to a fatal nerve disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is SOD1, short for copper, zinc superoxide dismutase 1. About 100 single-letter changes in its gene are known to cause the familial form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. In that disease motor neurons die and muscles waste away.

The changes are scattered across the whole protein, which makes their shared harm hard to explain. The team focused on oligomerization, the tendency of SOD1 copies to clump together. The full text gives the protein measurements and how mutants differ from the normal form. If stray clumping is a common thread among mutants, it offers one target for drugs across many forms of familial ALS.
plos-pone-0001777:
Sander L. J. Wijers, Patrick Schrauwen, Wim H. M. Saris, and their co-authors measured heat production in human muscle in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Mild cold and overfeeding raise energy expenditure in mammals, a process called adaptive thermogenesis. In small animals it comes mainly from mitochondrial uncoupling in brown fat, where energy is burned as heat instead of stored.

The team asked whether human skeletal muscle contributes through mitochondrial uncoupling of its own. They report that muscle uncoupling is associated with cold-induced adaptive thermogenesis. The full text gives the cold exposure tests and the muscle measurements. Muscle is most of body mass, so even a small uncoupling there could matter for weight control research.
plos-pone-0001877:
Takaoki Kasahara and co-authors tested a bold treatment idea in mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The mice carry a fault in the DNA of their mitochondria, the small power units inside cells, placed only in nerve cells. The fault models a human eye and muscle disease whose patients at times also have mood disorders.

The mutant mice showed acts much like those seen in bipolar illness, such as a warped daily rhythm. The team then gave the mice brief electric shocks to the brain, a lab form of a therapy used in human care. They report a marked effect on the odd acts. The work links faulty cell power to mood-like change.
plos-pone-0001977:
Jeremy Peirce and co-authors built a better math tool for mapping genes in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Advanced intercross lines are mouse groups bred over many generations. Their gene shuffling is dense, which lets traits be mapped to fine spots on the genome. Standard mapping methods from simpler crosses were often applied to them, followed by naive shuffle tests.

The pair of problems can bias results. Their method, called GRAIP, reshuffles genomes in a way that fits these lines, for both simulation and significance tests. Sharper tools mean gene hunts in mice land on the right spots more often.
plos-pone-0002077:
Debby Vissers and co-authors simulated preventive HIV drugs across whole epidemics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, means taking HIV drugs before exposure to block infection, and it looked promising, above all for women. Demand for rollout was expected the moment trials proved it works, so planners needed long-term forecasts.

The team simulated the impact of PrEP on HIV transmission and epidemics in Africa and India. Models can weigh how coverage, adherence, and risk change alter the gains over years. Forecasts like these help health systems spend on the mix of tools that cuts new infections most.
plos-pone-0002177:
Kristin Olesen and Anthony Auger studied how brain chemistry in newborn rats can switch on hormone receptors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hormone receptors in the growing brain shape cell processes that last into adult life, changing both behavior and body function. Earlier work suggested that dopamine, a brain messenger, can control progestin receptors in set regions of the adult brain.

The authors asked whether dopamine can also switch on estrogen receptors in the newborn female brain. They found that it does, in limited regions, and that this triggers a marker gene called Fos. The result shows hormone systems in the infant brain can be turned on by brain signals alone.
plos-pone-0002277:
Beth McNally, Joanne Trgovcich, Gerd Maul, and co-authors studied a cancer-linked protein found outside the cell nucleus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The PML gene was discovered through its part in a chromosome swap that causes a form of leukemia. Inside the nucleus, PML protein helps control cell growth, tumor suppression, and cell death.

A separate pool of PML sits in the cytoplasm, the cell's outer compartment. The team reports that this cytoplasmic PML helps cells resist viral infection. The finding gives an old, well-studied protein a second workplace and hints the cell stations some of its antiviral defense outside the nucleus.
plos-pone-0002377:
Xin and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Dedong Xin, Landian Hu, Xiangyin Kong, among others. Its subject is alternative Promoters Influence Alternative Splicing at the Genomic Level. More and more experiments have shown that transcription and mRNA processing are not two independent events but are tightly coupled to each other.

Both promoter and transcription rate were found to influence alternative splicing. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002477:
Amsili and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Shira Amsili, Hagit Zer, Stephan Hinderlich, among others. Its subject is uDP-N-Acetylglucosamine 2-Epimerase/N-Acetylmannosamine Kinase (GNE) Binds to Alpha-Actinin 1: Novel Pathways in Skeletal Muscle?. Hereditary inclusion body myopathy (HIBM) is a rare neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations in GNE.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002577:
Beveren, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Nico J. M. van Beveren, Lieuwe de Haan, among others. Its subject is a Visual Metaphor Describing Neural Dynamics in Schizophrenia. In many scientific disciplines the use of a metaphor as an heuristic aid is not uncommon.

A well known example in somatic medicine is the ‘defense army metaphor’ used to characterize the immune system. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002677:
In 2008, Seong Il Choi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about protein solubility and folding enhancement by interaction with RNA. The catalog record names Seong Il Choi first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. While basic mechanisms of several major molecular chaperones are well understood. A further point appears in the abstract. Here, we report a chaperone type of protein folding facilitated by interaction with RNA. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002777:
Lisandro Benedetti-Cecchi and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of neutrality and the response of rare species to environmental variance. Authorship is credited in the record to Lisandro Benedetti-Cecchi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Neutral models and differential responses of species to environmental heterogeneity offer complementary explanations of species abundance distribution and dynamics. A further point appears in the abstract. Under what circumstances one model prevails over the other is still a matter of debate. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002877:
Srinivasan Krishnamoorthy mapped a signaling network in fruit fly cells for PLOS ONE in 2008. Adding a phosphate group to proteins is one way cells switch signals on and off, and about a third of cell proteins carry such marks. The study focused on receptor tyrosine kinases, a key family of signal receivers.

Using Drosophila S2 cells with the ErbB1 receptor, the author charted which proteins gain phosphate marks after signaling starts. That chart is called a phosphor-proteome. The result reveals new network links, in the paper's own terms, and gives cell biologists a parts list for how this signal spreads inside the cell.
plos-pone-0002977:
Carlos Barcia, Nicholas Sanderson, Robert Barrett and co-authors watched T cells change astrocytes in 2008. Astrocytes are star-shaped brain support cells that usually swell in response to trauma, stroke, or degeneration. Their response to a direct immune attack by T cells was poorly understood.

Effector T cells form tight contacts called immunological synapses with target cells. The PLOS ONE study reports those contacts induce polarization of astrocytes, both in living animals and in dishes. That is a novel response mechanism to cellular injury, with relevance to brain diseases where T cells attack. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003077:
Vera Levina, Adele Marrangoni, Richard DeMarco and co-authors enriched lung cancer stem cells with drug selection in 2008. Cancer stem cells are thought to regrow tumors after chemotherapy, though direct confirmation was still forthcoming. The team asked whether drug treatment could enrich and maintain such cells.

They then examined the enriched cells' cytokine network plus tumor-forming and metastatic properties. Published in PLOS ONE, drug-selected cells model the survivors that relapse is made of. Studying them is a step toward treatments aimed at the cells chemotherapy leaves behind. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003177:
Michiteru Kitazaki, Hisashi Kobiki and Laurence T. Maloney test how depth cues affect lightness judgement in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. How light a surface looks is affected by how the scene is interpreted. Some evidence suggests perceived lightness under two-eyed viewing differs from that in actual scenes, while other reports say viewing conditions have little effect.

The authors compare pictorial depth cues, binocular disparity cues, and motion parallax cues in three-dimensional virtual scenes. Readers learn which kinds of depth information change how bright a surface seems. The work matters for vision science and for building virtual scenes that look right.
plos-pone-0003277:
Kellie J. Hall, Matthew T. Harper, Karen Gilio and colleagues analyse a kinase in platelets in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. PKC theta is a novel protein kinase C isozyme predominantly expressed in T cells and platelets. T cells lacking it show reduced activation, and mice lacking it are resistant to autoimmune disease, making it an attractive therapeutic target for immune modulation. Collagen is a major activator of platelets.

The team carry out a genetic analysis of the role of protein kinase C theta in platelet function and thrombus formation. Readers learn whether an immune drug target also affects clotting. That safety question matters before such inhibitors reach patients.
plos-pone-0003377:
Venkateswara Rao Simhadri and colleagues traced messages between immune cells in this 2008 paper. Dendritic cells are scouts that show threats to the rest of the immune system. Natural killer cells destroy infected or cancerous cells on contact. The study asked how a protein called BAT3 passes signals between these two cell types.

The scouts were found to shed tiny bubble-like packets loaded with BAT3. These packets, called exosomes, reach killer cells and switch on their response. The signal works through a surface sensor named NKp30 on the killer cells. The finding shows how immune cells can guide each other without direct contact.
plos-pone-0003477:
Nadège Bault, Giorgio Coricelli, and Aldo Rustichini studied how rank shapes choices in this 2008 paper. Animal societies rest on dominance orders, high over low. People likewise care about their standing among others. That care should bend economic choices, not just feelings.

Their work treats each person's payoff as tied to others' payoffs. Experiments showed social ranking changes what people pick. Gains feel smaller when a rival gains more. The results matter for pay, markets, and any group with a pecking order. Pay deals at work often turn on rank as much as on raw amounts.
plos-pone-0003577:
J. William Critchfield and co-authors mapped HIV-specific T cells in the gut in this 2008 study. The intestinal mucosa shows strong virus replication in HIV infection. It also suffers pronounced loss of CD4 T cells early on. HIV-specific CD8 T cells may modulate the disease course.

The team measured responses in the rectal mucosa during chronic infection. Their size and complexity reflected the patients' clinical status. Strong local battles mark how the disease is going. Vaccines may need to protect where the virus hits hardest. The gut is where HIV does much of its early and lasting damage.
plos-pone-0003677:
Anna Kuparinen, Robert B. O'Hara, and Juha Merilä published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. As organisms grow, they pass turning points such as maturation at rates that vary by chance. Earlier models of these transitions worked only in fixed time steps. The authors wanted a model that flows in continuous time.

They built probabilistic models for such ontogenetic transitions, keeping the randomness that real growth shows. The framework extends reaction norms, the patterns that link genes and environment to timing. It gives ecologists a sounder way to predict when individuals will make their big life changes.
plos-pone-0003777:
Chunyu Yang, Guangchun Cao, Yang Li, and colleagues published this waste treatment study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Black liquor is the alkaline wastewater left from pulping wheat straw for paper. Its high pH and heavy pollution load make it very hard to treat. It causes serious environmental problems.

The team built an alkaline consortium, a chosen crew of microbes that thrive in such conditions. They tracked how the crew's makeup changed while it treated black liquor with a very high pollution load. The study shows a designed microbe team tackling one of industry's toughest effluents.
plos-pone-0003877:
Joseph Kagaayi, Ronald H. Gray, Heena Brahmbhatt, and co-authors reported on infant feeding and HIV in 2008. Their PLOS ONE study followed babies born to HIV-positive mothers in Rakai District, Uganda. Mothers could feed by breast or by formula under a local program. Data comparing the two routes in real program settings were scarce.

The team tracked 182 infants and compared death rates between the feeding groups. They also tracked how many babies stayed free of HIV. Such evidence helps programs advise mothers where both feeding routes carry risks. The study adds ground-level data from rural Uganda to a hard policy choice.
plos-pone-0003977:
Olga Björklund, Johan Kahlström, Peter Salmi, and co-authors gave caffeine to pregnant mice in 2008. Worry persists about caffeine use in pregnancy and early infancy. Early exposure might leave lasting changes in behavior. The team gave pregnant mice modest caffeine doses of 0.3 grams per liter.

Their PLOS ONE article traces the effect to receptors on the mother. Caffeine acted on maternal adenosine A1 receptors, not the pups directly. Offspring still showed long-lasting behavioral changes afterward. The result reframes how early caffeine may shape the developing brain. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004077:
Bin Zhang and Jian-xing Ma studied a protective protein in eye cells in 2008. SERPINA3K is a serpin, a protein that blocks protease enzymes. Its levels fall in the retinas of diabetic rats. That drop may contribute to diabetic retinopathy, a blinding disease.

Their PLOS ONE article reports SERPINA3K prevents oxidative necrotic cell death. It does so by inhibiting calcium overload in the cells. Calcium flooding is a final common path to cell death. A natural protector against it could inspire new eye treatments. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004177:
Ghibom Bhak and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alpha-synuclein is the protein that clumps into Lewy bodies, the deposits found in the brains of people with Parkinson's disease. Learning how it forms amyloid fibrils, long ordered protein fibres, is key to any plan to stop the disease.

The team studied how shear stress, the force of flowing or stirred liquid, affects that process. They report that the protein first gathers into granules, and that this granular assembly speeds up fibril formation under shear. The finding shows how physical forces in a cell's world can hurry a disease protein along.
plos-pone-0004277:
Michel Henry and colleagues published this hepatitis B study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepatitis B virus DNA is vulnerable to editing by human APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases. These enzymes mutate viral DNA, though HBV is edited far less than HIV. The team analysed and compared editing by all seven APOBEC3 enzymes.

Using a quail cell line that makes no APOBEC of its own, they tested single-domain versions of each enzyme against HBV. They examined the recombinant nature of APOBEC3G, the family's best-known member. Mapping which enzymes can edit HBV clarifies a natural defence the virus must dodge.
plos-pone-0004377:
People who eat less often lose weight, then stall. Leanne Redman, Leonie Heilbronn, Corby Martin, and co-authors measured why, in free-living adults. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper came from the CALERIE study of calorie cutting. Forty-eight overweight adults, average age near thirty-seven, joined for six months. They were split into four groups with different intake targets.

Earlier work had not measured daily life responses in an objective way. The team tracked both metabolic change and behavior change. Bodies can burn fewer calories than expected. Habits can also shift in ways that blunt a diet. Knowing both responses helps explain stalled weight loss. It also helps set honest targets for diet programs.
plos-pone-0004477:
Nerve cells that serve the zebrafish sense of water flow are picky about direction, show Adele Faucherre, Jesus Pujol-Marti, Koichi Kawakami, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fish sense movement in water through a line of organs along the body, called the lateral line. Their sensors are hair cells, like those in our inner ear, with tiny bristles all tipped one way.

That shared tilt lets a whole group of hair cells read motion coherently. The team found the afferent neurons, which carry signals to the brain, are strict selectors: each connects to hair cells of one orientation only. Keeping the two directions in separate channels lets the fish tell which way the water moves. The rule may hold in ears as well.
plos-pone-0004577:
Making a step look taller can make people step more safely over it, show David Elliott, Anna Vale, David Whitaker, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tripping is a common factor in falls, which injure many older people. A typical safety strategy is to lift the foot higher over a step edge.

The team asked whether a visual illusion could increase the perceived height of a step. If the step looks bigger, people may clear it with more room to spare. Their title gives the outcome: the illusion led to safer stepping behavior. A painted pattern costs almost nothing. If it prevents even a fraction of falls on stairs, it is a cheap public health tool drawn from vision science.
plos-pone-0004677:
Yong Zhang and colleagues screened for insect only microRNAs in the silkworm for a PLOS ONE study in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny bits of RNA that tune how genes are used after they are copied. They play a large part in how insects grow and change form as they mature.

The team ran a large screen in the silkworm, a moth raised for silk for ages. They hunted for microRNAs found in insects but not in other animal groups. Such finds can reveal steps that guide larva to moth change. They may also offer targets for pest control that spare other species.
plos-pone-0004777:
Michalis Aivaliotis and colleagues profiled protein phosphorylation in an archaeon from the third domain of life, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Phosphorylation is a major control tag on proteins in complex cells. Its origin and evolution are open questions, and archaea hold a lead role in that debate as a distinct, ancient domain.

Many studies show archaeal proteins do carry phosphate tags. The team mapped tags on serine, threonine, and tyrosine in a salt loving archaeon. A full map tests how old this control system is. It may show that complex regulation predates complex cells. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004877:
Núria Gavara and Richard Chadwick studied collagen based mechanical anisotropy of the tectorial membrane and hair bundle coupling, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tectorial membrane in the mammalian cochlea displays anisotropy where mechanical properties differ along directions. Anisotropy arises from collagen fibrils organized in fibers running radially across the membrane in the inner ear. Shaping how sound driven motions couple rows of outer hair cells.

Directional stiffness tunes hearing sensitivity and frequency selectivity. Collagen architecture is functional, not incidental. Defects may explain some hearing losses. Bioinspired sensors could copy the design. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004977:
The midbrain holds important dopamine neurons. They sit in the substantia nigra and the ventral tegmental area. These neurons die in Parkinson's disease. Scientists grow similar neurons in culture to study them. Dario Greco and colleagues asked how faithful those cultures are. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009.

They compared gene expression in embryonic midbrain tissue with neuronal primary cultures. The profiles show where dish-grown neurons match the real thing. They also show where the cultures drift. The comparison guides better lab models of the dopamine system. That matters for Parkinson's research, which leans heavily on such cultures.
plos-pone-0005077:
Tumors often live in low oxygen. A protein called HIF-1 alpha is their master switch for surviving it. Ekaterina Moroz and colleagues built tools to watch that switch live. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They made two chimeric reporter systems. The reporters glow as HIF-1 alpha builds up or breaks down.

Real-time imaging follows stabilization and degradation in living cells. Many factors tune this protein in cancers. Watching it live reveals how cancer cells adjust the switch. Drug hunters gain a way to see their target in action. Compounds that destabilize HIF-1 alpha become easier to find. The tools serve both basic research and screening.
plos-pone-0005177:
All living things deal with carbon dioxide, which shifts back and forth into bicarbonate in the body. That shift is slow on its own, but enzymes called carbonic anhydrases speed it up. Elleuche and Pöggeler studied the beta form of these enzymes in the fungus Sordaria macrospora in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The pair found these enzymes play a part in building the fungus fruiting bodies and in helping spores sprout. So a gas-handling enzyme also guides growth and new life in this species. The finding widens what scientists expect these common enzymes to do inside cells.
plos-pone-0005277:
Antiretroviral therapy can suppress HIV, yet many treated patients still show abnormal immune activation and low CD4 counts. Jacobson and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether other herpesviruses help explain that lingering activation.

The team explored ongoing replication of cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and the Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus in suppressed patients. These viruses are common and can flare quietly. If they drive the activation, treating them could calm the immune system and protect the CD4 cells patients still need. These other viruses hide in most adults for life. Flare when the body is weak, so they are a smart place to look when the main virus is held down yet the body still burns with low-grade fire.
plos-pone-0005377:
Climate swings repeatedly expand and shrink where species can live. Those range shifts are proposed as a major force shaping life history traits and global biodiversity. Léotard and colleagues tested the idea in an equatorial three-species symbiosis in PLOS ONE in 2009.

In a symbiosis, three species live bound together, so one partner's spread affects all. Range expansion drove the evolution of dispersal traits in their system. The case links biogeography, where species live, to the evolution of how far their young travel. Three lives bound as one are a strict test of spread, since a slow partner can hold back a fast one. And the range edge is where such checks shape what lives where.
plos-pone-0005477:
Josefin Madjidian and Åsa Lankinen studied conflict between the sexes in a plant, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Males and females of a species can want different things from mating, and that clash can drive traits to change over time. Most tests of this idea had used animals, not plants.

Their work on an annual plant looked for signs that male and female traits push against each other over generations. Plants offer a fresh test because pollen and seeds play roles unlike those in animals. What they found helps show how wide the reach of sexual conflict may be.
plos-pone-0005577:
Jiayun Lu and co-authors studied a stem cell factor called SALL4 in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. SALL4 helps embryonic stem cells stay able to become any cell type. It also plays a role in leukaemia, where stem-like cancer cells keep growing.

The team searched for proteins that work with SALL4 and found a repressor complex it uses. Through that complex, SALL4 switches off two genes, PTEN and SALL1. Switching off PTEN, a brake on growth, may be one way SALL4 keeps stem cells, and cancer cells, dividing. A factor shared by stem cells and cancer stem cells is watched closely, since blocking it must not harm healthy tissue.
plos-pone-0005677:
Devi Stuart-Fox and colleagues studied lizards split into hidden lineages in a 2009 field and lab study. Gene tests now reveal many cryptic species: groups that look alike but differ deeply in their DNA. One such zone in this study mixes two lineages where their ranges meet.

Across that hybrid zone, the team compared body traits, parasite loads, and how well males compete. They ask whether the lineages have truly parted ways in form and habit, not just in genes. The answers help explain how new species form while still looking the same. They also warn that looks alone can hide real diversity.
plos-pone-0005777:
Suzana Gispert and co-authors followed aged mice lacking PINK1 in 2009, modeling a genetic form of Parkinson's disease. Loss of PINK1, a mitochondrial protein kinase, causes a recessive variant of the disease. The team bred mice without it and watched them into old age.

The mice developed a Parkinson-like phenotype with worsening mitochondrial faults, yet without the neuron death many expected. That split is telling: failing power plants alone can disturb movement before cells die. It suggests treatment windows may open earlier than neuron loss. The study refines what PINK1 loss does over a full lifespan.
plos-pone-0005877:
Venkata Sabbisetti and co-authors found in 2009 that a guardian protein keeps cells alive partly by switching on a fat-making enzyme. The protein p63, especially its delta form, is central to skin development and to many tumors. How it promotes cell survival was only partly mapped.

The team showed p63 drives fatty acid synthase, an enzyme that builds fats cells need to grow. Survival signals and fat supply turn out to be linked. Tumors often crank up fat synthesis, so the link may matter in cancer. The study fills a gap in how a major developmental protein sustains cells.
plos-pone-0005977:
A fungal colony is a web of threads with shared inner fluid, or so it seemed. Arend van Peer, Wally Müller, Teun Boekhout and colleagues revisited that view in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the fungus Schizophyllum commune, whose threads are split into rooms by walls called septa, each pierced by a large pore.

Fluid and even cell parts can stream through open pores, making the colony act as one body. Yet the team shows the fungus can close its septa when conditions call for it. That shutter control revises the old picture of an always-open colony and suggests fungi can seal off damage or stress room by room.
plos-pone-0006077:
TB can hide inside the body for years, dormant and shrugging off drugs. Chirajyoti Deb, Chang-Muk Lee, Vinod Dubey and colleagues built a better model of that hiding state in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper subjects Mycobacterium tuberculosis to several stresses at once in the lab, mimicking the harsh spots it meets inside a host.

The stressed germs became lipid-loaded, dormant and drug-tolerant, much like hidden TB in people. A faithful model is the missing tool in the hunt for drugs that kill latent germs, the main barrier to curing TB for good. The system lets teams screen compounds against the enemy in its toughest form.
plos-pone-0006177:
Breathing illnesses have long disrupted military missions, and troops abroad face extra risk. Bryony Soltis and colleagues surveyed United States troops sent to Iraq and Afghanistan for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Close living quarters, stress, and fresh exposure to germs all raise the odds of catching a chest illness while deployed.

Troops reported their own illness episodes and symptoms, giving rates and burden that records alone had missed. Few solid data existed on this problem before the survey. The results help medical teams plan supplies, rest, and prevention for future deployments. They also show how much duty time simple infections can quietly consume.
plos-pone-0006277:
H5N1 bird flu has grown steadily more deadly in poultry, and human cases keep mounting. Hongbo Zhou and colleagues focus on the neuraminidase protein, one of the virus's surface tools, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Its stalk region varies a lot between strains and may track with virulence.

A special stalk motif is responsible for increased virulence and disease severity, the title states. Pinpointing a short pattern behind deadliness helps surveillance labs flag dangerous strains early. It also gives vaccine and drug researchers a defined feature to watch. The result links a small structural detail to a global health threat.
plos-pone-0006377:
Radiation stress rewrites the small RNA controls inside cells. Nicole Simone and colleagues measured micro RNA expression after ionising radiation in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Micro RNAs are small, conserved, non-coding RNAs that adjust protein output and regulate many processes, including stress responses.

Oxidative stress from radiation altered the micro RNA profile, per the title. Those shifts may steer how cells survive or die after exposure. Radiation is used in cancer therapy, so response markers have clinical value. Micro RNA patterns could one day predict which tumors resist treatment.
plos-pone-0006477:
Daniel Glass and colleagues measured vitamin D and skin color in the United Kingdom for PLOS ONE in 2009. Vitamin D may protect against many diseases. Public health advice urges people to avoid sun to cut skin cancer risk. But avoiding sun may also lower vitamin D, with harms of its own. The balance may differ by skin type.

The authors report low vitamin D levels in fair skin types in the United Kingdom. That result is counterintuitive, since fair skin makes vitamin D more easily. Behavior, such as staying out of the sun, may outweigh biology. The study feeds a debate on how sun advice should vary between people.
plos-pone-0006577:
James Harper, Gillian Gile, Erick James, and colleagues questioned species definitions in microbes in PLOS ONE in 2009. For the majority of microbial eukaryotes, protists and algae, there is no clearly superior species concept consistently applied. In the absence of a practical biological species concept, researchers rely on morphology, outward form. The authors argue morphology is inadequate for species and genus delineation.

Their example comes from a paramecium-related group. Form can mislead because distant relatives converge and close relatives diverge. DNA-based evidence often redraws the tree. The paper is a call to rebuild microbial taxonomy on genetic grounds.
plos-pone-0006677:
Yukari Takahashi and colleagues studied two small RNA molecules in lung cancer cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. The molecules are microRNAs named MiR-107 and MiR-185. MicroRNAs are short strands that lower gene activity. They can silence a message or trigger its breakdown. Researchers suspected these two might slow cancer cell growth.

The team tested the microRNAs in human non-small cell lung cancer cell lines. Both molecules were able to induce cell cycle arrest. Arrest means the cells stop dividing at a checkpoint. Stopping division is one way a tumor's growth can be restrained. The findings suggest these microRNAs could inform future lung cancer research and treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0006777:
Art F. Y. Poon and colleagues built a grammar-based method for parsing social network surveys in PLOS ONE in 2009. People tend to form ties with others sharing their attributes. Some attributes are ambiguous, stigmatized, or illegal. They create hidden populations whose members are hard to identify. Surveys of such groups yield messy, incomplete network data.

The authors used stochastic context-free grammars to parse that data. Grammars, borrowed from language analysis, model structured patterns with randomness. Applied to networks, they can infer likely missing structure. Better parsing improves estimates of hidden population size and links. That helps health outreach reach groups that standard surveys miss.
plos-pone-0006877:
Aylin Yilmaz and colleagues measured an HIV drug in spinal fluid in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug is raltegravir, an integrase inhibitor. It was used in patients whose virus resisted other drug classes. HIV can shelter in the central nervous system. A drug must reach that shelter to work fully.

The team measured raltegravir concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Comparing the two shows how well the drug penetrates the nervous system. Poor penetration could leave a viral reservoir untreated. Good penetration supports regimens for patients with brain involvement. The measurements guide dosing where the blood-brain barrier limits access.
plos-pone-0006977:
Cunyou Zhao, Zhiwen Xu, Feng Wang, and colleagues studied a brain receptor gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene, GABRB2, builds part of the GABA A receptor, a key calming receptor in the brain. Quiet variants in this gene had been linked to schizophrenia. Those variants also tracked with how the gene's message is cut and joined.

The team examined splicing in one region, exon ten. They catalogued new isoforms, alternate forms of the gene's product. Then they weighed links between those forms and psychotic disorders. Such splicing shifts could change how the receptor works in the brain.
plos-pone-0007077:
Nicolas Moniaux, Christophe Nemos, Shonali Deb, and colleagues studied a transcription partner protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human PAF complex travels with RNA polymerase II as it reads genes. It regulates several steps of gene expression. In yeast, its counterpart controls a set of cell-cycle genes.

The team examined one member, hPaf1, in human cells. They found it acts as a regulator of cell-cycle progression. A factor that times both gene reading and division is a natural control point. Its failure could help explain how some cells slip into uncontrolled growth.
plos-pone-0007177:
Joydeep Mukherjee, Nicole Webster, and Lyndon E. Llewellyn wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on disease in a Great Barrier Reef sponge. The sponge is Rhopaloeides odorabile. Reports of marine sponge disease were rising worldwide when the study appeared, with risks for reefs and other sea life.

The authors purify an enzyme from a sponge pathogen and describe its properties in detail. The enzyme breaks down collagen, a tough structural protein. Their work gives marine biologists a concrete agent to study when they ask how sponge infections damage their hosts. The enzyme's traits are reported from the pathogen itself, not inferred from relatives.
plos-pone-0007277:
Justin A. Green, Chau T. H. Tran, Jeremy J. Farrar, and colleagues studied a steroid treatment for tuberculous meningitis in 2009. Adding dexamethasone to treatment reduces deaths from this brain infection. How the steroid produces that benefit was not known when the study began, leaving a gap in care.

Matrix metalloproteinases drive tissue damage in many inflammatory brain diseases. The authors measure their concentrations in spinal fluid during treatment. They relate those levels to clinical outcomes. Their PLOS ONE paper tests whether calming these enzymes explains part of the steroid benefit.
plos-pone-0007377:
David Fouchet, Guillaume Leblanc, Frank Sauvage, and colleagues modeled a cat virus across fifteen populations in 2009. Feline immunodeficiency virus spreads through bites between cats. Cat density and sex ratio can strongly affect how often cats fight, and hence how often the virus transmits between individuals in a population.

The authors use dynamic stochastic modeling to estimate population risk factors. Stochastic models include chance events, which matter in small populations. They apply the method to fifteen natural cat populations. Their PLOS ONE example shows how modeling can separate real risk factors from random variation.
plos-pone-0007477:
Marianne Seney and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on African mole-rats, rodents whose societies range from solitary living to fully eusocial colonies. The naked mole-rat, the most social species, shows almost no external difference between male and female genitalia. The team compared genital anatomy across species with different social systems. They asked whether anatomy tracks how a species lives.

Across the family, genital morphology followed social structure. The more eusocial the species, the smaller the sex differences tended to be. In colonies where most animals never breed, strong sexual signals may matter less. The pattern ties mating anatomy to social organization in a measurable way. It offers a rare case where society's shape is written on the body.
plos-pone-0007577:
Inna Djagaeva and Sergey Doronkin published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how neurons grow their branches. Dendrites, the branching arms that receive signals, must form precise shapes for the brain to wire correctly. Misshapen dendrites appear in several disorders of the mind, from schizophrenia to intellectual disability. The team studied a protein complex called the COP9 signalosome in fruit fly neurons. It is part of the cell's protein-recycling machinery.

The signalosome regulates dendrite growth in two directions at once. That dual control gives the neuron both a gas pedal and a brake from one complex. Balanced control produces the arbor shapes that synapses need. When the balance fails, the wiring suffers. The study helps explain a defect shared by many brain disorders. It also shows recycling machinery moonlighting as an architect of neurons.
plos-pone-0007677:
Lasse Folkersen and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns a DNA region tied to heart disease. Large scans had linked a stretch of chromosome 9, called 9p21, to coronary artery disease. How that stretch raised risk was still unclear.

The team studied gene activity data from five different sets and tied the risk versions to changes in gene use. They also found eight new splice variants of ANRIL, a long RNA made at that site. Those variants may be a step in the path from DNA to disease.
plos-pone-0007777:
William Farrugia and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks whether metal ions help an antibody grip its target. The target, Lewis Y, is a sugar marker found on most epithelial cancers. That makes it promising for antibody-based cancer therapy.

A humanized antibody against Lewis Y had already shown encouraging safety in trials. Antibodies read sugar clusters on cell surfaces, a hard recognition task. The authors explore how metallic ions might assist that recognition. Understanding the grip at atomic level could improve antibody drugs. It could also guide the design of new ones.
plos-pone-0007877:
Timothy Dunn and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines chemical signaling inside mouse eye cells. Retinal ganglion cells carry vision signals from eye to brain. During development, activity shapes how these cells grow and connect.

A key cascade uses calcium to switch on protein kinase A, an enzyme that relays signals. The authors found the calcium-driven rise in kinase activity is mediated by several adenylate cyclases. Those enzymes make the messenger molecule cAMP. Having multiple routes to the same switch adds robustness. The finding refines how scientists picture activity-dependent development in the visual system.
plos-pone-0007977:
Leo Garcia Flores and colleagues tried a new scan for pancreatic cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease is often found too late for surgery to help. Their scan used PET/CT imaging aimed at a sugar-binding protein that shows up in tissue around the tumor.

Lighting up the tissue near the tumor, rather than the tumor alone, may make small cancers stand out sooner. Early finds raise the odds that a surgeon can remove the growth in full. The early results support more testing of this aim-at-the-neighborhood approach in people at high risk.
plos-pone-0008077:
Gilles Guerrier and colleagues counted hunger and death among war-torn families in eastern Chad for PLOS ONE in 2009. Violence had driven more than two hundred thousand people from their homes in three years. Some lived in camps, others in villages or towns, displaced and host families side by side.

Surveys weighed children and gathered death records in each setting. Malnutrition and death rates told a grim, uneven story across the three kinds of place. Relief teams can use such maps to send food and care where the need is worst, rather than where access is easiest.
plos-pone-0008177:
Till Steiner, Yaochu Jin, and Bernhard Sendhoff presented a new computing method in PLOS ONE in 2009 called vector field embryogeny. The work deals with artificial embryogenies, computer systems that grow forms in steps like an embryo. Most such systems rely on maps of gene networks. Their method skips those maps entirely.

Instead, the approach shapes the flow of the system itself, known as its phase space. The authors showed the idea works by evolving cell differentiation, where cells take on distinct roles. Growing patterns emerged from the shaped flow. The result points to a fresh route for evolving complex forms in the computer.
plos-pone-0008277:
Takumi Kayukawa and Yukio Ishikawa studied cold hardiness in an insect in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The onion maggot, Delia antiqua, survives winter as a pupa. Pupae in winter diapause show strong cold hardiness. So do pupae acclimated to cold outside diapause. The team investigated which genes switch on during this hardening.

They linked a chaperonin protein to the insect's cold tolerance. The protein works by repressing the breakdown of actin at low temperatures. Actin gives cells their structure, so protecting it protects the cell. The finding explains one mechanism behind insect survival in winter.
plos-pone-0008377:
Wendy W. Hwang-Verslues and colleagues profiled breast cancer stem cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Cancer stem and progenitor cells can give rise to different forms of cancer. That heterogeneity was well shown in leukemia. For solid tumors, including breast cancer, the concept was not yet established. The team analyzed solid tumor cells using stem cell markers.

Profiling revealed multiple lineages of human breast cancer stem and progenitor cells. Distinct lineages could explain why breast cancers behave so differently. They might also respond differently to treatment. Identifying them is a step toward targeted therapy.
plos-pone-0008477:
Matthew Hemming and co-authors hunt for targets of an enzyme in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme is BACE1, also called beta-secretase. It cuts proteins near cell membranes and sheds their outer parts. BACE1 is best known for its role in Alzheimer disease. It makes the first cut that leads to amyloid buildup. But it likely cuts many other proteins too.

Using quantitative proteomics, the team list proteins cut by BACE1. Proteomics measures many proteins at once with high precision. A fuller target list helps explain what the enzyme does in health. It also warns what blocking it might disrupt in treatment.
plos-pone-0008577:
Viswanathan Palanisamy and co-authors study tiny vesicles in human saliva in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The vesicles are called exosomes. Cells release them, and they carry proteins and RNA to other cells. They occur in most body fluids, including milk, blood, and urine. Saliva exosomes had not been mapped in detail. The team collect them and study their structure at nano scale.

They also list the RNA and protein cargo the vesicles carry. That catalog shows what messages saliva exosomes could deliver. Such vesicles may serve as markers of oral and body health. They could one day carry drugs as natural delivery packets.
plos-pone-0008677:
Daniel Costa, Patrick Robinson, John Arnould, and colleagues tackled a tracking problem in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Biologists often follow seals and sea lions with ARGOS satellite tags. The tags report where an animal is, but each fix carries some error. Knowing the size of that error matters for any claim about travel or feeding.

The team compared ARGOS fixes with Fastloc GPS readings taken at the same time. GPS served as the trusted yardstick for animals swimming at sea. Their checks show how far off a satellite fix can be. Wildlife researchers can use those numbers to judge how much trust a track deserves.
plos-pone-0008777:
Victoria Gonzalo, Juan José Lozano, Jenifer Muñoz, and colleagues linked chemical tags on DNA to multiple colon tumors. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most cases of several separate colorectal cancers trace to inherited syndromes. Sporadic cases, with no family syndrome, were less understood. Faulty methylation tags near gene switches can silence protective genes. That silencing drives many colon cancers.
