The team compared tag patterns in patients with multiple tumors and controls. Certain promoters carried abnormal tags again and again. Those patterns may flag people who need closer screening. Finding them clarifies how sporadic multiplicity arises.
plos-pone-0008877:
Benjamin Groves, Hilde Abrahamsen, Heather Clingan, and colleagues found a brake on the cell's self-eating system. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Macroautophagy lets cells wrap and recycle their own worn parts. The mTOR pathway is one of its main drivers. Faulty control of this recycling links to cancer and brain diseases. A G-protein regulator called AGS3 was the suspect brake.

Raising AGS3 levels slowed the mTOR-driven recycling in their tests. The protein thus works against, not for, this cleanup route. A mapped brake helps explain how cells pace their recycling. It may also offer a handle for drugs in recycling-linked diseases.
plos-pone-0008977:
Arantza Rico and co-authors warned plant scientists about a side effect of a routine lab trick, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The trick, agroinfiltration, uses Agrobacterium bacteria to slip genes into tobacco leaves. Researchers use it to test plant genes quickly, including genes for fighting disease. The study used the tobacco species Nicotiana tabacum.

Leaves treated with the bacteria ended up with lower levels of the hormone ABA. The treatment also blunted salicylic acid, a defence signal plants raise against Pseudomonas bacteria. So the test method itself dampens the very defences researchers want to study. Anyone using the trick must allow for that hidden effect.
plos-pone-0009077:
Nigel Wood and co-authors gave enriched cages to mice bred with Huntington's disease and watched who benefited, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enriched housing means bigger cages with toys, tunnels, and chances to explore. Such housing improves brain function in lab animals and has been proposed as therapy. The R6/2 mouse is the standard model of Huntington's.

Benefits from enrichment were not the same for every mouse. Males and females responded differently to the livelier cages. The animals' exact genetic makeup also shaped the effect. A one-size therapy may fit poorly if sex and genotype steer the gains.
plos-pone-0009177:
Jeffrey H. Schwartz and colleagues published this archaeology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It asks a heated question about ancient Carthage, the Phoenician city in North Africa. Old accounts claimed the Carthaginians routinely killed infants as religious offerings. The authors tested that claim against the bones themselves.

Carthage had two kinds of burial ground. One held older children and adults, while the other, called the Tophet, held urns of cremated infant remains. By studying the ages and remains in those urns, the team judged whether the pattern fit sacrifice or natural infant death. Their answer was no: the remains do not support systematic sacrifice of infants.
plos-pone-0009277:
João Pedro Pereira, Jason Cyster, and Ying Xu published this immune cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Young B cells are born in the bone marrow, then leave to patrol the body. A fat-like signal called S1P guides older B cells out of lymph organs. Whether it also drives the first exit from the marrow was not fully known.

Using mice that lack S1P or its receptor S1P1 in set conditions, the team tested that exit step. They report a role for both the signal and its receptor in immature B cell egress. Completing that picture matters because B cell traffic shapes the whole antibody defense.
plos-pone-0009377:
Bernd Fritzsch and co-authors published this mouse ear study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene Prox1 helps build the lens, retina, pancreas, liver, and lymph vessels. It is also active in the inner ear's support cells and neurons. What exactly it does in the ear was the team's question.

Using standard and conditional mouse mutants, they removed Prox1 activity in the developing ear. Growth of the balance canals' cristae then faltered. Nerve fibers also failed to extend properly to the outer hair cells of hearing. The study shows one gene coordinating both the ear's balance and hearing wiring.
plos-pone-0009477:
Mara Marongiu and colleagues studied a protein that guides ovary growth in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein is FOXL2. Faults in it cause a syndrome with eyelid defects and can lead to early ovarian failure. The team found that FOXL2 gets tagged with small proteins called SUMO. This happens in both human and mouse cells.

The tagging changed how stable the protein is. It also changed where the protein sits in the cell and how well it works. So a small tag acts as a control dial on a key protein. Faults in that control could add to the diseases tied to FOXL2.
plos-pone-0009577:
Mirko Zimic and co-authors built a low cost microscope for tuberculosis work in PLOS ONE in 2010. Finding TB early saves lives, but many clinics in poor regions lack good equipment. One culture method, called MODS, grows the germ so it can be seen under a microscope. Inverted microscopes for that job are costly. The team designed a cheaper version for the task.

Their device lets lab staff spot the germ's early growth in culture. Lower cost puts the test within reach of more clinics. Faster diagnosis means faster treatment and fewer new infections. The paper is a piece of practical engineering aimed at a deadly, widespread disease.
plos-pone-0009677:
Jeremy Lundholm and co-authors tested plant mixes for green roofs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Green roofs cover buildings with living plants. They cool the building, soak up rain, and shelter urban wildlife. Not every plant mix does those jobs equally well. The team grew roofs with varied species and functional group combinations. They measured how each mix performed key ecosystem functions.

Certain combinations of species and groups outperformed others across several functions. Diversity in plant type, not just in species count, drove much of the gain. The results give planners an evidence based planting guide. Better mixes mean roofs that cool more, drain better, and support more life.
plos-pone-0009877:
Broken DNA strands are among the most dangerous injuries a cell can suffer. Donghong Ju and colleagues studied a repair pathway and a protein that must be cleared for it to work. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The repair route is nonhomologous end-joining, which glues broken ends back together. The protein is Rpn4, normally destroyed by the proteasome, the cell's disposal machine. When that degradation was inhibited, end-joining repair of double-strand breaks suffered. The result shows timing of protein cleanup matters for genome safety. Double-strand breaks can kill a cell if left unrepaired.
plos-pone-0009977:
PAX3 is a gene that helps build pigment cells early in life and stays active in adult skin. Sandra Medic and Mel Ziman mapped where it appears in normal skin and in moles and melanomas. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Melanocytes are the pigment-making cells of the skin. Melanocytic lesions include naevi, common moles, and melanomas, the dangerous skin cancers. Comparing PAX3 expression across all three shows where the gene switches behavior. Such maps help separate harmless moles from cancers. Skin color comes from melanin made by these cells.
plos-pone-0010177:
The authors were Shinsuke Ohnuki, Satomi Oka, Satoru Nogami, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study screened drug effects in yeast using images. Drug discovery depends on learning what a compound does inside cells and what it targets. New imaging tools can record many cell events at once, in fine detail and at large scale.

The team built a high-content, image-based screen to find drug targets in yeast. Yeast is cheap, fast, and shares much core biology with human cells. A screen that reads cell pictures can flag promising compounds and their targets early, before costly animal work.
plos-pone-0010377:
Daniel Weiller, Robert Märtin and Sven Dähne argued that movement should shape how senses encode space, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sensory systems aim to capture what matters for behavior. What matters depends on what an animal or robot can actually do. A sense that ignores its owner's abilities may waste effort on useless detail. The authors built that idea into a learning model.

In their setup, representations of sensory space formed with motor limits in mind. The resulting codes differed from those learned by senses alone. This matters for robotics, where cameras and limbs are designed separately too often. It also matters for brain theory, since bodies and senses evolved together. The paper asks designers to start from the whole agent, not the sensor.
plos-pone-0010477:
Jing Jie Yu and colleagues examined eye tumors in HIV patients in East Africa for PLOS ONE in 2010. Squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva, the eye's surface, had grown much more common there alongside HIV. Its behavior in that region seems distinct from elsewhere. Causes were suspected to involve both human papillomavirus and a growth receptor called EGFR. The team tested tumor samples for both factors.

Sorting out which drivers act in these tumors guides treatment choices. EGFR can be targeted by existing cancer drugs in some settings. HPV involvement would raise questions about prevention. The study serves a patient group often left out of cancer research. It also shows how infection and cancer intertwine in the HIV era.
plos-pone-0010577:
Jiabing Ji and Janet Braam introduced a new laboratory method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Geneticists often insert a known tag into DNA, then need to read the unknown DNA next to it. Finding that neighboring stretch has usually been slow and unreliable.

Their method, called restriction site extension PCR, reads outward from the tag in a more direct way. Tests showed it could recover flanking DNA quickly and in larger numbers than older approaches. A faster route from a tag to a full gene should help researchers link mutations to the traits they cause.
plos-pone-0010677:
Mark Littler, Diane Littler, and Barrett Brooks surveyed seaweeds on Saba Bank, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bank is a flat-topped seamount in the Dutch Windward Islands, twenty to forty-five meters deep in its shallow parts. Its plant life was among the least known parts of its reef system.

The team collected and named macroalgae across the bank's habitats. Many records were new for the area, and the flora proved richer than expected for a single seamount. Seaweeds feed and shelter much reef life, yet surveys often skip them. A full plant list makes the bank's living wealth harder to overlook in protection plans.
plos-pone-0010777:
Nuria Andreu and colleagues tuned glowing reporter systems for tuberculosis research, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycobacteria that make their own light let scientists follow infection without killing the animal or germ at each check. Standard light-making systems worked poorly in these waxy-coated bacteria, so the signal needed work.

The team tested several luciferase systems and adjusted how they are expressed. The best setups shone brightly and stayed stable in mycobacteria. Glowing germs can be counted quickly in drug and vaccine tests. A brighter, steadier signal shortens experiments and reduces the number of animals that long infection studies require.
plos-pone-0010877:
Timo Homeier, Torsten Semmler, Lothar Wieler and co-authors published this bacterial evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some E. coli strains leave the gut and cause disease in the brain, bladder, or blood, in both people and birds. A stretch of DNA called GimA, carrying an invasion gene, helps some of them enter brain lining cells.

The team screened hundreds of isolates from patients, animals, feces, and a reference collection for the GimA island. Alongside the full island and its complete absence, they found a third pattern: a short remnant, as if the island had been partly deleted. The full island appeared almost only in certain family lines of the bacterium. Homeier and colleagues use this patchy record to ask whether losing DNA tracks where a strain lives and what disease it causes.
plos-pone-0010977:
Patricia Guillaumot, Céline Luquain, Mouhannad Malek and co-authors published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cholesterol is vital in cell membranes, and its level is tightly controlled by mechanisms that are still partly unknown. Screening a special membrane fraction, the authors identified an uncharacterized protein and named it Pdro.

The protein sits mainly on late endosomes and lysosomes, the cell's sorting and recycling stations, anchored by fatty tags at one end. Changing its amount changed the cell's free cholesterol content. Guillaumot and colleagues also note that other groups found the same protein under different names, tied to cell movement machinery and lysosome control. Pdro emerges as a new handle on cholesterol balance, relevant to diseases from heart disease to rare storage disorders.
plos-pone-0011077:
Yeh, Xie, Langdon and colleagues reported a mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used mice bred to make extra amounts of a protein that triggers histamine release. Histamine drives many allergy symptoms, so the team wanted to see what too much of this factor does across the body.

By tracking the bred mice, the team charted wide effects linked to the extra protein. Their results help show how one immune factor can shape allergy and swelling in many tissues. The work gives later studies a clear animal model to test. It may also point toward treatments that calm an overactive immune response.
plos-pone-0011177:
Levi, James, Nelson and colleagues used fat derived cells to heal skull bone in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fat tissue holds stromal cells that can form other tissues. The team placed human cells of this kind into large skull defects in mice, wounds too big to heal on their own.

The human cells healed those critical defects by forming new bone. Using a patient's own fat as a source would ease supply and rejection worries. Skull repair after injury or surgery is a real clinical need. The result brings fat to bone repair closer to practical testing in people.
plos-pone-0011277:
Bergstedt, Tingskov, Thierry-Carstensen and colleagues ran a first human trial in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tuberculosis skin tests are old and often unclear, since prior BCG vaccination confuses results. The team tested a new reagent combining two proteins specific to the TB germ in volunteers for the first time.

A specific skin test could catch TB sooner and sort true infection from vaccine effects. That distinction matters in countries where BCG is routine. The trial checks safety and response as first steps toward clinic use. Better detection helps curb spread by finding infectious people earlier.
plos-pone-0011377:
Shuqi Xiao and co-authors read the full gene response of pig lungs infected with PRRSV in 2010. The virus causes a costly reproductive and lung disease in pigs worldwide, and vaccines control it poorly. Using deep sequencing, the team recorded which lung genes switched on or off across the whole genome during infection.

The response map revealed broad changes in immune and tissue genes as the virus took hold in the lung. Patterns in that map point to pathways the virus provokes or evades, and to stages where treatment might help most. Veterinarians and breeders gain a resource for picking drug targets and for breeding pigs that resist infection better. The study also shows how one deep sequencing run can replace years of gene-by-gene work in farm animal disease.
plos-pone-0011477:
Johan Lorenzen and co-authors followed kidney patients over time in 2010 to test whether repair cells in the blood predict heart trouble. Chronic kidney disease greatly raises the risk of heart attacks and strokes, beyond what standard risk factors explain. Endothelial progenitor cells, which help repair vessel linings, circulate in the blood and can be counted at a clinic visit.

The prospective study measured those cells and then tracked who suffered cardiovascular events during follow-up. Testing the idea prospectively, with the count taken before events occur, is what separates a real warning sign from hindsight. If repair cell counts forecast events, nephrologists gain an early-warning readout to guide closer monitoring and earlier treatment. The study design itself is the point: kidney patients need predictors proven by waiting and watching, not by looking backward.
plos-pone-0011577:
Thierry Chaminade and co-authors scanned people's brains in 2010 as they watched a humanoid robot move. Robots built like people are entering homes and hospitals, and designers need to know whether human social brains treat them as people. The team measured brain responses to the robot in the areas that read human emotional gestures, the movements by which people read feelings.

The neural verdict was mixed in an informative way: some social circuits answered the machine much as they answer a person, while others held back. That split predicts where human-robot interaction will feel natural and where it will feel eerie. Gesture designers can aim at the circuits that accept the machine, rather than polishing appearance blindly. The study also serves basic science, using the robot as a controlled, repeatable almost-person to probe how gesture perception is built.
plos-pone-0011677:
James Hadler and co-authors estimated how deadly the 2009 pandemic flu was in New York City, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Judging a new pandemic strain's severity quickly is vital for planning the response. A novel H1N1 virus was recognised in late April 2009, and the city saw an intense first outbreak peaking in late May.

Instead of counting only confirmed cases, the team used population estimates of flu-like illness from May and June. Dividing deaths by that fuller total gave more realistic fatality rates. Their accounting gave officials a truer sense of the virus's toll while the pandemic was still unfolding.
plos-pone-0011777:
Michael TeKippe and Alejandro Aballay compared immune defences in sterile worms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Making eggs and sperm costs resources that cannot then be spent on other trials. In the worm C. elegans, growing a germline cuts lifespan and raises the odds of falling to germs, so worms that lack a germline are oddly hardy.

The team infected germline-free mutants and mapped their response tools. The mutants used a mix of defences shared with normal worms and tools distinct to their state. That split lays bare the hidden immune cost of breeding in plain terms.
plos-pone-0011877:
James Boyd, Eric Oldenburg, and Geoffrey McMichael built in 2010 a color photo guide to how fall Chinook salmon embryos develop. Development speed in fish eggs depends strongly on temperature, summed as accumulated thermal units. Knowing the link lets biologists estimate when eggs in a natural gravel nest were fertilized.

Few staged photo references existed, so the team paired pictures of each embryo stage with the thermal units reached by then. A shared visual scale helps hatchery staff and field crews judge embryo age the same way. For wild salmon, better aging of eggs sharpens estimates of spawning time, which feed into river management and protection plans.
plos-pone-0011977:
Robert Glaser and Mark Meola reported in 2010 that a bacterium living inside insects helps them resist West Nile virus. Wolbachia is a widespread insect endosymbiont already known to raise virus resistance in fruit flies and in mosquitoes that do not normally carry it. The question was whether native Wolbachia does the same in its natural hosts.

In both Drosophila melanogaster and the mosquito Culex quinquefasciatus, hosts carrying their native Wolbachia resisted West Nile infection better. Culex mosquitoes spread the virus to people, so a natural resistance factor in them is more than a curiosity. It supports strategies that use Wolbachia to make mosquito populations poorer virus carriers.
plos-pone-0012077:
Maria Danoviz and co-workers tried in 2010 fat-based stem cells as a mending crew for hearts hurt by a heart attack, in rats. Heart cell grafts face a blunt flaw: most cells put in wash out or die in days. The team drew stem cells from rat fat, an easy source, and asked if soft gel-like helpers called biopolymers could keep more of the cells in place.

Put in with the gels, more cells stayed put, and the hurt hearts worked better than those of rats left with the harm alone. Heart shape and pump strength both moved the right way. A cheap, rich cell source joined to a stay-put trick meets the two big blocks at once, and points to heart mending built from a patient's own fat.
plos-pone-0012177:
Daniel Vilceanu and Cheryl Stucky investigated how mouse sensory neurons feel mechanical force, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Touch, pressure, and pain from squeezing or stretching all begin when force opens special channels in nerve endings. Which channel carries the main current in these neurons was still unknown, and one candidate was a channel already known for sensing irritating chemicals and cold.

They recorded the electrical currents that flow when sensory neurons are physically pushed, testing that candidate's role. Their measurements tie the candidate channel to part of the force response. Knowing the true touch sensors matters for treating pain where normal touch hurts, a problem current painkillers handle poorly.
plos-pone-0012277:
Hans Lomholt and Mogens Kilian sorted the acne bacterium's family tree in PLOS ONE in 2010. Propionibacterium acnes lives on nearly everyone's skin, sick and healthy alike, which long made its role in acne doubtful. The authors tested a sharper idea: only certain lineages of the species cause trouble, while their cousins live peacefully on clear skin.

Their population analysis found a distinct subpopulation and epidemic clones tied to acne. If the disease belongs to particular strains, treatment can aim at them instead of carpet-bombing the skin's whole community. It also explains decades of confusing results in which the same species seemed both guilty and innocent.
plos-pone-0012377:
Nathalie Stroeymeyt, Fernando Guerrieri, Jelle van Zweden and colleagues watched ants make fast choices in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Animals often must choose quickly, trading accuracy for speed when danger or hunger presses. Ants face such choices when picking a new nest or a food route, and each side of the body gathers its own clues.

The researchers tracked how ants weigh clues seen on each side when they judge a path. The ants combined the clues fast and still chose well, showing a neat way to beat the speed-accuracy trade-off. Their method may inspire designs for robot swarms and other systems that must decide well under time pressure.
plos-pone-0012477:
Claudia Hoffmann, Marlies Galle, Sabrina Dilling and colleagues studied how Salmonella triggers an inflammatory alarm in macrophages, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Macrophages are immune cells that eat invaders; when Salmonella injects proteins through its needle-like secretion system, the cell fires caspase-1, an enzyme that launches inflammation. A bacterial whip protein, flagellin, was thought to be required for that alarm.

The team showed the alarm can fire without flagellin when the bacterial effector SopE and the secretion system are at work. Redundant triggers make the alarm hard for bacteria to evade. Understanding the wiring helps explain severe Salmonella inflammation and may guide anti-inflammatory strategies.
plos-pone-0012577:
Delia Goletti, Alamelu Raja, Basirudeen Kabeer and colleagues tested a new TB marker in people living with HIV, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Standard TB blood tests rely on interferon gamma and lose sensitivity in people with weakened immunity, exactly the group most at risk of TB. An alternative marker, IP-10, is released in larger amounts and might read more reliably.

The team assessed whether IP-10 accurately detects the TB-specific immune response in HIV-infected persons. A dependable test for this group would close a dangerous diagnostic gap, since TB is a leading killer of people with HIV. Their evaluation informs which assays clinics should adopt for co-infected patients.
plos-pone-0012677:
Hilimire, Mounts, Parks and co-authors used scalp recordings to separate two forces that guide visual attention. Attention boosts what matters and filters the rest, but two ideas compete to explain it. One stresses how much an item stands out, the other where it sits in space.

Their 2010 brain-wave study timed the responses to tease those forces apart. The signals showed salience and space acting at different moments. Settling how attention splits its work helps explain disorders where focus fails, and sharpens basic vision science. Such timing work is hard to get from behaviour tests alone.
plos-pone-0012777:
Glasser, Taneri, Feng and co-authors used population models to compare targeted flu vaccination plans. Mathematical models suit this task because rival plans can be run on the same virtual population. Their 2010 study insisted the models be checked for credibility before their rankings are trusted.

They tested strategies that aim vaccine at different age or risk groups. Which group to favour depends on whether the goal is fewer deaths, fewer cases, or keeping schools and hospitals running. Their framework helps officials match a flu plan to a stated goal.  Several flu seasons of spread informed the model runs.
plos-pone-0012877:
Silveira, Barlow, Louzada and co-authors counted leaf-litter insects in Amazon forests with different fire histories. Fire is used across the Amazon to clear land for cattle and crops, and those fires often escape into nearby forest. Their 2010 study compared unburned forest with forest burned three times in seasonally dry areas.

They measured which factors set the abundance of arthropods living in fallen leaves. Leaf litter animals drive soil health and feed many larger species. Knowing how repeated fire thins them helps judge the true cost of escaped burns.
plos-pone-0319877:
Shengying Wan and colleagues measured the fruits of camphor trees from eleven source populations across Jiangxi Province, China, to map how much the species varies. One hundred seventy trees were scored on ten fruit traits, from size ratios to peel thickness and seed weight. Camphor is an economically important tree, and breeders need to know where the useful variation lives.

Nearly three-quarters of the variation sat between populations rather than within them, meaning the source stand matters more than the individual tree. Diversity scores were high overall, and peel thickness varied the most of any trait. For selecting superior planting stock, the message is to sample widely across provenances, since each holds a distinct slice of the species' variation.
plos-pone-0327077:
Meng-Jung Lin asked whether the body's molecular age clocks change how well older adults weather marriage's upheavals, such as widowhood or divorce. Using a large American retirement study of more than sixteen hundred older white adults. The team combined thirteen DNA-based ageing clocks with records of marital transitions, depressive symptoms, and death. They adjusted for genetic and social background.

Marital change itself tracked with more depressive symptoms but not, directly, with higher death risk, and it barely touched the clocks. The interesting action sat in the combinations: for death risk, several clocks significantly altered how transitions played out, mostly among men, with biologically older men paradoxically showing more resilience. Lin suggests the clocks may capture a lifetime's accumulated adaptation, not just wear, and calls the resilience reading a hypothesis worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0327277:
Abigail Kusi-Amponsah Diji and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE on outpatient care at a Ghanaian university hospital. Fragmented services and rotating doctors there break the bond between patients and providers. Twenty-eight people, clinicians and care recipients at the hospital in Kumasi, were interviewed in depth about the current system and a proposed Family Practice Model. That model would give each patient a dedicated doctor.

Two themes captured the mood. Participants described the present system as therapeutic disconnection: impersonal, rushed consultations, poor records, and never seeing the same provider twice, all eroding trust. Against that stood the wish summed up in the second theme, a doctor to call my own. Stakeholders backed a relationship-based model promising continuity, smoother processes, and long-term connection. The model, they conclude, could transform outpatient care and, by strengthening primary care, help Ghana toward universal health coverage.
plos-pone-0337677:
Tomohiro Udagawa and co-authors grow miniature kidney filters in a dish to test whether injury to some filtering cells spreads to their untouched neighbors. These podocyte cells wrap the kidney's filters, and their loss drives chronic kidney disease. The team mixed two mouse cell lines into mosaic organoids, one line vulnerable to a targeted toxin and one tagged and safe, then poisoned only the vulnerable cells.

Targeted cells were injured as intended, and their safe neighbors inside the same tiny filter also weakened, losing a key protein and quieting their identity genes. When the two organoid types grew side by side in separate clusters, no spread occurred. Udagawa and colleagues conclude the damage passes by direct contact within a shared filter, a mechanism that could help explain how kidney disease advances.
plos-pone-0338277:
Testing a patient's genes before prescribing can prevent bad drug reactions, but health systems ask whether the tests pay for themselves. Taichi Ochi and colleagues gathered seventeen earlier systematic reviews on that question into one umbrella review, published in PLOS One in 2026.

Searches across three databases, with a fresh update in 2025, fed the summary, and each review's quality was graded with a standard checklist. As the number of studies has grown, the balance of evidence has leaned toward the tests being worth their cost in several drug areas. The authors say cost questions should no longer block careful rollout where guidelines already support testing.
plos-pone-0342577:
Yutaro Nishikata and colleagues fed cholesterol-rich food to rats bred to have high blood pressure and strokes, and got a counterintuitive result. Cholesterol is normally a villain in heart disease, yet earlier reports said these rats lived longer on such a diet. Three groups of young rats ate plain food, cholesterol-enriched food, or the same diet plus a drug that blocks the body's own cholesterol making, for twelve weeks.

The cholesterol-fed rats ended with blood pressure about a tenth lower than controls, alongside wide changes in tissue fats, including plant sterols and lower levels of a fat linked to inflammation. Kidney tissue was also checked for damage. The rat paradox will not rewrite diet advice for people, but it shows cholesterol's effects depend heavily on context.
plos-pone-0343577:
Francisco Chamera and five colleagues work out how much fishing the catfish of Lake Malawi can bear, in this 2026 study of the lake's southeast arm. Catfish support a valuable commercial fishery, but effort has grown for decades. Using catch and effort records stretching back to the start of the century, the team applied a classic bioeconomic model that weighs stock growth against costs and prices.

Their analysis shows the stock survives only if yearly effort stays below a clear ceiling. The most profitable sustainable level sits far below current effort, at only a few hundred trips a year. Observed fishing far exceeds that level. The authors recommend deliberate cuts in effort so the fishery keeps producing both income and fish over the long term, rather than mining the stock down.
plos-pone-0346077:
Erica Christensen and colleagues tackle chronic wasting disease in this 2026 PLOS ONE wildlife study. The fatal prion disease spreads among deer through contact and through contaminated ground. The team followed mule deer fitted with GPS collars across Wyoming and tested them each year. It then modeled which landscape features raised the yearly chance of infection.

Deer favored spots near secondary roads, and those same spots carried higher disease risk, linking risk to how deer use the land. Risk also rose where the terrain collects moisture, even though deer did not prefer those areas, which points to prions lasting longer in damp ground. The findings aim to help managers target testing and disease control.
plos-pone-0346777:
Yingquan Ao and seven colleagues published this optics study in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rather than building a device, they used computer modeling to test a light filter made from stacked graphene sheets separated by thin insulating layers. The spacing between the layers changes gradually along the stack, a pattern called a chirped grating.

Their simulations show the stack lets longer wavelengths of light pass while blocking shorter ones, acting as a low-pass filter. The cutoff point and the width of the passing band can be adjusted by changing the number of layers, the spacing gradient, or the electrical state of the graphene. The authors suggest uses in spectral scanning and adaptive optics.
plos-pone-0347777:
Angelina Sutin and colleagues surveyed nearly two thousand adults on their sense of purpose in life and the strategies they use to handle stress. People with a strong sense of purpose tend to feel less stress, and the team tested whether better coping explains part of that link. Depression, anxiety, and current stress levels were also measured.

Purpose came with more active coping and more seeking of support, and with slightly less giving-up coping. Those ties looked much the same across age, sex, race, and education. One wrinkle mattered: among people currently in distress, purpose was linked to more disengaged coping, not less. The results caution against one-size advice, since coping habits seem to change under strain.
plos-pone-0347877:
Sabrina Harris and colleagues report a rare bright spot in climate change biology, from a gentoo penguin colony at Martillo Island, Argentina, near the species' northern limit. A time-lapse camera watched the colony from 2013 to 2024. Heat is dangerous for cold-adapted penguins, and the record includes chicks dying within the hour on a day that hit twenty-four degrees.

Across the study years the penguins advanced their breeding season by about two days each year. Breeding earlier means chicks fledge before the worst summer heat, cutting the number of dangerously hot days they endure. The authors are careful: hotter futures may overwhelm this shift. For now, a warming-driven change is shielding chicks instead of exposing them.
plos-pone-0348077:
Md Mafizer Rahman and colleagues built a maths model of dengue fever in Bangladesh that treats medical care as a moving part, not an afterthought. Many models assume everyone recovers alike, but their version separates people who recover on their own from those whose recovery depends on treatment. It also lets mosquito biting rise and fall with temperature. They fitted the model to case and weather data from each division of the country.

Where treatment was scarce, outbreaks peaked far higher, while prompt supportive care blunted epidemics even when transmission ran hot. Forecasts singled out metropolitan Dhaka as both a hotspot and the place where better treatment access would matter most. The authors offer the framework to other low-resource settings planning for seasonal surges.
plos-pone-0348177:
Xiuyu Tang and colleagues test how to keep small dental tools clean between patients in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. Reusable burs and flexible root-canal files must be cleaned before sterilizing, and keeping them moist after use stops debris from drying on. The team compared plain water, an enzyme cleaner, and a professional transport gel.

Instruments went through four rounds of use and reprocessing, then were checked under microscopes and with a test that detects leftover biological residue, plus surface imaging for wear and contamination. The professional moisturizer produced the cleanest instruments. The results give dental clinics practical guidance on a step that affects both patient safety and how long delicate tools last.
plos-pone-0348277:
Ayla Ahmed and co-workers study how smoke from home cooking fires relates to severe pneumonia in young Ugandan children. Pneumonia with low blood oxygen is a leading killer of children under five. Their 2026 study reviews cases at twenty hospitals, covering more than seven hundred children, and estimates each child's exposure from fuel type, cooking time, kitchen shape, and airflow.

Nearly every child lived with fine particle levels far above the world health limit. Higher exposure went with more breathing trouble, lower oxygen on arrival, longer oxygen treatment, and worse severity scores. Eye and nose irritation also rose with exposure. The links strengthen the case for cleaner stoves and better home ventilation in Uganda.
plos-pone-0348377:
Antje Lorenz and Elisabeth Beyersmann ran word-recognition experiments on how German speakers process compound nouns, words built from two nouns like water bottle. In German every noun carries a grammatical gender, and a compound takes the gender of its second part, its head. The question was whether the first part's gender also wakes up in the mind during reading.

Volunteers judged words flashed on a screen, preceded by the German word for the, matched either to the head's gender, the first part's gender, or neither. Primes matching the head sped recognition in both experiments; primes matching the first part did nothing. Minds, it seems, store the head's gender as the compound's own and let the modifier's gender sleep.
plos-pone-0348577:
Youssef El Khatib and Farangiz Mukhamedova propose a different goal for building investment portfolios, one that punishes wobble directly instead of rewarding return per unit of risk. Classic methods chase the best ratio of gain to volatility, which can still leave investors with deep drops. Their formula rewards expected return while dividing by portfolio volatility in a way that favours calm paths, and it stays inside mainstream preference theory.

In rolling tests on standard stock portfolios, with trading costs and no short selling allowed, the method produced clearly calmer results and shallower worst drops than the classic benchmark. Its average performance stayed in line with simpler strategies. The advantage held through the financial crisis, the pandemic crash, and the twenty twenty-two rate shock. The authors offer it to investors who value a smooth ride.
plos-pone-0348677:
Mohamed Metwaly and Abdullah Alshami map where ancient people likely settled around Al-Madinah in Arabia and which caravan routes fed the oasis city once called Yathrib. Their 2026 study scores the land with six factors, from slope to distance from water channels, then computes the cheapest walking paths toward major old sites and a coastal port.

Nearly a third of the study area rated highly suitable for settlement. Water access, gentle slope, and soil type governed the pattern most. Modeled routes matched known historical trade stations well when checked. The method can be reused across dry lands to predict where ruins wait and how goods once moved between desert wells.
plos-pone-0348777:
Ali M Alshhre reads sixty Saudi proverbs about women as a small archive of home life and nature. Proverbs come from the Saudi National Encyclopaedia regional records. Many use bread, heat, pots, pests, kohl, and henna to talk about mothers, wives, and home duty. Close reading joins feminist tools with attention to things and the living world.

Praise often hides a price. Sayings that honour mothers and home builders also lock women into heavy work and blame. Warning sayings police where women go, how they look, and how much freedom they claim, using images of want, risk, and loss. Everyday speech, the author shows, quietly governs gender through the language of the home.
plos-pone-0348877:
Nobukazu Nameki and co-authors solved the structure of a mouse protein piece bound to ubiquitin in 2026. The piece comes from proteins that help clear ribosomes stuck on faulty messages, a cleanup job vital to healthy cells, but its grip on ubiquitin was only guessed.

Using nuclear magnetic resonance, the team mapped the three helix bundle and its contact with ubiquitin's sticky patch, finding a grip much like that of known ubiquitin readers. One loop, though, had a distinctive double turn found in no close cousin. The detail refines ideas about how stuck ribosome cleanup crews recognise their targets.
plos-pone-0349377:
Wilson Castro and colleagues tested whether the electrical behavior of chicken breast meat can reveal its quality grade without cutting or tasting it. Ninety-six samples of Creole chicken were classed by acidity into the standard three grades: pale and soft, normal, and dark and dry. The team then swept the meat with radio-frequency signals and recorded how it stored and absorbed the energy.

The electrical spectra differed by grade, most clearly at low frequencies, where the dark, dry grade stood apart, and modeling separated two relaxation processes with grade-specific timing. Only three samples fell in the palest grade, so the authors call the work preliminary. A fast electrical probe that grades meat on the line would help producers sort quality without destroying product.
plos-pone-0349577:
Oswaldo Cadenas presents a streaming method for shrinking huge two-dimensional point sets without changing their convex hull, the smallest convex shape wrapping all the points. Hull calculations underpin mapping, graphics, and robotics, and on massive data most input points sit uselessly inside. His reduction examines points as they arrive in a single pass and discards only those provably interior, each backed by a local geometric certificate.

On synthetic data the filter kept only about one point in ten, and on large real-world sets under one in a hundred. Yet the hull of what remains is exactly the hull of the original. Throwing away the interior safely lets downstream hull algorithms run fast on streaming data that never fits comfortably in memory.
plos-pone-0349777:
Margarita Osuna and co-authors asked how the way diabetes and high blood pressure are counted changes later life estimates in Colombia, in 2026 work. Self reports and direct measures give very different rates, and policy built on the wrong one will mislead.

Using a national ageing survey from 2015, the team built rates three ways: reported diagnosis, measured risk, and both combined. They also split cases into controlled, uncontrolled, and unaware, then estimated years lived with each disease after sixty. Combined counting gave the longest time lived with diabetes. The spread shows why surveys should measure, not just ask, when planning care for older adults.
plos-pone-0349877:
Deaths recorded as involving antipsychotic medicines in England have been rising, and Muhammad Umair Khan and Syed Shahzad Hasan examined the pattern using national prescription data from 2015 to 2023. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered all seven English health regions.

Recorded deaths climbed from about ten to about fourteen per million prescribed items, growing a few percent each year. London saw the steepest rise while the Midlands fell. Poorer areas carried higher rates, and areas with larger Asian populations showed lower rates. The authors stress these records link medicines to deaths without proving cause, but the uneven map argues for closer local review of prescribing safety.
plos-pone-0350277:
Yizhou Chen and Jie Zhang surveyed more than three thousand Chinese university students to unpack why active students report fewer depressive symptoms. Exercise is known to protect mood, but the mental pathway was unclear. Their 2026 online survey measured activity levels, depressive symptoms, and grit, meaning the perseverance and passion people bring to long-term goals, then tested whether grit carried the effect.

More active students did report milder symptoms. Statistically, though, the whole benefit ran through grit: once grit was accounted for, activity alone showed no direct link to symptoms. The authors suggest that programs pairing exercise with grit-building elements, such as goal setting and persistence training, may protect student mental health better than exercise promotion alone.
plos-pone-0351077:
Prompt engineering became a public buzzword almost overnight. The term covers wording requests to AI systems skillfully. Reuben Ng and Ting Yu Joanne Chow analyzed the public conversation. They gathered nearly three hundred thousand English posts. The posts came from X and Reddit. All mentioned the term during one year from May 2023.

Discussion spiked around product news and viral claims. Themes and mood shifted quarter by quarter. Some posts hailed a new profession. Others mocked the hype. Sorting the chatter shows a public negotiating meaning in real time. The authors say educators should track such talk. Platforms should track it too. Fast-moving AI vocabulary enters everyday speech quickly.
plos-pone-0351177:
Reading with a toddler, pausing to ask questions and chat, is called dialogic reading. Ming Yean Sia and colleagues asked whether that early talk leaves a mark on the brain years later, in this 2026 PLOS One study following children from age two to age five.

Parents' engagement during shared reading was measured at two. At five, children's forehead brain activity was recorded with light-based scanners while they played a card-sorting game testing mental flexibility. More early dialogue went with stronger activity in regions handling planning and control, even after accounting for mothers' education and children's vocabulary. The authors suggest shared book talk helps build the brain's control systems.
plos-pone-0351477:
Mattia Ronca and seven colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for an imaging study of kidney tumors at the University Hospital of Bordeaux. Ordinary CT scans do not measure how stiff a tumor is, yet stiffness may help characterize tissue. Fifty adults scheduled for kidney tumor surgery will receive CT, MRI-based stiffness mapping, and ultrasound stiffness checks in the days before their operation.

Because this is a protocol, it sets out a plan rather than findings. The main aim is to learn whether plain CT density values can predict stiffness measured by the specialized methods, using machine learning models checked by repeated cross-validation. Secondary work will compare the imaging methods with each other and with the final pathology results, and judge how feasible the extra scanning is in routine care.
plos-pone-0351577:
Older adults on the edge of diabetes lose muscle and grow frail, and hard exercise is tough for many to keep up. Hui-Ying Luk and colleagues present the HEAT trial plan, in PLOS One in 2026, testing whether warming the legs locally can guard blood sugar and muscle, alone or before interval training.

Heat is expected to improve blood vessel growth and energy factories inside muscle, the same features that support sugar control. The two-phase trial compares real heat against a sham version, then checks whether heated muscle adapts better once training starts. The protocol reports design only; results will come later.
plos-pone-0351877:
Zeki Taş and five colleagues gather views on school sports from the people who live them in this 2026 study. Eighteen participants at one public high school in the Turkish province of Sakarya took part. Six were students, six were parents, and six were physical education teachers. Each group met separately for focus group interviews. The questions concerned how sports shape school achievement and commitment to school.

Across the three groups, sports were seen as a positive force. Participants linked participation to better perceived achievement. They also tied it to stronger attachment to school life. Because the study is qualitative, it reports perceptions rather than test scores. That is its strength. Policy about school sports usually counts medals or grades from above. These voices show how the value is actually experienced day to day, by teenagers, the parents cheering them, and the teachers organising it all.
plos-pone-0351977:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors retract a study of magnesium oxide nanoparticles made with the plant Saussurea costus. The study claimed the particles kill microbes and breast cancer cells. It also claimed uses in photocatalysis. After the work appeared, readers raised concerns about many of its figures. This notice withdraws the study in full.

The problems were not small slips. Panels overlapped with panels in other papers. Some overlapped with other panels in the same paper, under new labels. Still images of cells treated one way were presented as another way. Repeated patches showed inside single images as well. When the pictures carry the proof and the pictures are recycled, no claim in the study can stand.
plos-pone-0352577:
Daniel Wychrij and six colleagues test a broad fungal vaccine in monkeys in this 2026 study. Recurrent vaginal yeast infections trouble an estimated one hundred thirty-eight million women each year. Standard antifungal drugs often fail to stop recurrences. No fungal vaccine is approved anywhere. Rodent models translate poorly to human immunity. The team therefore built the infection model in Japanese macaques, then vaccinated the animals.

The macaques, like women, developed genuine infections with visible fungal filaments. Natural infection produced weak antibody responses. It also failed to protect against reinfection. Vaccination changed the picture. Immunised animals mounted strong antibody levels in blood and mucosal tissue. Their fungal burden after a fresh challenge dropped clearly. A single vaccine candidate guarding against many fungi could matter well beyond this one infection, and the primate model gives developers a realistic testbed.
plos-pone-0352677:
Selina Limmen and seven colleagues study how decisions get shared in children's physiotherapy. Their 2026 Dutch study ran in two phases. Six focus groups heard from adolescents, parents, and therapists separately. A survey of forty-six more therapists checked those findings. The goal was practical: when should families help decide, and what helps or hinders that teamwork?

Sharing, the groups said, can start at the very first meeting. Goal setting is a natural moment to involve children and parents. Involvement should then continue, adjusted to each family's wishes. Comparing treatment options, visit frequency, and home practice all invite joint choices. The team folded the lessons into an existing goal-based decision model. They also matched rollout strategies to known implementation barriers. Young patients get a real voice, without dumping adult-sized responsibility on them.
plos-pone-0352877:
Khurshid Ataniyazov and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One genetic study of high blood pressure in Uzbekistan. The study region is Karakalpakstan. The Aral Sea crisis hit that area hard, and salty conditions strain health there. The team compared more than six hundred patients with high blood pressure to one hundred eighty controls. They tested nine gene variants tied to blood pressure control.

Six of the nine variants linked to the disease after strict checks. Some raised risk, and others seemed protective. The team also checked effects across sex, age, and weight groups. A seventh variant looked promising before the strict checks, but did not survive them. The authors say so plainly. They present the findings as a regional genetic profile. It may help explain why high blood pressure is so common in this stressed region.
plos-pone-0352977:
Almalki and colleagues surveyed burnout among front-line clinic staff in Al-Khobar, Saudi Arabia, in a 2026 study. More than one hundred doctors, nurses, and other providers completed a standard burnout inventory. About one in five met the study's burnout mark.

Feeling detached from patients scored highest, followed by emotional exhaustion. Exhaustion ran higher in women, in lower-paid staff, and in those seeing many patients daily. Some drivers were personal and some were workload based, the authors note. Cutting patient load pressure and supporting lower-paid staff are concrete steps clinics can take before burnout drives skilled workers away.
plos-pone-0353177:
Yinqin Liu and colleagues use worldwide health data to chart a neglected overlap: heart failure caused by long-term lung diseases. Their 2026 PLOS ONE analysis covers adults aged fifty-five and older across three decades, from 1990 to 2021. The lung conditions involved include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, scarring lung diseases, and dust-related lung damage.

Total cases and years lived with disability climbed sharply over the period, even though rates per person changed only modestly. The burden grew steepest after age seventy-five and ran higher in men than in women. Mapping where this combined burden concentrates can help health systems plan clinics, staff, and long-term care for ageing populations.
plos-pone-0353277:
Muhammad Ahsan ul Haq and four colleagues redesign an electric motor so it needs no brushes or separate exciter, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering paper. Their wound-rotor synchronous machine uses a stator winding split into two unequal sections. That imbalance creates an extra magnetic ripple, which a second winding on the rotor harvests and converts to direct current to power the rotor's own field winding.

Simulations of an eight-pole design validated the scheme. Against the existing design, the new machine produced slightly more power and torque while drawing about half the input current — and it runs from a single inverter instead of two. Brushless, efficient motors of this kind suit pumps, fans, and electric drivetrains.
plos-pone-0353377:
Ibrahim L Kadigi, Lazaro Kagata, and Stefan Sieber simulated rice farming across Tanzania. They tested which input combinations best protect harvests as the climate shifts. Their 2026 study drew on a national farm census of more than six thousand rice farms. It modeled yields under uncertainty. Farms were sorted by seed type and fertilizer practice, on the mainland and in Zanzibar.

Improved seeds paired with manufactured fertilizer performed best. That pairing gave a real chance of top yields. It also gave the lowest risk of falling below food security lines. Local seeds responded weakly even when fertilized. Organic fertilizer helped soils more than immediate harvests. Mainland farms gained far more than Zanzibar's. The authors recommend prioritizing farmer access to improved seed and fertilizer.
plos-pone-0353477:
Trinidad and colleagues, in a 2026 review, gather what schools have done to teach swimming over the past twenty-five years. Swimming lessons build child development and help prevent drowning, yet programs vary widely. The team searched major research databases and screened studies by set rules, keeping sixteen that fit.

Most programs focused on technique and practical skills, with little link to the wider school curriculum and limited input from physical education teachers. Work centered on younger children, from infants through primary school, and was scarce at secondary level. Program length, session frequency, content, and testing tools all differed a lot between studies. The authors conclude that school swimming needs stronger backing from institutions, better teacher training, and a more joined-up approach for each age stage. Without that, they argue, gains in water safety and skill will stay patchy.
plos-pone-0353677:
Maher Abdessater and five colleagues test whether one day of simulation training can prepare new doctors for a common bedside procedure, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Inserting a urinary catheter is routine, but most complications come from beginners. Forty fresh interns at a university hospital first answered a knowledge and confidence survey — only a small minority felt ready, and basic facts about catheter sizes and technique were widely missed.

After lectures, videos, and hands-on practice on male and female models, knowledge, confidence, and self-belief scores all jumped sharply. Six months later the group had performed hundreds of real catheterisations with a high success rate and few complications. Practice off the patient, the authors conclude, pays off on the ward.
plos-pone-0353777:
Alrashood and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Saudi Arabia, ask whether artificial intelligence in science teaching can strengthen, rather than dilute, students' cultural identity. Forty-seven experienced science teachers in two regions were interviewed and observed in class. The worry behind the study is that imported digital tools may flatten local culture out of lessons.

Teachers did not see AI as a mere delivery pipe for facts. They described using it to root science ideas in local settings, stories, and values, making lessons more interactive and group-based, and helping them judge learning in more responsive ways. The authors are careful: these are teachers' perceptions and observed practices, gathered through an inductive thematic analysis, not proof of student outcomes. They frame AI as a cultural bridge when teachers steer it deliberately, and call for designs that build local content in from the start.
plos-pone-0353877:
Xolelwa Dyani, Olanrewaju Oladimeji, and Moreoagae Bertha Randa publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for strengthening school teams that support teenagers' mental health in South Africa's Gauteng province. About one in seven adolescents worldwide lives with a mental health condition, and schools are where help can reach them earliest. The study focuses on the support teams already inside secondary schools.

The plan unfolds in stages: questionnaires to map how common learners' difficulties are, a review of existing interventions, then interviews with team members about what works and what fails. From that evidence the team will build and roll out a quality-improvement intervention. The protocol matters because it designs the fix with the schools, not for them.
plos-pone-0354177:
Shaoshuai Hou and six colleagues study how to quieten herringbone planetary gearboxes, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering paper. These compact gear systems drive wind turbines, aircraft engines, and ship propulsion, but vibration and noise limit them. The team examined a design whose teeth are staggered in phase between the two halves of the herringbone pattern, and derived formulas for how mesh stiffness changes over time.

Staggering the teeth clearly improved vibration behaviour in their models. Speed changes and manufacturing errors mattered too, and one error type, a tangential slip on a single tooth, dominated the rest. The findings give gearbox designers a practical lever for smoother, longer-lasting transmissions.
plos-pone-0354277:
Sukpornsawan and colleagues, in a 2026 study, explore how computers can recognize antibiotic packages in Thai pharmacies. Look-alike packaging is a safety risk when staff check medicines by eye under time pressure. Their approach reads both the look of a package and the words printed on it.

Thirty-six products were photographed and measured for traits such as image complexity, how much of the package is printed area, and how confidently a text reader could read the words. A clustering method sorted the packages into nine groups with shared traits. Packages in a middle range for complexity and printed area were recognized most consistently, and text reading confidence mattered too. A second analysis rated which groups used their inputs most efficiently. The authors offer their framework as a structured way to judge packaging for automated checking systems.
plos-pone-0354377:
Oluwakemi Tomobi and co-authors tested clinical simulation as a booster for basic science learning among pre-health students. Interest in science fades through schooling in the United States, most sharply for underrepresented students, and weak science foundations block health careers. Their 2026 study added team-based emergency simulations after traditional lectures.

Students rotated through healthcare team roles in four scenarios, from drug overdose to stroke and cardiac emergency. Checklists assessed their performance, and tests before and after measured understanding and recall. Tomobi and colleagues examined whether the format was feasible and welcomed by students. They frame simulation as an equity tool: vivid practice may hold the students whom lectures alone lose.
plos-pone-0354477:
Verma and colleagues present a 2026 profile of WHiSE 2.0, a study of Indigenous people who use drugs in three northern Ontario cities. Indigenous people face deep health gaps tied to colonial history. The study, led with Indigenous guidance, asks what harm reduction, meaning steps to cut the harms of drug use, looks like in their lives.

About three hundred fifty people in Sudbury, Thunder Bay, and Sault Ste Marie answered an hour-long survey. Most identified as First Nations. Housing was shaky for many: large shares slept on the street, in shelters, or on couches. Smoking drugs was the most common route, with injecting also common. Even so, most people knew what harm reduction meant, and most had been tested for HIV and hepatitis C. Many took part in ceremonies, and some said cultural teachings shaped their safety practices. The profile sets up follow-up work on regional service gaps.
plos-pone-0354677:
Youngjae Lee and four colleagues published this 2026 pilot trial on helping older adults recover balance after a trip. Thirty community-dwelling volunteers practiced either a simple step training that needs no special gear, standard treadmill trip training, or no training, then faced induced trips on a laboratory walkway.

The step training group recovered with a longer and faster first step than the untrained group. Lee cautions that the sample was small and harness use differed between groups. Still, a low-cost routine that sharpens the rescue step could bring trip training beyond specialized labs if a bigger trial confirms it.
plos-pone-0354877:
Jenny Paola Alfaro-García led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of how dengue virus can damage blood vessel walls from a distance. Fluid taken from infected cells was applied to vessel lining cells, and gene activity plus computer network modeling traced the response over time.

The fluid briefly switched on inflammation, then turned toward repair and tissue rebuilding, while pushing lining cells toward a different cell identity. Two molecules, a signaling protein and a structural one, sat at the network's center. Alfaro-García links this sequence to the leaking vessels of severe dengue.
plos-pone-0354977:
Aditi Moudgil, Shalli Rani, and Fazlullah Khan tackle computing decisions for connected vehicles in this 2026 paper. Cars now offload heavy computation to roadside edge servers, but someone must decide which tasks go where, fast, and in a way engineers can audit. Their framework optimizes task placement and resource allocation together, driven by an algorithm they call GTGO, and adds a module that explains how much each decision variable mattered.

As the number of task-generating vehicles grew, the framework improved overall system welfare by roughly a fifth over baseline approaches and cut average task delay a lot. The optimizer settled quickly, within a few dozen rounds, and the explanations came without hurting performance. The authors present the package as a clear option for smart transport systems.
plos-pone-0355277:
Helene Smith and co-authors interview professional staff about why women in and just out of prison in New South Wales, Australia, struggle to get contraception care. Women with prison histories face higher rates of pregnancy and abortion and poorer birth outcomes than other women, pointing to unmet need. A dozen health and case staff described what helps and what blocks care during custody and the fragile weeks after release.

Staff pictured fertility as interrupted by prison itself, then swamped by unstable housing and competing demands after release. They asked for options that are easy to reach, reversible, and gentle, plus counseling that respects the woman's own timing. Inside prison, service structure itself blocked access in ways the interviews detail. Smith and colleagues argue release planning must treat contraception as core health care.
plos-pone-0355377:
Qianqian Jia and colleagues run in 2026 a blinded trial of a chest wall nerve block for patients having keyhole surgery to clear the bile duct. One group received the block guided by ultrasound before general anaesthesia, and the other received none. Pain scores and use of a patient controlled pain pump in the first day were the main measures.

Pain at rest and on movement was lower in the block group at several early time points, and pump use fell as well. The block covered the expected skin zones, and one strong pain drug was needed less during surgery. By one day, pain scores no longer differed.
plos-pone-0355477:
Shazia Humayun and co-authors asked whether feeling called to one's work lifts whole teams, not just individuals. They surveyed workers in Pakistani manufacturing, gathering answers from nearly two hundred employees grouped in forty-nine teams. Their 2026 study drew on field theory to trace how personal calling might travel into team results.

Calling did reach team performance, and the bridge was collaborative crafting, where teammates reshape their work together in a self-managing way. The effect grew stronger where leader-member exchange, the quality of the boss-worker relationship, ran high. Humayun and colleagues say calling research should move up a level: meaning at work pays off partly through what teammates build jointly.
plos-pone-0355677:
Jong Yun and colleagues present in 2026 a trial plan for patients having stomach cancer surgery in Korea, testing whether extra protein in vein feeding aids recovery. People having planned removal of the stomach will receive either protein rich or standard vein feeding around surgery. Feeding goes through a vein in the arm for several days.

The main check compares how well the body holds onto nitrogen, a sign of protein balance, a few days after surgery. Other checks cover nutrition, muscle size, blood sugar, problems after surgery, and return to function. As a protocol, it gives methods and reasoning, not results.
plos-pone-0356177:
Tao Zhao and five colleagues test how printer settings affect the strength of 3D-printed carbon fiber composites, in this 2026 study. Their material mixes continuous carbon fiber into a common biodegradable plastic and is printed layer by layer. The team varied the printer nozzle size and the share of fiber in the part, then pulled specimens apart and examined the breaks under an electron microscope.

Parts with fiber snapped with almost no stretching, while plain plastic deformed visibly first. The larger nozzle produced much stronger parts, and strength rose steadily as fiber content increased, thanks to even fiber placement and tight bonding between fiber and plastic. Weighing strength against cost, the authors name a mid-level fiber share as the sweet spot. They see the lightweight, partly plant-based composite suiting uses from vehicle parts to custom medical devices.
plos-pone-0356277:
Zahra Toghiyani and co-authors asked what shapes sexual joy for newlywed couples in Iran. Social rules and private life both play a part, but local proof was thin. Their 2026 study spoke with thirty-one newlyweds, some as couples, till no new themes came up in the talks.

Three themes ran through the talks. Rules learned before marriage, with strong taboos, still weighed on couples. Each partner's deep beliefs about sex shaped ease and hopes. Power and choice formed the third theme: who starts, who decides, and how fair it feels. Toghiyani and colleagues say classes before marriage should deal with these social and private layers head-on, not teach body facts alone.
plos-pone-0356377: Shallal and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on students teaching bioethics to fellow students. The teaching happened during clinical rotations, when students work with real patients. From this case study, the authors draw three lessons meant to travel to other schools. They frame the lessons with a tool called CFIR, used to study how new practices take hold.
plos-pone-0356477:
Xinru Guo and three colleagues ask whether a soy compound changes how a blood marker of vessel stress relates to heart risk, in this 2026 analysis. The marker, called EASIX, reflects stress on the endothelium, the lining of blood vessels. The team compared people's estimated ten-year cardiovascular risk across levels of genistein, a plant compound from soy, measured in urine. Statistical models adjusted for other influences and tested how the relationships curved.

Higher vessel stress scores went with higher estimated risk overall. The link differed modestly by genistein level: a significant interaction appeared, though the association was only slightly weaker in the high-genistein group, and the shape of the curve differed between groups. The authors are explicit that these are hypothesis-generating findings from a single analysis, not evidence that soy intake changes anyone's risk.
plos-pone-0356777:
Maciej J Ejsmond led a team of six authors studying common eider ducks in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Ducklings of this sea duck can suffer from a lack of thiamine, a vitamin vital for nerves and energy. The team asked how the mother's diet affects that risk in her young.

Ejsmond's group found that risk rises when females eat large prey. That prey-size link gives conservation staff a concrete dietary factor behind poor chick health. Where eider numbers are falling, understanding food links helps target protection. The study also shows how a mother's foraging choices, shaped by changing seas, can pass effects to the next generation before the ducklings feed at all.
plos-pone-0356877:
Luya Yang, Min Zhang, and Yaxian Gao built a three-part system for spotting defects on steel plate surfaces in real time. Flaws hide in low-contrast images on the factory floor. Genuine defect photos are also scarce. Their 2026 study attacks both problems. An adaptive step boosts contrast by merging color channels by information content. A generative network then synthesizes extra defect examples for training.

The detector itself is a slimmed-down version of a current YOLO model. It uses ghost convolutions and attention to stay fast. Together the pipeline lifted detection accuracy by several points. It cut parameters by about a fifth. It reached strong scores at a few milliseconds per image. Steel makers could run such a system on the line without slowing production.
plos-pone-0357077:
The PLOS One Editors retracted this systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026. The review had pooled studies claiming that sensory art therapies ease anxiety around root canal treatment in highly anxious dental patients. A retraction means the journal has withdrawn the article as unreliable, and its conclusions should not be used.

Editors found the review lumped together very different interventions, from virtual reality and aromatherapy to yoga and aerobic exercise, so any pooled effect could not be credited to a specific therapy. Several included studies also failed the review's own eligibility rules, enrolling routine dental patients or testing exercise rather than art therapy. With its evidence base misassembled, the analysis could not support its claims.
plos-pone-0357277:
Kristina Anna Djupvik Aakvik leads a team of eight linking birth records to later physical activity in Norway, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Babies born early face many health questions, and whether they grow into less active children and adults was unclear. The researchers joined the national birth registry to a large regional health study, giving nearly thirteen thousand participants aged thirteen to fifty-two whose movement was measured by wearable sensors for a week.

Each extra week of gestation predicted slightly more light activity per day, an effect clearest in females, and more total activity among adolescents. Birth weight, by contrast, showed no relationship with later movement once examined on its own. The differences per week are small, but across a population they suggest early birth leaves a faint, lasting fingerprint on everyday activity. The authors frame it as one more reason to support activity in those born preterm.
plos-pone-0357377:
Mingyu Ji and coauthors published a 2026 diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE on a single-tube test that names six common respiratory pathogens at once. Since the COVID pandemic, respiratory infections have resurged, and treatment depends on knowing which germ is responsible. Their assay combines real-time PCR with melting-curve analysis of fluorescent probes, distinguishing two flu types, respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, adenovirus, and a mycoplasma bacterium in one run.

Against a panel of fifty-seven other pathogens, the test never gave a false identification, and it detected each target at very low copy numbers. Repeat measurements were tight and consistent. On several hundred throat samples, it matched or beat a commercial kit, with agreement statistics near perfect, and it proved more sensitive for several of the targets and more precise for rhinovirus. The assay is proposed for hospital laboratories needing fast, high-throughput answers during respiratory virus season.
plos-pone-0357577:
Melissa Lagger and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a Swiss cohort study on a timely question. Do GLP-1 receptor agonists, the blockbuster diabetes and weight-loss drugs, affect pancreatic cysts that can turn cancerous?? These cysts, called IPMNs, are increasingly common findings, and the same drugs are now taken by millions, yet their effect on existing pancreatic lesions is unknown. Three Swiss hospitals will pool records from 2010 to mid-2026.

Patients will be sorted into four groups by drug exposure and cyst status, and cyst progression will be judged by international radiological criteria. The study also tracks tumor markers, pancreatitis episodes, progression to advanced precancer or cancer, and operations triggered. The authors are frank about limits: with only a few dozen patients expected in the key group, the study may be too small for firm answers. Even so, a carefully measured signal beats the current evidence vacuum.
plos-pone-0357977:
Anvar Sadath and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a systematic review on what happens after non-suicidal self-injury. Self-injury without intent to die is common in young people and linked to later suicide attempts, but past reviews blurred distinct outcomes together. The planned review insists on time order, including only studies where self-injury clearly came before a later attempt or death.

The team will search five major databases for observational studies, with two reviewers extracting data and rating bias independently. Because the studies will likely differ too much for pooled statistics, results will be synthesized as a structured narrative. The review will also track whether features of the self-injury, such as frequency or method, track with graver later outcomes. The registered protocol's sharper focus, its authors hope, will improve risk assessment and safety planning in clinics.
plos-pone-0358077:
M. Kristen Hall and coauthors published a 2026 cell study in PLOS ONE on how sugar chains on proteins shape neuroblastoma, a childhood nerve-cell cancer. Cancers often carry simpler sugar coatings, and the team focused on the enzyme that starts branching these chains. Using gene editing, they crippled that enzyme in a human neuroblastoma cell line, then compared growth, sticking, and invasion against the original cells.

The mutants carried more of the simple sugar type and fewer branched forms, and restoring the enzyme reversed that. Their growth changed surprisingly: slower when sparse and unattached, yet faster in crowded dishes and three-dimensional cell balls. They also clung together more strongly and invaded more aggressively. Fed a growth signal, the mutants responded far more strongly than the parent line. Weakening this enzyme, they say, makes these cancer cells more dangerous in several ways, a caution for sugar-targeting therapies.
plos-pone-0358177:
Kevin Thomas leads a team of eight laying out the PANEM trial in PLOS ONE in 2026, a large test of digestive enzyme supplements after stomach removal surgery. Patients who lose part or all of the stomach often digest food poorly, because meals and pancreatic enzymes no longer meet in the right order. Weight loss, discomfort, and fatty stools follow. Whether routinely swallowing replacement enzymes with meals improves life quality has never been settled in a proper trial.

PANEM will enroll one hundred eighty-eight adults across several centers and assign them by chance, in secret, to enzyme capsules or identical placebos taken with meals. The main yardstick is cancer specific quality of life, especially physical functioning, after six months. Weight, extra nutrition use, and blood measures of nourishment count as secondary outcomes. The protocol gives surgeons and dietitians the design from which a long missing answer should come.
plos-pone-0358477:
Dipika Chandra leads a team of five reviewing why elderly villagers in Bangladesh struggle to use primary health care, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The reviewers registered their plan, searched several databases in March 2026, and sifted more than two thousand articles down to nineteen that met their rules. Barriers were then sorted through a social ecological lens, which stacks causes from the individual outward to national policy.

Five levels of obstacle emerged. Personal barriers included failing physical capability, empty pockets, and not knowing what services exist. Family barriers included weak family connection, relatives controlling health decisions, and gender inequality inside the household. Organizational, community, and policy barriers stacked above those. The authors argue that fixing clinics alone will not move elderly patients who are stopped first at home. Effective reform in rural Bangladesh must work on every level of the stack at once.
plos-pone-0358777:
Yan Zhu and four colleagues tackle a weakness in synthetic voices that must sound emotional, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Zero shot systems can copy a new speaker. Yet feelings often blur into the words. Their fix separates the two streams. Text meaning and emotional tone travel through parallel attention paths and merge only at a controlled gate, so neither corrupts the other during generation.

They also built a fine grained emotion space of sixteen classes, sorted from pitch and energy patterns in speech. During training, the system dwells on its hardest examples. Samples with unusually high loss get extra weight. Tested on speakers the system had never heard, using a standard emotional speech collection, it produced words with a low error rate and clean sound measures. The design targets expressive voices for media and assistance tools.
plos-pone-0358877:
