Md Parvej Hussain leads a team of six measuring how a small start in life shadows children's nutrition across South Asia, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The authors used recent demographic and health surveys from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and the Maldives. They matched children of low birth weight with similar children of normal weight. The total passed one hundred forty-seven thousand cases. Then they compared five forms of malnutrition.

About sixteen percent of the children had been born small. After matching, low birth weight was significantly associated with every form examined: stunting, wasting, underweight, having at least one form, and suffering several at once. The pattern held country by country with one exception, wasting in Bangladesh and the Maldives, where the link lost significance. The authors say preventing low birth weight itself, through maternal care, is the lever that moves all five outcomes together.
plos-pone-0359277: Santo and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the microbes of the horse gut. They profiled the small compounds those microbes make along the whole digestive tract. Horses were fed in three ways: pasture, hay, or rations with added oats. Diet shapes the gut's chemistry, and those compounds affect the horse's health. The profiles give vets and owners a fuller picture of feeding effects.
plos-pone-0359577: Kotan and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on filling gaps in health data. Records often miss values, and the reason for the gaps changes what fix works. The team tested a method called CHIT, a cyclical hybrid approach, under three missing-data patterns. They used health data sets as the test ground. Honest tests of gap filling matter because filled values quietly shape later findings.
plos-pone-0359777:
David Calzada, Laura Martín-López, and Jerónimo Carnés published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, the house dust mite whose droppings trigger many allergies. The authors use genetic and microbiomics approaches to monitor the growth of mite cultures and the environmental influences on them.

Laboratories grow these mites to produce allergy test and treatment materials, so culture quality matters. Tracking both the mites' genes and their microbes can reveal why batches thrive or fail. Allergen manufacturers and researchers standardizing mite material are the readers for monitoring methods of this kind.
plos-pone-0360077:
Randa Al-Kharabsheh and Muayyad Ahmad built in 2026 a large scale artificial intelligence analysis to predict which neurology patients will return to hospital without planning to. Unplanned readmissions are costly and often signal that something in the first stay or the discharge plan went wrong. The authors use CHAID decision trees, a method that sorts patients into risk groups through a branching series of questions.

A decision tree has an advantage over many AI tools: doctors can read its reasoning and see which factors drove a prediction. If such a model proves accurate, hospitals could aim follow up calls, home support, and medication reviews at the patients most likely to bounce back. The work joins a wider push to make hospital prediction tools explainable.
pmc-10517477:
Alowais, Alghamdi, Alsuhebany, and co-authors survey how artificial intelligence is entering clinical practice. Health care is complex for patients, doctors, and hospitals alike. The authors argue that fast gains in these computer systems could improve care and daily life for patients if used well.

Inside, the review walks through where such tools can plug into medical work, from reading scans to easing routine tasks. It also weighs the care needed before hospitals trust them widely. For clinicians and students, the piece offers a broad, plain map of a fast-moving field and the choices it now forces.
pmc-13399477: breeding health services the team in full study fertility desires, birth control needs, and actual use patterns of mixed HIV care and family planning services among women living with HIV. This research team with care surveys patient preferences. The 2026 Europe PMC paper in full reports the service findings. It guides person-focused program design. Fertility remains deeply desired. Care becomes mixed. Service use becomes with care studied.
pmc-13403377: Pseudomyxoma peritonei — tumor heterogeneity and its microenvironment dissected by single-cell transcriptomics. Xi Li, Lei Wang, Lei Ai, and others sequence the cells. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is rare-cancer genomics. It maps the jelly-belly tumor cell by cell.
pmc-13403477: Wound care biomaterials scientists rigorously test the cytocompatibility, enzymatic biodegradation kinetics, and intrinsic antioxidative potential of novel alginate-based advanced wound dressings. The team with care test the natural polymer. The 2026 Europe PMC paper fully presents the material testing. It strongly supports medical wound care applications. Alginate is a naturally derived polysaccharide. Biocompatibility proves excellent. Healing potential becomes clearly demonstrated.
pmc-13407577: The team test photobiomodulation effects on trapezius myofascial pain in a randomized sham-controlled trial. The light therapy targets muscle pain. The 2026 Europe PMC paper presents trial results. It evaluates noninvasive treatment. Myofascial pain burdens many. Light therapy offers hope. Evidence guides use.
pmc-13408277: Gastroenterologists provide compelling real-world evidence that water exchange colonoscopy much helps adenoma catching rates weighed to conventional ways. The team prospectively compare catching results. The 2026 Europe PMC paper fully studies comparative effectiveness. It strongly supports wider water exchange adoption. colon adenomas precede invasive cancer. lifted catching ultimately saves lives. way picking matters.
pmc-13408577: Ultra-high-performance concrete — its compressive strength designed and predicted by a hybrid experimental and machine learning framework. Mohamed Ayman and Amr ElNemr build the framework. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is concrete ML. It machine-learns concrete strength. Concrete, UHPC.
pmc-13409277: British joint disease research epidemiologists in full study Behçet's syndrome disease research across England using large-scale real-world look-back primary care cohort data. The team with care estimate national rate and new-case rate. The 2026 Europe PMC paper in full reports the epidemiological findings. It informs niche service planning. Behçet's disease is truly rare. English public data are now available. Healthcare services become rationally planned.
pmc-13410577: Africa's emerging role in precision oncology was explored through translational insights from functional genomics. The continent's contributions were highlighted. The finding guides global oncology. African genomic diversity holds untapped keys to cancer biology. Rix highlighted Africa in precision oncology. Genomic diversity needs global inclusion.
pmc-13415277: Rye chromosome arm 1RS — its introgression enhancing climate resilience in German winter wheat. Yeneneh Bekele-Reba, Lorenz Bülow, Anne Zaar, and others introgress the arm. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is wheat genetics. It ryes German wheat resilient. Wheat, winter.
pmc-13417477: Endodontic surgery can preserve bone with piezoelectric devices. The bone window technique was reported. The innovation guides dentistry. Piezoelectric surgery spares bone. Tooth preservation needs surgical innovation. Natural bone preservation needs piezoelectric precision. Bone window techniques preserve anatomy. Apical surgery needs bone-sparing techniques.
pmc-13418377: Surgery can impair cognition in older patients through neuroinflammation. The authors showed human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells via beta-NGF alleviate cognitive impairment after tibial fracture surgery by regulating a neural pathway. pmc-13650677: In 2026, a team published Tumor-intrinsic execution of interferon-γ-associ. The work broke new ground. Time has kept the file intact through the years. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
pmc-2573877:
Searle, Mitnitski, Gahbauer, and co-authors set out a standard procedure for creating a frailty index. Frailty in ageing can be measured by counting health deficits a person has accumulated. Such an index can be built from most ageing study databases, yet methods varied between teams.

The authors describe, step by step, how to build one in a consistent way. Their analysis is a worked example others can follow. A shared standard lets clinics and researchers compare frailty scores across studies, improving prediction of falls, hospital stays, and care needs in older adults.
pmc-3637477:
Fenton and Kim carry out a systematic review and meta-analysis to revise the Fenton growth chart for preterm infants. Growth charts help clinicians judge whether a premature baby is growing as expected. The earlier 2003 chart needed updating against newer data and standards.

Their revision harmonises the preterm chart with the World Health Organization growth standard and smooths the join between the two. It draws on pooled preterm growth data to set the curves. A sound chart matters daily in neonatal units, guiding feeding decisions for the smallest and most fragile patients.
pmc-4054777:
Dixon, Patel, Welsch, and their colleagues reported in 2014 on a drug effect that kills certain cancer cells. A cell surface system swaps cystine from outside the cell for glutamate from inside. That exchange is tied to many diseases, and drugs that block it strongly had long been sought but not found.

The team showed that blocking the exchange can trigger stress in a cell structure called the endoplasmic reticulum. It can also drive ferroptosis, a form of cell death that depends on iron. The work points to a fresh way to attack cancer cells that rely on this exchange to survive.
pmc-4325677:
Burgess and Thompson wrote in 2015 about multivariable Mendelian randomization. The standard method uses gene variants tied only to one risk factor to estimate its causal effect on disease. Some variants, though, affect several traits at once, a property called pleiotropy.

The paper shows how such multi-effect variants can still be used well. By modeling several risk factors together, researchers can separate their effects instead of discarding useful variants. Triglyceride levels and other blood fats are a case where traits overlap heavily. The approach widens the questions Mendelian randomization can answer about what truly causes disease.
pmc-4521077:
Gasparrini, Guo, Hashizume, and their colleagues studied temperature and death risk in 2015 across many countries. Earlier studies had estimated early deaths from heat or cold in single countries. None had assessed the whole temperature range in a systematic way across different climates.

The team pooled data from many populations exposed to varied weather. They quantified how much mortality is attributable to high and low ambient temperature overall. Such a global picture shows that cold and heat both carry burdens, in proportions that differ by place. Public health plans for hotter futures need that full-range evidence, not heat alone.
pmc-5161777:
Liu, Oza, Hogan, and their colleagues updated estimates in 2016 of causes of death in children under five. Child survival improved remarkably between 1990 and 2015. Still, the Millennium Development Goal target of cutting under-five mortality by two-thirds was not achieved globally.

The team updated their annual estimates of child mortality and its causes for 2000 to 2015, by country and region. Knowing whether children die of pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria, or newborn conditions directs aid to the right tools. The analysis also speaks to the Sustainable Development Goals that followed. It gives governments a scorecard for where child health gains are real and where they stall.
pmc-6124377:
Steven Wingett and Simon Andrews described FastQ Screen, a quality control tool, in 2018. Sequencing projects usually map reads against one reference genome. That habit can hide the fact that DNA came from the wrong species or a contaminated source.

FastQ Screen maps a sample of reads against many genomes at once. The split of hits shows whether the sample matches its claimed origin. Sudden hits to other species flag contamination early, before months of analysis rest on bad data. Core facilities run it as a routine sanity check on incoming sequencing runs.
pmc-7162477:
Junling Gao, Pinpin Zheng, Yingnan Jia, and coauthors studied mental health and social media during the Wuhan outbreak in 2020. Huge numbers of citizens followed the crisis on social media for hours daily. The authors asked what that exposure did to mental health.

In a large cross-sectional survey of Chinese adults, anxiety and depression were common. Frequent social media exposure was linked to higher odds of both, even after other factors were weighed. The authors suggest that crisis communication should limit rumor and overload. The paper was an early warning that information habits shape outbreak mental health.
pmc-7488777:
Arang Rhie and colleagues introduced in 2020 a tool called Merqury for judging the quality of a newly assembled genome. Modern long read methods can now produce assemblies that rival or beat the official reference genomes. That success creates a problem, because the usual way of checking an assembly, comparing it with the reference, stops working when the new one may be better.

Merqury checks an assembly without any reference, by comparing short DNA words called k-mers between the assembly and the raw reads. From that comparison it estimates accuracy, completeness, and whether the two copies of each chromosome were kept apart. Genome projects use such checks to prove their assemblies can be trusted before others build research on them.
pmc-7763177:
Matthew Young and Sam Behjati presented SoupX in 2020, a method for cleaning a common flaw in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Droplet based methods read the RNA inside single cells, but they assume every RNA strand captured came from a cell. In practice, loose RNA floating in the sample gets captured too, blurring the true signal from each cell.

SoupX estimates how much of that background contamination is present and subtracts it from the results. The authors show how the correction sharpens the picture of what each cell is actually doing. Single-cell studies guide research on development, immunity, and cancer, so removing this silent distortion improves conclusions across a fast growing field.
pmc-7857477: A 2026 investigation into Asymmetry and evolution over a one-year perio yielded fresh results. The methodology was sound. Readers worldwide can access it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
rosenroth-kabbala-denudata-1677:
Christian Knorr von Rosenroth unveils Kabbalah in Kabbala Denudata, in Latin from 1677. Vast renderings of the Zohar and kindred writings fill its tomes. Christian readers gained their first full road into Jewish mysticism through this massive, learned, and daring work of translation and commentary from Sulzbach.

Leibniz read it, and occultists mined it for centuries afterward. The Sefirot, the worlds, and the soul's exile unfold in Latin dress here. It became the cornerstone of Christian Kabbalah in the West. All later occult Kabbalah drinks from this spring in some measure, the book through which Europe learned to dream in Hebrew letters.
sefer-yetzirah-kalisch-1877:
Isidor Kalisch translated the Sepher Yetzirah into English in 1877, with a preface, notes, and glossary. His Book on Creation was the first English rendering of the text. The Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, is the earliest surviving work of Jewish mysticism, compact and cryptic.

It teaches that God formed the world through thirty-two paths of wisdom: ten sefirot and the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Letters combine like gates and walls in its strange, exact system. Kalisch, a rabbi and scholar in America, opened the little book to English readers. Later students of Kabbalah all start somewhere near this text. Its few pages have drawn centuries of commentary.
seiss-miracle-in-stone-1877:
Joseph Seiss, a church chief in the United States, read the Great Pyramid as a sign from God in A Miracle in Stone, out in 1877. Seiss took the claims of Smyth and gave them a pulpit voice. The stone heap, he held, holds dates and truths of the Good Book in its halls and sums.

Crowds in the United States bought the book in droves. It took a British stone school and made it a theme for sermons there. Seiss writes with warmth and zeal. His work marks the point where stone lore met mass faith.
the-compleat-chymist-1677: The Compleat Chymist, 1677. The complete chemist. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume twenty-seven of Casanova's memoirs: the old rover looks back. The long tale nears its close. A great life's last pages. Twenty-seventh volume: the old rover remembers, last bright pages, the old rover looks back.
tob-10477:
All sixty-six books of the King James Bible stand complete here, from Genesis to Revelation, in the translation first published in 1611. A committee of translators, working under King James I, produced the version whose phrases entered English itself. Expressions like a thorn in the flesh and the powers that be come from its pages.

Old Testament history, poetry, and prophecy give way to the Gospels, Acts, letters, and Revelation. Four centuries on, its cadences still shape how millions hear Scripture, whether or not they attend church. No other single book has influenced English literature, law, and everyday speech as deeply or for as long.
tob-10577:
A long gospel bearing the name of Barnabas, the companion of Paul, survives in Italian and Spanish copies from late medieval times. It presents Jesus as a prophet who foretells the coming of Muhammad. Mainstream scholars judge it a medieval work, not an early gospel.

Its Jesus denies being the Messiah or the Son of God and escapes the cross while another dies in his place. Those claims match Islamic teaching and clash with all early Christian records. Cherished in some Muslim circles and rejected by most scholars, the book stays among the most argued-over of all claimed gospels.
tob-14477:
Henry Steel Olcott, co-founder with Helena Blavatsky of the Theosophical Society, kept a diary of the movement's birth. Old Diary Leaves turns that diary into a history told by a man who was there. Olcott was an American lawyer, soldier, and journalist before he was an occultist.

He recalls the first meetings in New York, the move to India, the masters and marvels claimed around Blavatsky, and the work of building lodges worldwide. His tone is plain and often wry, even about wonders. As the participant's own memory of the early society, the volumes remain a first source for its history.
tob-4146-15477:
Volume four of Ganguli's Mahabharata carries the epic from book thirteen to its close in book eighteen. The aged Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, delivers long teachings on dharma, the law of right conduct. Those lessons form one of the epic's great storehouses of wisdom.

In time the Pandavas lay down their kingdom and walk toward the mountains and heaven. A stray dog joins them and proves more than he seems. One by one the heroes fall on the road. The longest story ever told ends quietly, with the claim that truth alone endures. Ganguli's full translation remains a landmark of patience.
tob-4177:
Catherine of Siena, a dyer's daughter who became a counselor to popes, dictated her Dialogue in states of prayer in the 1370s. She speaks with God the Father, and he answers at length. The record here follows the 1919 checked edition of her spiritual testament.

The talks range over the soul's growth, the corruption of the church, and the call to reform it from within. Catherine's image of Christ as a bridge between heaven and earth carries the whole design. Her tone is fierce, tender, and utterly assured, often in one page. Few medieval women wrote with such authority, or kept it.
tob-4277:
Lewis Spence, a Scottish writer on myth and folklore, turned to Mexico for a study devoted only to its gods. Where his companion work on Mexico and Peru told the myths, here the focus stays on the divine cast itself. Each major deity of the Aztec world gets close attention.

Readers meet the feathered serpent, Tezcatlipoca the smoking mirror, and Tlaloc the rain god, along with many lesser powers. Spence explains what each god ruled, how priests honored them, and what their images meant. The result is a clear guide to a faith that Spanish conquerors worked hard to destroy.
tob-9052-15477:
Ganguli's fourth volume closes the Mahabharata with books thirteen through eighteen. Bhishma, the dying elder, teaches dharma from his arrow bed: how kings should rule, how people should give, forgive, and prepare for death. His lessons form a small library inside the epic.

At last the Pandava heroes renounce the world and climb toward heaven, falling one by one on the road. A faithful dog walks with them to the end. The poem closes on how to die well and what survives a person. With this volume, Ganguli's immense labor of translation stands complete.
turgenev-virgin-soil-1877:
Virgin Soil, Turgenev's last novel, appeared in 1877 and is given here in R. S. Townsend's translation of 1917. Young Nezhdanov joins the populist movement, whose members went to the people with hopes of rousing the peasants. He lodges as a tutor on an estate while spreading pamphlets in secret.

Beside him, Mariana shares his ideals and his growing doubts about their mission. The peasants prove wary, officials close in, and Nezhdanov's faith in himself gives way. Turgenev treats the young rebels with sympathy and clear sight at once. The novel records a real movement of the 1870s at close hand. Townsend's version stands as a distinct translation beside Garnett's.
un-ga-res-55-177:
Guatemala's fifth year of peace brought a fresh UN mandate in Resolution 55/177, passed in December 2000. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2000 by a vote of 1999. In late 1999, the land held its first general vote since the peace was signed. Power passed in peace from one chief to the next, a mark of real growth toward a free state open to all.

Yet core parts of the peace still waited to be done, the text stresses. A fresh timetable from the follow-up team was called for. Both sides had asked the UN to back the firming of peace to 2003. The mission's tenth and eleventh reports on human rights are weighed in the text.
un-ga-res-a-69-77:
One of the UN's three arms bodies has gone quiet, and Resolution A/69/77, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, takes stock of it. The Disarmament Commission is the Assembly's own debate body on arms, set up to study questions in depth and to send firm counsel back. The Assembly had the commission's report before it, and recalls the bids of 2006 to make its work bite.

The text notes a blunt fact: in fifteen years, the commission has sent no firm counsel to the Assembly at all. Its revival is urged for the next three-year cycle. Talks should be tight and aimed at results. Background papers from the UN's disarmament study arm may help spark the debate back to life.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 55/177 was adopted on 19 December 2000. It carries the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala into its fifth year. The mission monitors the peace settlement that ended the country's civil war. The Assembly draws on the mission's verification reports and on reporting by the Secretary-General and Guatemala's peace commission.

The mandate is renewed for the whole of 2001. The resolution notes the national elections held in late 1999 and the peaceful transfer of power that followed. It calls on both the government and the former insurgent movement to meet their remaining peace commitments. That way the accords can be fully carried out. Continued verification gave the settlement an external check while its hardest reforms were still pending.

Resolution 69/77, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the report of the Disarmament Commission. It notes that the Commission has produced no substantive recommendations in fifteen years. It encourages work to revitalize it. It sets its next substantive session for 6 to 24 April 2015. A report is due to the Assembly's seventieth session.
un-sc-res-1377:
Foreign ministers of the Security Council met on 12 November 2001 to declare a common stand on terrorism. Two months after the September attacks, the Council recalled resolutions 1269 (1999), 1368 (2001), and 1373 (2001). It declared that acts of international terrorism form one of the most serious threats to peace and security in the twenty-first century. Such acts, it said, challenge all states and all of humanity.

The declaration condemns all acts, methods, and practices of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, whatever their motive. Financing, planning, and support for terrorism are declared contrary to the Charter, like the acts themselves. The Council says a sustained joint effort by all member states is essential to beat the threat. It calls on states to join the anti-terrorism conventions as soon as possible. It also links the fight to easing regional conflicts and tackling development problems.
un-sc-res-1477:
The Rwanda tribunal needed a new pool of temporary judges in 2003. Nominations for ad litem judges had reached the Secretary-General. On 29 April 2003 the Security Council forwarded the list to the General Assembly. The tribunal's statute sets that step. The Assembly would elect from the names sent. Candidates came from many states across Africa, Europe, and beyond.

Ad litem judges sit for single trials rather than full terms. They let a busy court run more cases at once. The Arusha tribunal faced a heavy docket from the 1994 genocide. Extra judges were key to its plan to finish trials on schedule. The forwarding act is brief, but it staffed real courtrooms.
un-sc-res-1577: Resolution 1577 dates to 2005 in the Council's numbered output, and this entry reproduces the record text via Wikisource. Votes on such texts need nine of fifteen members, with no permanent member opposed. What passed that bar is preserved here in full, so readers can weigh the decision in the members' own chosen words.
un-sc-res-1677:
Violence shook Timor-Leste in late April 2006, and the Council reacted within weeks. On 12 May 2006 it extended the United Nations Office in Timor-Leste, UNOTIL, until 20 June. The government in Dili had opened an inquiry into the April incidents. The Council noted that step. It stayed committed to lasting stability in the young country.

The Secretary-General owed an update by 6 June 2006. It would cover the situation and the future United Nations role after UNOTIL ended. The Council urged Timorese institutions to tackle the causes of the violence. UNOTIL would help within its current mandate. Events soon forced a far bigger mission than anyone planned that May.
un-sc-res-1777:
UNMIL's next year came with planned cuts on 20 September 2007. The Secretary-General's report of 8 August 2007 guided the Council. Liberia's police were being rebuilt and deployed, and a new army was taking shape. Governance gains and control over natural resources continued. Ex-combatants still needed steady jobs. UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire mission coordinated across the border.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2008. It endorsed the Secretary-General's advice for a staged reduction of the mission's troops, by some 2,450 over the year. A cut of about 498 in the police element was endorsed as well. The Secretary-General would track progress against core benchmarks, from security handover to the rule of law. The Council planned to review his findings before the mandate expired. Liberia's calm held through the drawdown, a sign the peace had begun to carry its own weight.
un-sc-res-1877:
On 7 July 2009, the Council acted on the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal by adopting Resolution 1877. The court had admitted it could not finish all its work by 2010. Three permanent judges had resigned. Appeals work was set to swell once the last trials ended.

The Council extends the terms of the sitting permanent and temporary judges to 31 December 2010. Judges named to fill the empty seats get the same term. The Secretary-General may add one extra temporary judge for a short period, above the normal cap of twelve. The statute is amended so trial judges can move up to the Appeals Chamber as cases close. The court must still finish as fast as it can.
un-sc-res-277:
Southern Rhodesia's white regime proclaimed a republic in March 1970. The move aimed to cement its illegal rule. On 18 March 1970 the Security Council condemned the proclamation. It restated its line of resolutions against the regime since 1965. Sanctions already in force stayed in effect. Reports from the sanctions committee informed the decision. Spain cast the lone abstention.

No state could recognize the illegal regime or help it. Acts of its officials and bodies deserved no recognition anywhere, courts included. Britain held the primary duty to let the people of Zimbabwe choose self-determination. The text tightened the legal isolation of the Smith regime. Majority rule in Zimbabwe still took another decade to arrive.
un-sc-res-377: Security Council business produced Resolution 377, catalogued in this library as a 1975 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-477:
Security Council Resolution 477, adopted on August 14, 1980, recommended Zimbabwe for membership in the United Nations. The southern African land had won legal independence from Britain that April, after a long guerrilla war against the white minority regime that had called the country Rhodesia. Free elections brought Robert Mugabe to power as the first prime minister of the new state.

The Assembly seated Zimbabwe eleven days later. The council's brief text closed a fifteen-year saga in which the UN had treated Rhodesia's rebel regime as illegal and backed sanctions against it. Few admission votes carried such a sense of a wrong formally undone and a people's long fight recognized.
un-sc-res-77: Work on limiting conventional weapons reached the Council in the autumn of 1949. Its Commission for Conventional Armaments had sent a second progress report. The report covered the first items of the commission's plan of work. On 11 October 1949 the Council told the Secretary-General to pass the papers on. The General Assembly and member states would receive them. The record of the Council's own debate went along. The short act kept the disarmament file moving between bodies.
un-sc-res-977: Holding number 977 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1995 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1377, adopted unanimously on 12 November 2001 at a meeting of foreign ministers, is a declaration on terrorism issued two months after the September 11 attacks. It builds on the binding counter-terrorism duties the Council had imposed in September. Ministers declared that acts of international terrorism rank among the gravest threats to world peace in this new century.

The declaration calls terrorism a challenge to all states and to humanity, and condemns every act, method, and practice of it as criminal and unjustifiable, whatever the motive. Financing, planning, and support for attacks are likewise condemned. It argues that only a sustained, comprehensive campaign, with every member state taking part under the Charter and international law, can defeat the threat.

A long slate of names fills most of this text. They are picks for stand-in judge at the Rwanda war crimes court. The court sat in Arusha, Tanzania. It tried the men blamed for the 1994 mass killings. Full-time judges could not hear all the cases. Stand-ins filled the gaps. Resolution 1477 passed with no dissent on 29 April 2003.

The Council sent the slate to the General Assembly. The Assembly would vote the judges in. The names came from all over the world. Chad, Turkey, Cameroon, Uganda, and Poland are among the states on the list. Some picks would never sit. The slate had to be wide so the Assembly could choose. The text is dull at a glance. It still shows the vast, slow grind of bringing a genocide to trial.

Burundi's United Nations operation, ONUB, is extended until 1 June 2005 in this text of 1 December 2004. The mission had deployed in June 2004 to support the Arusha peace process. Burundian parties had since agreed a power-sharing deal in Pretoria, and parliament had adopted an interim constitution in October giving guarantees to all communities.

ONUB stays in place to help carry the transition through to free and fair elections. Governments and parties in the region are urged to reject violence and cooperate with ONUB and the Congo mission in ending impunity. Congo and Rwanda are called on to help Burundi complete the inquiry into the Gatumba massacre and bring those responsible to justice.

Timor-Leste's slide into crisis bought its UN office a month of life in 2006. On 12 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1677. Clashes inside the young state's security forces had erupted in late April. The text names the incidents of 28 and 29 April. People had died, and thousands had fled their homes in Dili. The state the UN helped build looked fragile.

The text extends the small UN office, UNOTIL, just to 20 June 2006. The Secretary-General must report by 6 June on the state of play. His report must also scope the UN role past that date. The government and state bodies must tackle the roots of the violence, with the office's help. A far larger mission followed within weeks.

Uganda's path into the United Nations runs through Resolution 177, adopted on 15 October 1962, with every member in favor. The Council had examined the East African country's bid for membership. Uganda had become independent from Britain only days earlier, on 9 October, and joining the UN was among the first acts of the new state.

In a single operative sentence, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Uganda. That recommendation was the required first step, because the Charter gives the Assembly the final vote on new members but only on the Council's advice. The brief record captures Uganda taking its place in the wave of African states entering the UN in the early 1960s.

Resolution 1777, adopted on 20 September 2007, extends the UN mission in Liberia while approving its gradual slimming. The Secretary-General's August report described steady government progress against corruption and in recovering control over natural resources. The Liberian police were being rebuilt, equipped, and deployed, and restructuring of the armed forces had begun, though much remained to do.

UNMIL's mandate was renewed until 30 September 2008. With that year secured, the Council endorsed the Secretary-General's plan for a phased drawdown of the mission's troops and police as Liberian forces took over. It pressed Liberia and its partners to speed up police and army reform and the building of a national security framework.

The Yugoslavia tribunal's bench is reinforced and its judges extended in Resolution 1877, adopted on 7 July 2009. Its Completion Strategy Report admitted it could not finish work in 2010, three permanent judges had resigned, and the Appeals Chamber faced a rising workload.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the Trial Chamber permanent judges and all ad litem judges, serving and unassigned alike, until 31 December 2010. It runs until their cases finish, if that is sooner. The Appeals Chamber judges' extension will be reviewed by 31 December 2009. It lets the Secretary-General appoint ad litem judges beyond the statutory twelve, up to thirteen at a time until the end of 2009, so a reserve judge can sit. It amends Article 14 of the Statute. Up to four extra permanent judges can join the Appeals Chamber as their trials complete. They include judges drawn from the Rwanda tribunal.

Rhodesia's white rulers claimed the rank of a republic in 1970. The move aimed to lock in rule by a small white class. The Council's bans had not yet brought the revolt to an end. Some states still traded with the banned regime. South Africa and Portugal kept it fed. Resolution 277 passed on 18 March 1970 by fourteen votes to none. Spain held back.

The claim to republic rank was damned as void. No state could grant the regime a nod of law. All ties had to snap: trade, posts, and travel links alike. Cars, trains, and planes to the land were to halt. South African police and troops had to leave at once. Aid for Zambia, hurt by the bans, was urged. States had to report their steps by 1 June.

Western Sahara, a territory on the coast of West Africa ruled by Spain, drew the Council's attention in the autumn of 1975. Spain had written to the Council about the situation. Rival claims to the territory were raising the temperature in the region. Resolution 377 was adopted by consensus on 22 October 1975.

Acting under Article 34 of the Charter, the Council decided to look into the dispute. That article lets the Council investigate situations that might endanger peace. The Secretary-General was sent on a mission to the area and to the parties concerned. The Council appealed to all of them to show restraint and moderation. Calm conditions would let the mission go ahead well. The General Assembly's decisions on the territory, including its call for decolonization, stayed fully in view.

The shelf label on this text points at Jerusalem. The page itself tells a far happier tale. Zimbabwe had just won its freedom. White rule in Rhodesia ended after a long bush war. Free polls in 1980 chose a black-led state. Its bid for a UN seat came next. Resolution 477 passed with no dissent on 30 July 1980.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Zimbabwe. The Assembly did so weeks later. Robert Mugabe led the new state at its birth. The seat closed one of Africa's last colonial files. Few votes in 1980 carried such joy. A state the UN had shunned as a rebel colony now took its lawful place in the hall.

Paperwork moved the early arms debate forward in 1949. The Commission for Conventional Armaments had delivered its second progress report. Annexes covered the first items of its work plan, settled back in August 1948. Resolution 77 was adopted on 11 October 1949. Nine members voted yes, with the Ukrainian and Soviet delegations abstaining.

The Secretary-General was told to forward everything to the General Assembly. The report, its annexes, and the Council's own debate record all went across. The Assembly would read them for information. Nothing was decided about weapons themselves. The text captures the UN's division of labor. The Council's commission studied conventional arms, then reported upward to the full membership.

The war crimes court for Rwanda needed a home, and the Council chose one on 22 February 1995. The court had been set up the previous November, by Resolution 955. It would try those behind the genocide of 1994. The choice of its seat had been left to the Council. Resolution 977 was adopted unanimously.

On the advice of the Secretary-General, the Council decided that the court would sit at Arusha. Arusha is a town in the United Republic of Tanzania. The choice depended on proper arrangements between the United Nations and Tanzania's government. Those arrangements had to be acceptable to the Council. Rwanda's government had said that it would work with the court. Fixing the seat let the new tribunal start building its courtrooms, staff, and case files.
webster-displaying-of-supposed-witchcraf:
John Webster, a physician and schoolmaster, published The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft in 1677. The huge book sets out to debunk supposed witchcraft by natural causes alone. Webster had seen the trials up close in the north of England, and he writes as a doctor who trusts observation over accusation.

He explains fits, visions, and strange cures by disease, fraud, and fear. Case after case receives a physical reading. The work is the great Restoration skeptical summa, massive and methodical. Webster answers Glanvill point by point in the same years. His Displaying shows how far a determined natural philosophy could go in emptying the witch belief of its evidence.
works-on-phrenology-physiology-and-kindr: Works on Phrenology, Physiology, and Kindred Subjects, 1877. The kindred works. This book preserves that catalogue. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
wright-philosophical-discussions-1877:
Chauncey Wright was a sharp American thinker whose work spread mostly through essays and talk. After his early death, Charles Eliot Norton edited his Philosophical Discussions in 1877. Wright had defended Darwin in America with unusual force. Charles Sanders Peirce counted him as a mentor and sparring partner.

The essays take up evolution, science, and the methods by which minds gain truth. Wright writes plainly and cuts hard against loose or wishful reasoning. His pages show the tough style that shaped the first American pragmatists. The volume preserves a mind that print almost lost. It explains his quiet fame among peers.
zola-lassommoir-1877:
Zola opens L'Assommoir with Gervaise waiting up for Lantier until two in the morning. For a week he has sent her to bed with tales of hunting for work. That night she thinks she sees him enter a bright ballroom with Adele, a pretty brunette.

He sleeps out for the first time, and Gervaise wakes at five in wild sobs. Her bare furnished room holds a broken bureau, three straw chairs, and a greasy table. Hope still lies ahead: honest work builds her a small laundry in time. Her husband's drinking then dissolves it all, in the starkest portrait of drink and poverty in French letters.
